Takes part in designing the discharge plan and coordinating services (686.6(a)(2)(ii)(e)).
Prepares the health summary and medication transfer.
Never pressure a person to stay and report any wish to leave to the Residence Manager.
Helps identify the destination and arranges services and follow-up.

documentation: Discharge File with the Administrator's written confirmation of the criterion
Written notice to the person and supporters, with delivery date and language
Discharge plan and planning meeting attendance record
Record of the team's recommendation and of any against-recommendation review, with the person's decision
Objection record and outcome (APP-01)
Health summary, medication transfer record and records-transfer log
Personal funds accounting and belongings receipt
Follow-up contact record
Vacancy report to OPWDD

policies.title: Review and Appeal of Plans of Services and Placement Decisions
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Residence Manager, program planning team members and all staff at [AGENCY NAME]'s OPWDD-certified IRA who receive or process an objection, request for review or appeal.
policies.purpose: To give individuals, parents, guardians and correspondents a clear way to ask for review of, object to and appeal the plan of services and placement decisions, in line with the Commissioner's regulations, and to show where each subject required in the policy and procedure manual is addressed.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(iii) (review and appeal procedures available to individuals and their parents, guardians or correspondents, including but not limited to appeal of the plan of services and placement decisions, in conformance with the regulations of the commissioner) and 686.6(b)(3) (the written policy/procedure manual and its contents).

(1) Right to participate, object and appeal. Each individual has the right to a written individualized plan with the right to participate in it, to object and to appeal (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(4)). Individuals and their parents, guardians and correspondents may appeal the plan of services and any placement decision, including admission, transfer, discharge and a decision to decline admission. The right to request an alternative residence is also protected (633.4(a)(4)).

(2) Objections follow 14 NYCRR 633.12. Objections are handled under 633.12 and the Commissioner's regulations, and [AGENCY NAME] follows the steps and timeframes in the current regulation text. The Administrator keeps the current text of 633.12 in the policy file, and enters each timeframe on the Objection Log when an objection is received. [AGENCY NAME] does not set shorter deadlines for the person than the regulation allows.

(3) Appeal information. At or before admission, and again after any change, each person receives appeal information in his or her primary language (633.4(a)(8)). Interpreters are provided at no charge (633.4(a)(15)). Individuals are told how to reach the persons and agencies to which complaints may be made, both on admission and when the contacts change (633.4(a)(12)).

(4) No reprisal. A person who raises a concern, objects, appeals or files a grievance faces no reprisal (633.4(a)(4)). Rights are not limited as a threat, as retribution or for discipline (633.4(a)(7)).

(5) Rights modifications and the plan. A modification of an HCBS right needs a specific assessed need and justification in the person-centered service plan (14 NYCRR 636-1.4; see RIT-02). The person may appeal it under this policy. The plan is updated when it is ineffective and on reassessment of functional need (Subpart 636-1).

(6) Record access. Written requests for access to the clinical record are handled under Mental Hygiene Law 33.16. A denial may be reviewed by the OPWDD Clinical Record Access Review Committee (633.4(a)(10); see REC-08).

(7) Manual contents (686.6(b)(3)). The written policy and procedure manual contains the following required areas: (i) admission and discharge of individuals, in ADM-01 to ADM-03, DIS-01 and DIS-02 (and SUP-01 to SUP-03 for supportive IRA); (ii) administration of records, in REC-01 to REC-08; (iii) emergencies and disasters, in EMR-01 to EMR-03 and IRA-04; (iv) health and safety issues, in HS-01 to HS-07 and IRA-01 to IRA-03; (v) personnel, in PER-01 to PER-08; (vi) review and appeal procedures for concerns of individuals and their correspondents, in this policy and APP-02; (vii) community involvement of staff and individuals, in COM-01; and (viii) individuals' involvement in community residence activities, in DEC-01. The manual is maintained under POL-02 and POL-03.

definitions.definition: A request that a decision on the plan of services or placement be reviewed again, by a person other than the one who made the decision.
Any statement, spoken or written, that a person, guardian or correspondent disagrees with a plan of services or placement decision. Handled under 14 NYCRR 633.12.
The written individualized, person-centered plan that describes the person's goals, supports and services (REC-01).
A decision on admission, declining admission, transfer, room assignment, discharge or move to another residence.
Any adverse action, threat, loss of privilege or change in treatment because a person objected, appealed or complained.

procedures: Information at admission: At or before admission, and after any change, the Residence Manager gives each person, and the parent, guardian or correspondent as available, the written statement of how to ask for review and appeal the plan of services and placement decisions. It is given in the person's primary language, and the Residence Manager explains it verbally. The recipient signs for it.

Posting: The Residence Manager posts the review and appeal information, the grievance contacts (APP-02) and OPWDD's information line, (866) 946-9733, 44 Holland Avenue, Albany, NY 12229-0001, in an accessible place and in accessible formats. [AGENCY NAME]'s internal contact is [APPEAL CONTACT NAME AND PHONE].

Receiving an objection: Any staff member who hears an objection or appeal request must accept it in any form (verbal, written, signed, gesture, through an advocate or supporter). The staff member records what was said, with date and time, and passes it to the Residence Manager the same day. Staff may not discourage a person from objecting.

Logging and deadlines: The Administrator opens an entry on the Objection Log within one business day. The entry records the date received, the person, the decision objected to and the person's requested outcome. The Administrator enters each timeframe from 14 NYCRR 633.12 on the log and calendars it.

Acknowledgment: The Administrator acknowledges the objection in writing, and verbally if needed, in the person's primary language, and tells the person who will review it and what the next steps are. The person may have a supporter, advocate or family member help throughout.

Interim protection: While the objection is pending, no change that is the subject of the objection takes effect unless there is immediate danger to health or safety (EMR-01) or a court orders otherwise. In an emergency the Administrator documents the reasons and tells the person right away.

Review: A reviewer who was not involved in the original decision (an administrator, the governing body or the person identified in the current text of 633.12) examines the plan, the reasons for the decision and the person's views. The reviewer meets the person and listens to his or her reasons.

Plan reconsideration: If the objection is to the plan of services, the program planning team meets with the person and reconsiders the plan, including whether it is ineffective or whether functional needs have been reassessed (REC-01). Changes are documented in the plan.

Written decision: Within the timeframes in 633.12, the reviewer gives the person, and the guardian or correspondent as available, a written decision with reasons and with information on how to take the matter further, including further appeal levels under the Commissioner's regulations and the OPWDD contacts above.

Rights modifications: If the objection concerns a limitation of a right, the reviewer checks that the limitation is documented, individual, time-limited and for clinical purposes only (633.4(a)(3)), and that there is a specific assessed need and justification in the plan (636-1.4). Any limitation that does not meet these tests is ended at once (see RIT-02).

Record access: If a person is denied access to the clinical record, the Residence Manager gives the person written notice of the right to have the denial reviewed by the OPWDD Clinical Record Access Review Committee and the contact to use (REC-08).

No reprisal: The Administrator tells all staff, at orientation and annually, that retaliation for an objection or appeal is prohibited and will result in discipline (PER-07). The Administrator checks in with the person within [NUMBER] days of the decision to make sure there has been no retaliation.

Alternative residence: If a person asks for an alternative residence, the Administrator tells the care manager the same business day. The request is documented in the person-centered plan along with the alternatives considered (DIS-01, DIS-02).
Manual availability: The Administrator keeps the manual current and complete under 686.6(b)(3), with each subject area in the cross-reference above, and makes it available as required by POL-03.

Annual review: Each year the Administrator reviews the Objection Log for timeliness, outcomes and patterns, and reports to the governing body and the quality improvement process (GOV-02). Where objections have exposed problems with plans or placement practices, the Administrator proposes corrective action.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the process, keeps the Objection Log and the timeframes, assigns an uninvolved reviewer and ensures written decisions and non-retaliation.
Gives the information at admission, accepts objections, supports the person and updates the plan.
Accept and pass on any objection the same day and never discourage or retaliate.
Reviews the decision independently and issues the written decision within the regulatory timeframes.
Receives the annual summary and ensures the manual is maintained (POL-01).
May object and appeal at any time, with the supports they choose.

documentation: Signed receipt of appeal information, in the person's primary language
Objection Log with dates and 633.12 timeframes
Staff record of each objection and the written acknowledgment
Reviewer's notes and written decision
Revised plan of services, where changed (REC-01)
Record of any interim emergency action and its reasons
Follow-up record on non-retaliation
Annual objection summary to the governing body and quality improvement
Manual cross-reference showing where each 686.6(b)(3) subject area is addressed

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All staff and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME]; all individuals living in the IRA and their parents, guardians, correspondents, advocates and health care proxy agents
policies.purpose: To give every individual, and every parent, guardian or correspondent, a safe, accessible way to raise a concern or complaint and get a timely answer without fear of reprisal. To separate grievances from allegations of abuse or neglect, which must go to the state hotline.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(iii) (review and appeal procedures available to individuals and their parents, guardians or correspondents) and the 686.6(b)(3)(vi) manual-content area (review and appeal procedures for concerns of individuals and their correspondents). Plan-of-services and placement appeals are handled under APP-01, and this policy works alongside it. [AGENCY NAME] lets any individual file a grievance without reprisal (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(4)). Complaint contacts are given to each individual and correspondent on admission, and again whenever the contacts change (633.4(a)(12)). An individual may also object to a plan or rights limitation and use the objection process under 633.4(a)(9) (objections under 633.12). Interpreters and other language assistance are provided at no charge (633.4(a)(15)). No one is retaliated against, disciplined, or has services, rights, privileges, or staff attention reduced for raising a concern. Staff are told that retaliation is misconduct. Allegations of abuse, neglect or other reportable incidents are NOT grievances. They are reported at once to the Justice Center VPCR hotline at 1-855-373-2122 (24 hours; Relay: dial 711 and give the number), and handled under REC-05 and REC-06. A concern that is both a grievance and a possible reportable incident is reported first and then handled under both policies.

definitions.definition: Any complaint, concern or dissatisfaction raised by or for an individual about services, staff, the residence, rules, charges, rights or the treatment of the individual. It is not an allegation of abuse or neglect.
A person, such as a family member or friend, who has been identified to receive information and to speak for an individual who has no guardian.
Any adverse action, threat, or change in treatment taken because someone raised a concern, including reduced choices, discipline, discouragement, or changes to schedule, room or staff.
An event that a mandated reporter must report to the Justice Center VPCR hotline when there is reasonable cause to suspect it, including suspected abuse or neglect.
The person [AGENCY NAME] designates, [GRIEVANCE COORDINATOR NAME], to receive, log and track grievances. If the concern is about that person, the Administrator takes the role.

procedures: On or before admission, the Residence Manager gives each individual and their guardian or correspondent the written complaint-contact sheet, explains it in plain language and in the person's primary language or preferred communication method, and documents this in the record (633.4(a)(12)).

The contact sheet lists: the Grievance Coordinator ([GRIEVANCE COORDINATOR NAME], [PHONE]); the Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]); OPWDD at (866) 946-9733 and 44 Holland Avenue, Albany, NY 12229-0001; the Justice Center VPCR hotline at 1-855-373-2122 (Relay: dial 711 and give the number); and any advocacy contact the individual chooses ([ADVOCACY OR SELF-ADVOCACY CONTACT]).
The Residence Manager posts the contact sheet in a place the individuals can easily see and reach. It is available in large print, plain language, picture format and translated versions on request.

The Administrator updates the sheet within 5 business days of any change to a contact. The Residence Manager then gives the new sheet to every individual and correspondent and documents that they received it, as 633.4(a)(12) requires.

A concern may be raised verbally, in writing, by gesture or assistive communication, through an advocate, or by a parent, guardian or correspondent. Staff must not require a written form. Any staff member who hears a concern writes it on the Grievance Intake Form the same shift and gives it to the Residence Manager.

Staff first decide whether the concern may involve abuse, neglect or another reportable incident. If so, the staff member calls the VPCR hotline at 1-855-373-2122 immediately, protects the person, notifies the Residence Manager, and follows REC-05 and REC-06. Staff must not investigate first or wait for supervisor permission.

The Grievance Coordinator logs every other grievance in the Grievance Log within 1 business day, assigns a tracking number, and tells the person how it will be handled. The coordinator also tells the person they may have someone of their choice help them.
Where the person can be helped immediately, such as a request for a different snack or a room-temperature problem, the Residence Manager resolves it right away and records the resolution in the log.

For all other grievances, the Grievance Coordinator acknowledges receipt to the person and any correspondent within 2 business days, in the person's preferred communication method, using an interpreter at no charge if needed (633.4(a)(15)).

The Residence Manager or the Administrator reviews the grievance, speaks with the person, and gathers facts. The review is done by someone who was not involved in the matter. Where possible, the Administrator is the reviewer if the Residence Manager is involved.

The Administrator gives the person and correspondent a written, plain-language response within 14 calendar days of receipt (the agency standard). The response states what was found, what will be done, who is responsible, and by when. If more time is needed, the Grievance Coordinator tells the person why and gives a new date.

The response tells the person they can ask for a review by the Administrator or the governing body, can contact OPWDD at (866) 946-9733, can object to a plan or rights limitation as set out in 633.4(a)(9), and that using these routes will never lead to reprisal.

If the grievance involves a plan of services, placement or rights modification, the Grievance Coordinator also starts the review and appeal steps in APP-01 and RIT-02, and tells the person's care manager.
The Administrator checks within 10 days after resolution that the action promised was done and asks the individual whether they are satisfied. Results are recorded in the log.

The Administrator watches for retaliation. For 90 days after a grievance, the Residence Manager checks in with the individual at least weekly and records any signs of changed treatment. Any suspected reprisal is investigated, and if it may be abuse or neglect it is reported to the VPCR hotline.

Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually (PER-02). They are told that raising concerns, and helping others to raise them, is protected, and that interfering with a grievance is grounds for discipline.
The Administrator reviews the Grievance Log quarterly for trends. Findings go to the governing body and the quality improvement process (GOV-02), without identifying details beyond what is needed.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy, reviews grievances, issues written responses, checks for retaliation, and reports trends to the governing body.
Logs and tracks grievances, sends acknowledgments, keeps the contact sheet current, and makes sure interpreters and communication supports are used.
Gives the contact sheet at admission and after any change, posts it, resolves concerns on the spot, and monitors the individual after a grievance.
Accept concerns in any form, report potential abuse or neglect to the VPCR hotline immediately, and never retaliate.
May raise a concern at any time, in any way, and may use outside contacts.

documentation: Signed or witnessed acknowledgment that the complaint-contact sheet was given on admission and after each change
Grievance Intake Forms and Grievance Log with tracking number, dates, reviewer, outcome and follow-up
Written responses to individuals and correspondents
Interpreter or communication-support use
Retaliation monitoring notes
Quarterly trend review summary and governing body minutes
Training attendance records

policies.title: Community Involvement, Integration and Employment Choice
policies.applies_to: All staff and volunteers; all individuals living in the IRA; families, guardians and correspondents
policies.purpose: To direct staff and individuals toward activities that build and sustain the residence's ties with its neighborhood and community, to support each person's own goals for community life, work and relationships, and to make sure no one is isolated or has community access limited without a documented, assessed need.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(iv) (community involvement, providing direction to staff and individuals as to the type of activities that will promote and nurture the involvement of the community residence with the neighborhood and community) and the 686.6(b)(3)(vii) manual-content area (community involvement of staff and individuals). [AGENCY NAME] delivers services in the most integrated setting appropriate to each person and supports each person to use community resources like other residents of the neighborhood. The person-centered plan documents that the individual chose the residence and which alternatives were considered (14 NYCRR Subpart 636-1). Services are delivered in integrated community settings, and the agency will not isolate individuals. Individuals choose how they spend their time, with whom, and where, including work, volunteering, school, faith, recreation and visits. Any limit on community access, such as a restriction on going out unsupervised, visitors or travel, is a rights modification. It is allowed only with a specific assessed need and justification in the person-centered service plan (636-1.4), and it must follow 633.4(a)(3) (documented, individual, time-limited and for clinical purposes only) and RIT-02. Rights are never limited for staff convenience, as a threat, as retribution or for discipline (633.4(a)(7)).

definitions.definition: A setting that gives individuals the same access to the community as people without disabilities, including opportunities to work, live, shop, worship, and use services in the community.
Neighborhood and community events, relationships, groups, volunteering, employment, recreation, faith activities, and civic life that individuals and the residence take part in.
A limit on an HCBS right or on community access that needs a specific assessed need, justification and documentation in the person-centered service plan (636-1.4).
The staff member, [COMMUNITY LIAISON NAME/TITLE], who builds and keeps relationships with neighbors and local organizations.

procedures: Before admission, the Residence Manager meets with the individual and their family or guardian to learn the person's interests, past community ties, faith, work or school goals, favorite places, and preferred routines, and records them in the person-centered plan.

The plan documents that the individual chose this residence and which alternatives were considered (Subpart 636-1). If the individual cannot say so, the plan records who helped decide and what the person showed they preferred.

Within 30 days of admission, and at each plan review, the Residence Manager and the individual identify at least [NUMBER] community activities, such as clubs, volunteering, faith, recreation, library, shopping and civic groups, that the person wants to do. These are written into the plan with the staff support needed.

The Administrator designates a community liaison. Within 90 days of opening, the liaison introduces the residence to neighbors, the local police and fire departments, faith and civic groups, businesses and the local municipality. The liaison also gives a contact name and number for neighbor concerns.

The Residence Manager schedules staff and transportation so that individuals can attend activities when they want, including evenings and weekends, and not only on a fixed group outing schedule. Individuals are not required to go with housemates.

Staff support individuals to use public transit, local stores, banks, libraries, parks and other community services, and support skills training so the person can do this as independently as possible.

The Residence Manager asks about and supports employment choice: work in the community, supported employment, volunteering, school or day services. Information is given in an accessible form, and referrals are made to the care manager and local providers. Choices of work or day activities are made by the individual and are not controlled by staff schedules.

Staff support relationships, visits and contact with family and friends, and support dating and intimate relationships as the person chooses, following RIT-01. The residence is not isolated or closed to visitors.
Staff do not segregate or label individuals in the community. Staff help the person to be seen as a neighbor, and use respectful language.

Each shift, the staff member on duty records on the daily activity note which community activities each individual did, who went, how the person took part, and any support needed (see REC-01). The Residence Manager reviews the notes weekly.

If an individual's community access appears to need a limit, the Residence Manager does not impose one. Staff ask the care manager and the person's planning team to assess the need. A limit may start only after the specific assessed need and justification are written into the person-centered plan (636-1.4), the person or guardian has consented, and the steps in RIT-02 are done. Each limit is time-limited and reviewed on the schedule in RIT-02.

The Residence Manager reviews the daily notes monthly. If an individual is rarely leaving the home or going to the same few places, the Residence Manager meets with the person within 14 days to ask why, offer options and change the plan if the person wants.

The Residence Manager and the community liaison keep a Community Involvement Log of neighborhood contacts, events attended, invitations received and neighbor concerns. Concerns are answered within 5 business days, in line with confidentiality rules (REC-03).

Staff and individuals are encouraged to take part together in neighborhood activities, such as block events, volunteering and faith services, and to invite neighbors to the home where the individuals want. Staff do not share personal information about individuals with neighbors without authorization.

The Administrator reviews the Community Involvement Log and the participation data every quarter. The review looks at each individual's integration and employment goals, and the results go to the governing body and into quality improvement (GOV-02).
Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually (PER-02), including that limiting community access for staff convenience is not allowed (633.4(a)(7)).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures resources, staffing and transportation for community involvement; reviews data quarterly; approves any rights modification steps with the planning team.
Develops each person's community goals with them, schedules support, reviews daily notes and starts the review if access appears limited.
Builds and keeps neighborhood and community relationships and handles neighbor concerns.
Support individuals to take part in the community as they choose and record participation each shift.
Choose activities, work and relationships, and tell staff what they want.

documentation: Person-centered plan section showing choice of residence and alternatives considered
Community, employment and relationship goals and supports in each plan
Daily activity notes showing community participation
Community Involvement Log, neighbor contact records, and event records
Any rights modification documentation under 636-1.4 and RIT-02
Quarterly review summary and governing body minutes
Training records

policies.title: Individual Participation in Day-to-Day Decisions
policies.applies_to: All staff and volunteers; all individuals living in the IRA; guardians, families and correspondents
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals, in accordance with their capability, contribute to decisions about daily life in their home, including menus, schedules, house activities and décor, and that their involvement in neighborhood and community activities is supported and recorded.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(v) (the means whereby individuals, in accordance with their capability, contribute to the decision-making process relative to day-to-day activities at the community residence, and individual/staff involvement in neighborhood/community activities) and the 686.6(b)(3)(viii) manual-content area (individuals' involvement in community residence activities). This is the individuals' home. They take part in decisions about what they eat, when they get up and go to bed, how they spend the day, how their rooms and shared spaces look, house activities, house meetings, and who visits. Staff give information and support in each person's preferred way so that each person can take part to the fullest of their capability, and they do not decide for a person who can decide for themselves. Individuals have access to food at any time. Any restriction on food access must be the least restrictive possible, justified under 14 NYCRR 636-1.4 through the person-centered planning process, and documented in the plan (OPWDD HCBS access-to-food guidance; 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)). Rights are never limited for staff convenience, as a threat, as retribution or for discipline (633.4(a)(7)). Individual and staff involvement in neighborhood and community activities is recorded as described in COM-01 and in this policy.

definitions.definition: Routine choices about daily life, including meals and snacks, wake and sleep times, clothing, schedules, outings, chores, room décor, use of shared spaces, visitors, and house activities.
Each person takes part as fully as they can, with the information, time and communication supports they need. It does not mean decisions are withheld because of a disability.

definitions.term: Access to food at any time
definitions.definition: The individual can get food and drink whenever they want, with no set meal-only times, unless a justified, documented person-centered restriction is in place.
A regular meeting where individuals discuss and decide on house matters, with support to take part.

procedures: At admission and at each plan review, the Residence Manager asks each individual about daily routines and preferences (sleep times, meals, hobbies, privacy, chores, visitors, décor) and writes them in the plan in the person's own words, with support as needed.

Each individual chooses their own bedroom décor, bedding and personal items, and has a say in colors, furniture and arrangement of shared areas. Staff help carry out the choices within safety codes (see HS-07).

The Residence Manager holds a house meeting at least monthly, scheduled when individuals can attend. Staff use pictures, plain language, assistive technology and one-to-one sessions so each person can contribute. Each person may also give input outside meetings.

Menus are planned with the individuals each week. Individuals choose meals and snacks, help shop and cook as they wish, and may substitute. Staff record the choices on the menu record. Where a modified diet is ordered, staff follow HS-05 and still offer choices within it.

All individuals may get food and drink at any time, including between meals and at night. Food is kept in an accessible place. Staff do not lock the kitchen or food, set 'closed kitchen' hours, or withhold food as a consequence.

If a person's team believes a food restriction is needed for health or safety (for example, a medical condition), the Residence Manager asks the nurse and care manager to assess it. A restriction begins only after the least restrictive option is chosen through person-centered planning, with a specific assessed need and justification in the plan (636-1.4), consent as required, and a time limit and review date (RIT-02).

Individuals set their own daily schedules, including waking, bathing, meals, leisure, and bedtime, within their plan and any health needs. Staff schedules and routines are arranged around the individuals, and not the other way round.
Staff offer real choices for outings, activities and house events. Each person decides whether to join. Staff do not require group participation and do not penalize a person who declines.

Individuals decide on chores and household tasks to the extent of their capability. Chores are voluntary teaching and skills activities listed in the plan, and are never used as discipline or a condition of services.

Staff support individuals to make decisions by giving information in an understandable way, allowing enough time, and checking understanding. If a person wants to make a choice that staff think is unwise, staff explain the risks and support the person to make an informed decision. The Residence Manager records the discussion and consults the nurse and the planning team where health or safety is involved (see DEC-02).

No staff member may remove or restrict a choice, privilege or right as a threat, retribution, discipline, or for staff convenience (633.4(a)(7)). Staff who see this happening report it to the Residence Manager or Administrator. If it may be abuse or neglect, staff call the VPCR hotline at 1-855-373-2122.

Each shift, staff record on the daily note the decisions each person made, such as meals, activities and schedule, and each person's participation in neighborhood and community activities with any staff involvement, as set out in COM-01.

The Residence Manager keeps house meeting minutes recording topics, individuals' decisions and follow-up actions, and posts decisions in an accessible form. Decisions made are put into practice within 14 days where possible, and individuals are told when they cannot be and why.
If an individual's choices are being overridden or they are not taking part, the Residence Manager meets with the person within 7 days, changes supports and updates the plan.

The Administrator reviews house meeting minutes, menu records and daily notes quarterly, and checks with individuals about whether they feel in control of their home. Results go to quality improvement (GOV-02).
Staff are trained at orientation and annually (PER-02) on supporting choice, communication supports, access to food and the limits on rights restrictions.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure policies, schedules and staffing support individual choice; reviews records quarterly; approves any person-centered restriction process.
Holds house meetings, records preferences, supports choice in menus, schedules and décor, and starts reviews of any proposed restriction.
Offer choices, give information in the person's preferred way, record decisions and participation each shift, and never limit rights for convenience.
Assesses health-related food or activity concerns and advises on least restrictive options.
Take part in decisions to the fullest of their capability and tell staff their wishes.

documentation: Person-centered plan preferences and choices
House meeting minutes and follow-up actions
Menu planning and food choice records
Daily notes showing decisions made and participation in community activities
Any food restriction or rights modification documentation under 636-1.4 and RIT-02
Quarterly review summary
Training records

policies.title: Informed Consent, Health Care Proxy and Decision-Making Support
policies.applies_to: All staff, nurses and volunteers; all individuals living in the IRA; guardians, correspondents, health care agents and families
policies.purpose: To make sure that individuals decide about their own health care, treatment and services to the extent they are able, with the support they need; that the right people consent when a person cannot; and that health care proxy, choice of providers and consent for restrictive behavior interventions are handled lawfully.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(v) (the means whereby individuals, in accordance with their capability, contribute to the decision-making process relative to the day-to-day activities at the community residence). Capable adults make their own decisions about their health care, medication, treatment and services, and [AGENCY NAME] does not substitute its judgment for theirs. Individuals have the right to choose their physician and dentist and to use a health care proxy (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(4) and (a)(11)). Where a person is not able to give consent, the agency involves the person's legal guardian, health care agent or other legally authorized person, as the person's legal status requires, and still seeks the person's own views and assent. Staff follow OPWDD's health care proxy and do-not-resuscitate requirements, and no staff member independently decides to start or withhold life-sustaining treatment. Behavior interventions that include restrictions need informed consent and review by the Informed Consent Committee under 14 NYCRR 633.16, and are never started on staff authority alone. Disclosure of health information to people outside the care team requires a valid written authorization under 45 CFR 164.508, unless the law permits otherwise (see REC-03). Written requests for access to the clinical record are handled under 633.4(a)(10).

definitions.definition: A person's voluntary agreement to a treatment, service or restriction after being told, in understandable terms, what it is, the benefits, risks and alternatives, and the right to refuse.
A written document in which an adult names a health care agent to make health care decisions if the person loses the ability to decide.
A court-appointed guardian, health care agent, or other person with legal authority to consent for an individual.
The committee under 14 NYCRR 633.16 that reviews and approves behavior interventions that are restrictive or intrusive before they are used.
A person's agreement or cooperation when they cannot give legally valid consent. It is sought even where someone else consents.

procedures: At admission, the Residence Manager and the nurse find out each person's legal status (own decision-maker, guardian, health care agent, correspondent) from the person's records and the care manager, and record who may consent to what. They file copies of guardianship papers and any health care proxy in the clinical record.

The Residence Manager assumes each adult can make their own decisions unless a court has ruled otherwise or a clinical assessment shows otherwise. Staff do not decide that a person lacks capacity on their own.

Before any treatment, new medication, procedure or service is started, the nurse or other qualified person explains it in plain language and in the person's primary language or communication method, with an interpreter at no charge (633.4(a)(15)). The person's questions are answered and the person's decision is recorded.

Staff give each person time and communication supports (pictures, plain-language summaries, a trusted person present) so they can take part in decisions to the fullest of their capability. A person's decision is respected even if staff or family disagree, unless a legally authorized representative has the right to decide.

Where a person cannot consent, staff obtain consent from the legally authorized representative before non-emergency treatment, document who consented and when, and still tell the person what is happening and ask for their views.
Emergency treatment is not delayed to get consent. Staff call 911 and follow EMR-01, and notify the representative as soon as possible afterward.

Individuals choose their own physician and dentist (633.4(a)(4)). Staff help the person find and get to providers they choose and do not require use of agency-preferred providers. The choice is recorded.

The nurse offers each adult information on health care proxies and, if the person wants, helps them complete one with a qualified person, without pressuring them. Copies are kept in the record and sent with the person to hospitals and appointments. Staff follow the proxy agent's decisions as the law requires (633.4(a)(11)).

Staff follow OPWDD's do-not-resuscitate requirements. Staff do not make or change any DNR decision. Any question about resuscitation status goes at once to the nurse and Administrator, and an order is honored only when it was made through the required process and is in the record.

No behavior intervention with a restriction is used until the planning team has completed a functional behavior assessment, the intervention is in the behavior support plan, the individual or authorized representative has given informed consent, and the Informed Consent Committee has reviewed it under 633.16. See BEH-01 and BEH-02.
Consent and refusal for medications are handled under REC-07. A person's refusal is recorded and reported to the nurse and prescriber, and staff do not hide medication in food or force it.

Written requests by an individual or representative to see the clinical record are given to the Administrator the same day and handled under 633.4(a)(10). If access is denied, the person is told in writing they may ask for review by the OPWDD Clinical Record Access Review Committee.

Staff release health information to anyone outside the care team only with a signed authorization that meets 45 CFR 164.508, or as otherwise permitted by law (REC-03). The authorization states what, to whom, for what purpose, an expiration, and the right to revoke.

The Residence Manager reviews each person's decision-making status, consent forms, proxies and provider choices at each plan review and at least annually, and updates them when a person's status or wishes change.

Staff who think a representative is not acting in the person's interest tell the Residence Manager and Administrator. The Administrator contacts the care manager and, where needed, seeks legal advice or other appropriate help. Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported to the VPCR hotline at 1-855-373-2122 under REC-06.
Staff are trained at orientation and annually (PER-02) on consent, supported decision-making, health care proxy and the limits of their role.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this policy, handles record-access requests and legal-status questions, and ensures Informed Consent Committee review before restrictive interventions.
Explains treatments and medications, supports health care proxy completion, verifies consent before treatment, and is the contact for resuscitation-status questions.
Records legal status, consent and provider choices; makes sure supports for decision-making are used; reviews annually.
Respect individuals' decisions, never coerce, report concerns, and never decide consent or resuscitation status.
Make decisions within their legal authority and in line with the person's wishes and best interests.

documentation: Legal status and decision-maker record for each individual
Guardianship papers and health care proxy copies
Signed consent and refusal records
Physician and dentist choice record
Informed Consent Committee approvals
HIPAA authorizations and clinical record access requests with responses
Annual review notes
Training records

policies.category: Administration of records, incidents/abuse and medication (686.6(a)(2)(vi))
policies.title: Plans of Services: Development, Implementation and Daily Documentation
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Residence Manager, nurse, direct support professionals, and all individuals with their planning teams
policies.purpose: To make sure each individual has a written, person-centered plan of services that they helped develop, that it is carried out, and that daily documentation shows the services given and supports the Medicaid rate code billed.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(vi) (requirements for the administration of records) and 686.6(a)(2)(vi)(a) (plans of services). Each individual has a written individualized plan with the right to participate, object and appeal (14 NYCRR 633.4). The plan follows the person-centered planning requirements of 14 NYCRR Subpart 636-1: it records that the individual chose this residence and which alternatives were considered, and it is updated when it proves ineffective and on reassessment of functional need. Any modification of an HCBS right needs a specific assessed need and justification in the plan (636-1.4) and is handled under RIT-02. The plan includes the person's protective oversight plan (IRA-02) and a current fire-evacuation evaluation (IRA-04). Staff document each day's services in the daily record. Daily service notes must support the rate code billed (service day, therapeutic/non-medical leave day, or retainer/medical leave day). OMIG disallows a claim whose documentation does not match the rate code billed, so documentation accuracy is a compliance requirement, not only a record-keeping one. Appeals of the plan and placement are handled under APP-01.

definitions.definition: The written individualized plan that sets out the person's goals, assessed needs, supports, services, health and safety needs, and any rights modifications, developed with the person.
A dated, signed record each shift of the services provided, the individual's participation and condition, and any notable events.
The Medicaid billing code for the daily unit of residential habilitation: service day, therapeutic/non-medical leave day, or retainer/medical leave day.
A day a person is away for medical reasons, such as a hospital stay, for which the bed may be held and billed under the retainer rate code, subject to the annual cap in OPWDD guidance (see GOV-03).
The individual, family or guardian, care manager, Residence Manager, nurse, direct support staff and others the person chooses.

procedures: Before or at admission, the Residence Manager obtains the current person-centered plan, assessments and care manager information, and sets an initial team meeting date in line with OPWDD and care manager timelines (ADM-02).

The Residence Manager invites the individual, guardian or correspondent, care manager, nurse and any others the person wants to the planning meeting. The meeting is held where and when the person can attend. Information is given in plain language, and an interpreter is provided at no charge (633.4(a)(15)).

The team develops the residence's part of the plan, including the person's goals in their own words, daily support needs, health needs, behavior supports if any, community and employment goals, and the supports and training staff will give.

The plan records that the individual chose this residence and which alternatives were considered (Subpart 636-1). For individuals who cannot say so, it records who helped decide and the person's expressed preferences.
The plan includes the individual's protective oversight plan (IRA-02) and a current fire-evacuation evaluation (IRA-04). The Residence Manager checks that both are filed in the plan and current.

The individual is told of the right to participate in the plan, object to it, and appeal. The Residence Manager gives the individual and representative a copy of the plan and the appeal process (APP-01). Any objection is recorded and sent to the Administrator the same day, and handled under 633.4(a)(9) and APP-01.

Any proposed limit on a right goes through RIT-02, and the plan must show the specific assessed need and justification (636-1.4) before it starts. Limits are never based on staff convenience (633.4(a)(7)).

The Residence Manager assigns staff to carry out each part of the plan, trains them on the plan before they work alone with the individual, and records the training. Direct support professionals are told of the person's support strategies in a short, usable form that is kept in the staff area.

Staff complete a daily service note each shift, in ink or in the approved electronic system, before the end of the shift. It records the date, the person, the services and supports provided against plan goals, the person's participation and mood, health observations, community activities, medications given (cross-referenced to the medication record), and any incident. Entries are signed with name and title.

Staff record the correct rate-code status of each individual for each day: service day (person in the residence receiving services), therapeutic/non-medical leave day, or retainer/medical leave day. They record where the person was and why, for example hospital or home visit. The Residence Manager checks the status against the note before the monthly billing review.

Staff do not create, change or back-date notes. A late entry is marked 'late entry' with the actual date and time. A correction is made by one line through the error, with initials, date and the corrected text. Electronic corrections keep the audit trail.

The Residence Manager reviews all daily notes weekly for completeness, plan alignment, and the accuracy of rate-code status, and signs the review. Gaps are fixed within 3 business days and are discussed with staff.

Each month, before billing, the Administrator or designee compares daily notes with rate-code status for each person and each day. Any day that is not supported by documentation, or does not match the code, is corrected or not billed. Retainer days are counted against each person's annual cap in accordance with current OPWDD guidance (see GOV-03).

The Residence Manager reviews the plan at least [REVIEW FREQUENCY, e.g., every six months] and also at any time the plan is not working or a person's needs change. When the plan is ineffective or a reassessment of functional need shows changed needs, the team updates the plan promptly (Subpart 636-1). Updates are signed and distributed to the person, representative and staff.
The Residence Manager records progress toward each goal each month, and brings concerns to the team and the care manager.
Plans, notes and rate-code documentation are kept in the individual record and retained and protected under REC-03 and REC-08. Billing and documentation reviews are reported under GOV-03.
Staff are trained at orientation and annually (PER-02) on plan implementation, documentation standards, and the link between notes and billing.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures every individual has a current plan, carries out the monthly rate-code review, and corrects documentation gaps before billing.
Convenes planning meetings, ensures the plan includes required components, trains staff on the plan, and reviews daily notes weekly.
Contributes health information, protective oversight and health supports to the plan.
Carry out the plan and complete accurate, timely, signed daily notes with correct service status.
Take part in planning, and may object to or appeal the plan.

documentation: Current person-centered plan with choice-of-residence and alternatives-considered statement
Protective oversight plan and fire-evacuation evaluation filed in the plan
Plan review meeting records, objections and appeals
Staff training on the plan
Daily service notes with rate-code status
Weekly note review sign-offs and monthly note-to-billing reconciliation
Rights modification documentation under 636-1.4

policies.category: Administration of records, incidents/abuse and medication (686.6(a)(2)(vi))
policies.title: Personal Funds and Financial Records
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Residence Manager, direct support professionals, finance staff, and all individuals living in the IRA and their representatives
policies.purpose: To protect each individual's money, to make sure the individual controls their money to the extent of their capability, and to keep complete, accurate and secure financial records, with clear staff accountability when the agency handles funds.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(vi)(b) (person's financial records) and is written under 14 NYCRR 633.15 (management of personal funds), which applies to all OPWDD-certified residential facilities. Individuals have the right to use their own money (633.4(a)(4)). Where [AGENCY NAME] manages funds, it acts as a fiduciary under MHL 33.07(e). The agency offers each individual the option to set up separate accounting as required by SSL 131-o. These written procedures cover security, staff accountability, paper and electronic recordkeeping, usage, and monitoring of personal allowance and other income. Personal allowance is the monthly income portion for the individual's personal spending. Each person's funds are tracked separately and are never combined with another person's or the agency's. Cash and cash equivalents, including prepaid cards, are locked with limited access. A ledger records every receipt, disbursement and cash balance. Cash above the cash cap needs a documented specific purpose and is held no longer than 14 days. Cost of care charged to an individual is limited to the maximum under 14 NYCRR 635.9 and SSL 131-o, which is the Level II SSI combined payment level minus the SSL 131-o minimum personal allowance. Supervised IRAs are responsible for the required supplies and services under 635.9, and the agency may not charge individuals for them out of their personal allowance. OPWDD is amending Part 633 to add or amend section 633.9 on representative payees for residents of certified residences, with conforming changes to 633.15. The agency will apply the adopted rule text when it takes effect and update this policy at that time (see POL-02). Financial records are kept 4 years.

definitions.definition: The monthly income portion set aside for the individual's personal spending, after the cost of care.
Handling, holding or accounting for an individual's money by the agency. SSL 131-o requires the agency to offer to set up separate accounting.
Prepaid cards, gift cards, and similar items that can be used like cash. They are treated as cash for security and recordkeeping.

The maximum cash the agency may hold on site for an individual under OPWDD guidance, [CASH CAP AMOUNT per current OPWDD guidance]. Amounts above it need a documented specific purpose and are limited to 14 days.
A person or organization appointed to receive and manage an individual's Social Security or SSI benefits for the individual.
The charge to an individual for room, board and required services, capped under 14 NYCRR 635.9 and SSL 131-o.

procedures: Before admission, the Administrator gives the individual and their representative written information on supplies and services the agency provides and the charges, in line with 633.4(a)(4)(xv) and ADM-03. The information states how cost of care is set under 635.9 and that it never exceeds the maximum (Level II SSI combined payment level minus the SSL 131-o minimum personal allowance).

At admission, the Administrator identifies each person's income sources (SSI, SSDI, earnings, other) and who receives them (the person, a family member, a representative payee, or the agency). The Administrator records this in the financial record. If the agency is asked to be representative payee, the Administrator follows Social Security Administration requirements and the adopted OPWDD rule on representative payees (633.9) once it takes effect.

The Administrator offers the individual, in writing and in plain language, the choice of having the agency manage their personal allowance with separate accounting, or managing it themselves or with support (SSL 131-o). The individual's or representative's decision is signed and filed. The person may change it at any time.

Where the agency manages funds, the Administrator opens a separate ledger for each person (paper or electronic), and where an account is used it is in the person's name or held in trust, never commingled with agency funds.

Cash and cash equivalents are kept in a locked box or safe, in a locked room or cabinet. Only the Residence Manager and one designated alternate hold keys or codes. The key log shows who accessed the box and when. Keys and codes are never shared and are changed within 1 day when someone leaves or loses access.

Each person's cash is kept in a separate, labeled envelope or compartment. Each receipt and disbursement is entered in that person's ledger the same day, with date, amount, source or purpose, the balance, the signature of the staff member, and a second staff signature for each transaction over [DOUBLE-SIGNATURE AMOUNT].

Every spending transaction is supported by a receipt. Where a receipt cannot be given, the staff member writes a note that the person or a witness signs. The person is shown the transaction and the new balance and decides how their money is spent, with support as needed. Staff never use a person's funds for agency expenses, staff items or items the agency must supply under 635.9, and never borrow or lend a person's money.
Prepaid cards and gift cards are logged as cash on the ledger, with card number (last 4 digits), value loaded, each purchase and the remaining value. They are stored with the cash.

The Residence Manager does not keep cash for an individual above the cash cap. Where a larger amount is needed for a specific purpose, such as a major purchase or a trip, the Residence Manager writes the purpose, amount and expected date on the ledger and has the Administrator approve it. The extra cash is held no more than 14 days, after which it is spent for the stated purpose or deposited.

Two staff, one of them the Residence Manager or designee, count each person's cash and reconcile it against the ledger at least weekly and at each shift change when cash is moved. Both sign. Any discrepancy is reported to the Administrator the same day. If theft or exploitation is suspected, the Administrator reports to the VPCR hotline at 1-855-373-2122 and follows REC-05 and REC-06, and the individual is reimbursed promptly while the matter is reviewed.

The Administrator or a person independent of daily handling reconciles the ledgers, receipts, bank statements and cash on hand each month, signs the reconciliation, and reviews it with the governing body at least quarterly. Findings are corrected within 14 days.

At least once a year, the Administrator and the Residence Manager meet with each individual (and representative) whose allowance the agency manages to review the annual personal expenditure plan: what the person wants to spend on, savings goals, clothing, recreation and trips, and any changes in income. The plan is signed and filed, and changed when the person's wishes change.

Each person receives a statement of their account at least monthly in a form they understand, and may see their ledger and receipts at any time on request. Staff must give access promptly and never use access to funds as a reward or consequence (633.4(a)(7)).

The Administrator tracks Social Security, SSI and other income reporting duties, such as changes in income, resources or residence, and carries them out on time. The agency does not hold a person's resources above SSI limits without a plan, and tells the representative and care manager if a person's savings approach a limit.

When a person leaves the residence or dies, the Administrator closes the ledger within 5 business days, gives the person or the legal representative all funds with a final accounting, and handles funds after death as required by law (see EMR-03 and DIS-02). Signed receipt is obtained and filed.

Staff who handle funds are trained at orientation, before they handle any money, and annually (PER-02) on these procedures, key control, ledgers, prepaid cards, exploitation signs and reporting duties. The training is documented.

The Administrator updates this policy within 30 days after OPWDD adopts the amendments to 633.9 and 633.15 on representative payees, and sooner if the new rules require changes before then (POL-02). Financial records are kept for at least 4 years and for longer where another law or open audit requires (REC-08).

responsibilities.duty: Acts for the agency as fiduciary, makes the SSL 131-o offer, approves cash above the cap, performs monthly reconciliation, and reports suspected exploitation.
Controls keys and cash, ensures ledgers and receipts are current, supports individuals' spending decisions, and does weekly counts.
Record each transaction accurately, follow security and receipt rules, never borrow or use funds for other purposes, and report discrepancies.
Review monthly reconciliations and quarterly findings.
Decide how their funds are used to the extent of their capability, review statements, and raise concerns.

documentation: Signed notice of charges and cost-of-care disclosure
SSL 131-o offer and the person's decision
Income sources and payee record
Individual ledger of receipts, disbursements and balances
Receipts, key-access log, prepaid card log
Weekly cash counts and monthly reconciliation
Approvals and 14-day tracking for cash above the cap
Annual personal expenditure plan
Monthly statements to individuals
Closing accounting and receipts
Staff training records
All of the above retained for at least 4 years

policies.category: Administration of records, incidents/abuse and medication (686.6(a)(2)(vi))
policies.title: Confidentiality and Protection of Individuals' Records (Privacy and HIPAA)
policies.applies_to: All employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors of [AGENCY NAME], and all paper and electronic records about individuals living in the IRA
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy of every individual living in the residence and to make sure information about the individual is used and shared only as the individual permits or as the law requires or allows.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(vi)(c), confidentiality and protection of individuals' records. Each individual has the right to confidentiality (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(4)). [AGENCY NAME] keeps all information about an individual confidential and shares it only (a) with the individual's written authorization, given by the individual or the individual's legally authorized representative, or (b) when law permits or requires it. Examples are treatment and care coordination, required reports to OPWDD and the Justice Center, and emergencies. [AGENCY NAME] follows the federal privacy rules at 45 CFR Part 160 and 45 CFR 164.530 to the extent they apply to it. These cover a designated privacy official, workforce training, safeguards, a complaint process, sanctions, no retaliation, and documentation of the privacy policies. HIV-related information is confidential under 14 NYCRR 633.19, Public Health Law Article 27-F and 10 NYCRR Part 63. It is released only as those rules allow. Written requests by an individual for access to the clinical record are handled under Mental Hygiene Law 33.16 (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(10)) and REC-08. Families and others are notified of and given access to incident information as Jonathan's Law requires, as described in REC-05. Staff are advised of these rights (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(6)). Breaking this policy is grounds for discipline, up to termination.

definitions.definition: Any information that identifies an individual or could reasonably be used to identify one, including name, photograph, diagnosis, services, medications, incident information, finances and HIV-related information. It may be written, electronic or spoken.

A signed, dated, written permission from the individual or the legally authorized representative that names what may be released, to whom, for what purpose, and for how long. The individual may revoke it in writing.
The least amount of information a person needs to do a specific job or task.
The person [AGENCY NAME] designates to run the privacy program and receive privacy complaints.
Any use, access or disclosure of confidential information that is not permitted by this policy or by law.

procedures: 1. The Administrator names a Privacy Officer, [PRIVACY OFFICER NAME], [PHONE]. The name and phone number are posted in the staff office and given to every individual and representative at admission.

2. At hire, and again each year, every employee, intern, volunteer, consultant and contractor is trained on this policy and signs a confidentiality statement. The Residence Manager files the signed statement in the personnel file (PER-06). No one may work with individuals until it is signed.

3. At or before admission, the Residence Manager gives each individual and representative a plain-language written notice of the individual's confidentiality rights and how [AGENCY NAME] uses and shares information. It is given in the person's primary language or with communication support (RIT-03). The signed acknowledgement goes in the individual's record.

4. Access is limited by job role. Direct support staff see the information needed to support the people on their shift. Clinical, administrative and billing staff see only what their tasks require. The Privacy Officer approves access and removes it when a person changes roles or leaves.

5. Paper records stay in a locked cabinet or room in the staff area. They are never left open in common areas, vehicles or the kitchen. Items used daily, such as the medication record and plan summary, are kept in the locked staff area and returned after use.

6. Electronic records require a unique user ID and password. Staff never share log-ins. Screens lock automatically. Devices are encrypted where feasible. Identifiable information is never sent by personal text, personal email or social media. Staff use only [AGENCY NAME]-approved secure systems.

7. Staff discuss individuals only in private places and only with people who need to know. They do not discuss individuals in public places, with friends or family, or in front of other individuals or visitors.

8. Staff do not confirm to a caller or visitor that a person lives in the residence. They take a message and pass it to the individual or the Residence Manager. Visitors are handled under RIT-01 and the individual's wishes.

9. Before releasing information outside [AGENCY NAME], the staff member checks the identity of the requester and confirms a valid authorization or a legal basis, and discloses only the minimum necessary. The Residence Manager records the date, recipient, what was released and the authority in the individual's disclosure log.

10. HIV-related information is kept separate within the record. Only staff who need it for care or safety may see it, and it is released only with a specific release or as 14 NYCRR 633.19, Public Health Law Article 27-F and 10 NYCRR Part 63 permit. A staff member unsure whether a release is allowed asks the Privacy Officer first.

11. Photographs, video and audio recordings of individuals, and any posting on websites or social media, require the individual's written consent. Staff may not take images of individuals on personal devices.
12. Written requests for the clinical record are forwarded to the Privacy Officer the same day and handled under REC-08. Staff may not refuse a request or tell a person to ask later.

13. Notice and access to incident information for parents, guardians and other eligible family members is given under Jonathan's Law and REC-05. The Incident Review Coordinator confirms that notice is given and documents it.
14. Records taken off site, for appointments or the day program, are limited to what is needed, carried in a closed container, kept with the staff member and returned the same day.

15. Staff who see or suspect a privacy breach tell the Privacy Officer immediately and no later than the end of the shift. The Privacy Officer investigates, limits the harm, documents the findings, and notifies affected individuals, representatives and agencies within the time federal and state law require.
16. Individuals, family and staff may complain about privacy practices to the Privacy Officer or through APP-02. No one is retaliated against for raising a privacy concern.
17. Contractors, consultants and vendors who handle individuals' information must sign a confidentiality agreement or business associate agreement before they receive access.
18. Paper records are shredded and electronic media are securely wiped when destruction is allowed under REC-08. Each destruction is logged.

19. The Privacy Officer audits access logs, record security and disclosure logs at least quarterly. The Privacy Officer reports results and corrective actions to the Administrator and into the quality review (GOV-02). The privacy policies and related documentation are kept in writing as 45 CFR 164.530 requires.

responsibilities.duty: Appoints the Privacy Officer, provides secure storage and systems, and applies sanctions for violations.
Runs the privacy program, trains staff, approves access, investigates breaches and complaints, and audits compliance.
Enforces safeguards on site, obtains acknowledgements and signed statements, and keeps the disclosure log.

responsibilities.role: All staff, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors
responsibilities.duty: Protect confidential information, use it only as the job requires, and report suspected breaches immediately.

documentation: Signed staff confidentiality statements and privacy training records
Individual's signed acknowledgement of the confidentiality notice
Signed authorizations and the disclosure log
Breach reports and investigation findings
Access audit reports and corrective action records
Confidentiality or business associate agreements with contractors

policies.category: Administration of records, incidents/abuse and medication (686.6(a)(2)(vi))
policies.title: Statistical Information and Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, Incident Review Coordinator, Residence Managers and all staff who record incidents or notable occurrences
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] accurately coordinates, collects, releases and tracks statistical information and sends the reports OPWDD requires on time.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(vi)(d), coordination, collection, release and tracking of statistical information. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] designates one Statistical Information Coordinator, [STATISTICAL INFORMATION COORDINATOR NAME], [PHONE]. The Coordinator coordinates collection, controls release and tracks all statistical information. Reportable incidents and serious notable occurrences are entered in OPWDD's incident reporting system and updated at least monthly until closure (14 NYCRR 624.5). Serious notable occurrences include every death regardless of cause and sensitive situations as defined in REC-05 (14 NYCRR 624.4). Minor notable occurrences are recorded in a log kept by the Coordinator (14 NYCRR 624.4, 624.5). Statistical data given to anyone outside the agency, other than required reports to OPWDD or other regulators, is de-identified unless the privacy rules in REC-03 permit otherwise. The Compliance Officer will confirm in writing whether any additional Part 686 recordkeeping or reporting requirements apply to [AGENCY NAME]. This policy will be revised if any do.

definitions.definition: Counts and rates drawn from records, such as numbers of incidents by type, location, shift and individual, injuries, deaths, medication errors, admissions, discharges and staff training completion.
An event that must be reported to the Justice Center VPCR and to OPWDD under 14 NYCRR Part 624.
A death of any individual regardless of cause, or a sensitive situation, including a possible criminal act by an individual (14 NYCRR 624.4).

Suspected theft or financial exploitation over $15 and up to $100 (isolated, no card involved), or an injury needing treatment beyond first aid by a physician, dentist, physician assistant or nurse practitioner (14 NYCRR 624.4).
The person named by the Administrator to coordinate, collect, release and track statistical information.

procedures: 1. The Administrator names the Statistical Information Coordinator and a backup in writing. The names are on the staff contact list and in the incident file.
2. Staff complete the incident or notable occurrence report form for every event before the end of the shift. They give it to the Residence Manager, who forwards it to the Coordinator the same day.

3. The Coordinator classifies each event as a reportable incident, serious notable occurrence, minor notable occurrence or other event, using the definitions in REC-05 and 14 NYCRR 624.4. A question about classification goes to the Administrator the same day. When in doubt, the event is reported at the higher level.

4. The Coordinator confirms that reportable incidents and serious notable occurrences were reported immediately to the CEO or designee and to OPWDD. The Coordinator confirms that minor notable occurrences reached the CEO or designee within 48 hours (14 NYCRR 624.5). The Coordinator records the date and time of each notice on the tracking sheet.
5. The Coordinator or designee enters each reportable incident and serious notable occurrence in OPWDD's incident reporting system and keeps the confirmation record.

6. The Coordinator updates every open entry at least monthly until the case is closed. The Coordinator keeps a tickler list of due dates and reviews it weekly. If an update would be late, the Coordinator tells the Administrator at once.
7. The Coordinator keeps a log of minor notable occurrences with the date, individual, event, notice date and follow-up. The log is reviewed each month with the Administrator.
8. Every death is entered as a serious notable occurrence even if it is also a reportable incident. A death that is also a reportable incident is reported both ways (14 NYCRR 624.4; EMR-03).

9. By the 10th day of each month, the Coordinator compiles a statistical summary for the prior month. It covers incident and notable occurrence counts by type, location, shift and individual, injuries, medication errors, elopements, restraint use, and open and closed investigations. The Coordinator also compiles trends against prior months.
10. The Coordinator gives the monthly summary to the Administrator. Each quarter the Administrator presents the summary and trends to the governing body and the quality improvement review (GOV-02).

11. Release: only the Coordinator or the Administrator releases statistical information outside the agency. Regulator requests are answered by the deadline in the request, and the Coordinator keeps a copy of what was sent and the date. Other requests need the Administrator's written approval. Data released without an authorization is de-identified (REC-03).
12. The Coordinator checks the data for accuracy by comparing the log against incident reports and the OPWDD system each quarter. Errors are corrected and the correction is noted.
13. The Coordinator keeps incident statistics, logs and system confirmations under the retention rules in REC-08 and does not destroy them without the Administrator's approval.

14. The Compliance Officer reviews OPWDD guidance and this policy at least annually and records any change in required reports. The Compliance Officer also confirms in writing whether additional Part 686 recordkeeping or reporting requirements apply. Required changes are made through POL-02.

responsibilities.duty: Names the Coordinator and backup, reviews monthly summaries, approves outside releases and reports to the governing body.
Classifies events, enters and updates the OPWDD system, keeps the logs, compiles summaries and controls release.
Makes sure staff complete reports the same shift and forwards them to the Coordinator the same day.
Checks reporting requirements annually and audits data accuracy.
Report every event on time and accurately.

documentation: Incident and notable occurrence reports
Reporting and update tracking sheet with notice dates and times
Minor notable occurrence log
OPWDD incident system confirmations and monthly update records
Monthly and quarterly statistical summaries
Log of statistical information released outside the agency

policies.category: Administration of records, incidents/abuse and medication (686.6(a)(2)(vi))
policies.title: Incidents, Allegations of Abuse, Notable Occurrences and Investigations
policies.applies_to: All employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident, allegation of abuse and notable occurrence is reported on time, recorded, investigated, reviewed and used to prevent a repeat.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(vi)(e), incidents and allegations of abuse. It is the written policy on reporting, recording, investigation, review and monitoring required by 14 NYCRR 624.5(a)(1). All employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors must report. Anyone with reasonable cause to suspect a reportable incident reports it immediately to the Justice Center Vulnerable Persons' Central Register (VPCR) at 1-855-373-2122, which is staffed 24 hours a day (Relay: dial 711 and give the number). Reporting may be delayed only to protect someone's safety or to call 911, and the VPCR report must be made within 24 hours of discovery. Reportable incidents and serious notable occurrences go immediately to the CEO or designee and to OPWDD. Minor notable occurrences go to the CEO or designee within 48 hours (14 NYCRR 624.5). Employees are told that every reportable incident is investigated, and that an investigation continues to a substantiated or unsubstantiated finding even if the employee leaves [AGENCY NAME]. Parents, guardians and other eligible persons are notified of incidents and given access to information as Jonathan's Law requires. The Incident Review Coordinator keeps the current notice timeframes from the statute and 14 NYCRR 624.5 on file. Retaliation against anyone who reports is prohibited (PER-03).

definitions.definition: An event that must be reported to the Justice Center VPCR and to OPWDD under 14 NYCRR Part 624, including abuse and neglect and significant incidents. Deliberate inappropriate use of restraint is abuse or neglect, and inappropriate use of restraint is a significant incident. Unauthorized absence, choking and larger thefts are reportable incidents under 14 NYCRR 624.3.
The death of any individual regardless of cause, or a sensitive situation (14 NYCRR 624.4).

As [AGENCY NAME] defines it, and to the extent not already a reportable incident: (1) a possible criminal act by an individual, as 14 NYCRR 624.4 requires; (2) an arrest of, or police investigation involving, an individual or a staff member on duty; and (3) an event likely to bring media attention or serious public concern to the residence or an individual.

Suspected theft or financial exploitation over $15 and up to $100 (isolated, no card involved), or an injury needing treatment beyond first aid by a physician, dentist, physician assistant or nurse practitioner (14 NYCRR 624.4).
[ADMINISTRATOR NAME], or the person [AGENCY NAME] has named in writing to receive incident reports, including after hours: [ON-CALL DESIGNEE NAME], [PHONE].
An employee or volunteer of a certified or operated facility who must report reasonable cause to suspect a reportable incident.

procedures: 1. Make everyone safe first. Any staff member who sees or learns of an incident provides first aid or calls 911 if anyone is in danger or injured, and separates the individual from any alleged abuser.

2. The staff member who discovered or suspects a reportable incident calls the VPCR at 1-855-373-2122 immediately. If calling 911 or safety actions must come first, the VPCR report is still made as soon as possible and always within 24 hours of discovery. Telling a supervisor does not meet the duty to report. Each mandated reporter must make or confirm the report personally.
3. The staff member writes down the VPCR call date and time and the report or confirmation number, and gives them to the Residence Manager.

4. The staff member notifies the CEO or designee immediately by phone of every reportable incident and every serious notable occurrence, at any hour. The Residence Manager or on-call designee makes the notice if the staff member cannot.
5. The CEO or designee, or the Incident Review Coordinator, reports each reportable incident and serious notable occurrence to OPWDD immediately through OPWDD's incident reporting system.

6. Minor notable occurrences are reported to the CEO or designee within 48 hours. The Residence Manager sends the written report to the Incident Review Coordinator, who adds it to the minor notable occurrence log (REC-04).
