7. Preserve evidence. Staff do not clean the scene, move or discard items, or alter records. They secure relevant documents, schedules, video and medication records and give them only to investigators and the Incident Review Coordinator.

8. Every employee involved writes a factual statement the same shift. The statement says what was seen and heard, with dates and times, and does not offer conclusions. Staff do not discuss the event with each other before giving the statement.

9. The Residence Manager protects the individual. The Residence Manager arranges any medical care needed (EMR-01), emotional support, and communication help, and offers to help the individual contact family, an advocate or Justice Center staff. The Residence Manager removes staff accused of abuse from direct contact with the individual until the Administrator decides on the next step. The Administrator determines the safeguards and documents them.

10. Notice to families: the Incident Review Coordinator makes sure parents, guardians and other eligible persons are notified, and offered access to information, within the timeframes in Jonathan's Law and 14 NYCRR 624.5. The notice date, method and recipient are documented. [AGENCY NAME]'s standard is to notify the same day whenever practicable.

11. Investigation: the Administrator assigns a trained investigator who has no involvement in the event. The investigator follows 14 NYCRR 624.5 and cooperates fully with the Justice Center, OPWDD and law enforcement, and does not interfere with their investigations. The investigation continues to a substantiated or unsubstantiated finding even if the employee has resigned or been terminated.

12. The investigator interviews witnesses, reviews records, and writes a report with findings and recommended actions, and gives it to the Administrator within the timeframe set by the Justice Center, OPWDD or the Administrator, whichever is shortest.
13. The Incident Review Coordinator updates every open entry in the OPWDD system at least monthly until closure (14 NYCRR 624.5) and records each update date.

14. The Incident Review Committee, made up of the Administrator, the nurse, the Program Director and the Residence Manager, reviews each incident. It decides on corrective actions, such as staff retraining, supervision changes, plan of services changes, or environmental changes. The Administrator assigns owners and due dates, and the Coordinator tracks them to completion.

15. Employee consequences: substantiated findings lead to discipline up to termination. A final Category 2 finding reported through the Staff Exclusion List check is not an automatic bar to employment, but it is a factor in hiring and continued employment decisions (PER-04). The Administrator documents the decision.
16. Each month the Coordinator analyzes incidents for patterns by individual, location, shift and staff, and reports to the Administrator. The analysis feeds the quality improvement review (GOV-02).

17. All employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors receive written notice of this policy at hire and each year. The notice states that each person must report, that every reportable incident is investigated, and that no one will face retaliation for reporting in good faith.

18. The Incident Review Coordinator files incident reports, VPCR confirmation numbers, statements, investigation reports, family notices and corrective action records. They are kept in a secure incident file kept separately from the individual's regular record and are retained under REC-08.

responsibilities.role: All employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors
responsibilities.duty: Report reasonable cause to suspect a reportable incident to the VPCR immediately and always within 24 hours of discovery, tell the CEO or designee, protect the individual, and cooperate in the investigation.
Ensures safety and first aid, collects statements, secures evidence, notifies the CEO or designee, and carries out protective actions.
Receives immediate reports, ensures OPWDD notice, assigns investigators and approves protective and corrective actions.
Enters and updates OPWDD reports, tracks deadlines, ensures family notice, and keeps the incident file.
Conducts an impartial investigation through to a finding and writes the report.
Reviews each incident, decides corrective action and monitors completion.

documentation: Incident or notable occurrence report form
VPCR call date, time and confirmation number
Record of notice to the CEO or designee and to OPWDD
Written staff statements
Investigation report with finding and corrective action plan
Monthly OPWDD system update record and closure confirmation
Family notice record under Jonathan's Law
Signed staff acknowledgement of the reporting duty

policies.category: Administration of records, incidents/abuse and medication (686.6(a)(2)(vi))
policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Mandated Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, interns, volunteers, consultants, contractors and individuals living in the residence
policies.purpose: To prevent abuse, neglect and exploitation of individuals, to make sure staff recognize and report them, and to train staff and individuals in safety and protection.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(vi)(e), incidents and allegations of abuse. Each individual has the right to freedom from abuse, corporal punishment, unnecessary mechanical restraint and unnecessary medication (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(4)). Rights may not be limited for staff convenience, as a threat, as retribution or for discipline (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(7)). Employees and volunteers are mandated reporters (Justice Center, Mandated Reporters). A mandated reporter with reasonable cause to suspect a reportable incident reports immediately to the VPCR hotline at 1-855-373-2122 (24 hours; Relay: dial 711 and give the number). Reporting may be delayed only for safety or to call 911, and the report must be made within 24 hours of discovery. Deliberate inappropriate use of restraint is abuse or neglect. Inappropriate use of restraint is a significant incident (OPWDD Part 624/625 Handbook). [AGENCY NAME] trains all employees, volunteers and others as 14 NYCRR 633.8 requires. Self-protection training is provided to individuals identified by the program planning team. Detailed reporting, recording and investigation steps are in REC-05.

definitions.definition: Any act or failure to act that harms an individual physically, sexually or emotionally, including corporal punishment, verbal or psychological abuse, and deliberate inappropriate use of restraint, as defined by the Justice Center and OPWDD.
A failure to provide the supervision, care or services an individual needs, which results in or is likely to result in harm.
Taking or misusing an individual's money, property, benefits or labor, including theft, coercion, or use of the individual's cards or accounts.
A person required by law to report reasonable cause to suspect a reportable incident. This includes employees and volunteers of certified or operated facilities.
The team that develops and reviews the individual's plan of services, including the individual, family or representative of the individual's choice, and staff (REC-01).

procedures: 1. Before any employee, intern, volunteer, consultant or contractor has unsupervised contact with individuals, the Administrator confirms clearance under PER-04 and the Residence Manager gives a written statement of mandated reporter duties. The person signs it, and the Residence Manager files it in the personnel file.

2. Within 3 months of hire or the start of volunteering, and each year after, the Training Coordinator trains all employees, volunteers, consultants and contractors who work with individuals. The initial training covers human growth and development, characteristics of the individuals served, promoting positive relationships, abuse prevention, identification, reporting and processing, laws and policies on protection from abuse, incident reporting, and safety and security procedures including fire safety (14 NYCRR 633.8(b)(1)). The annual retraining covers positive relationships, abuse prevention and reporting, laws and policies, incident reporting, and safety and security including fire safety (14 NYCRR 633.8(b)(2)).

3. The Training Coordinator also trains staff on preventing and managing significant-risk body substance exposure, including HIV (14 NYCRR 633.8(a)(1)(viii)-(ix)). This training is part of orientation and is repeated each year (PER-02).

4. The Training Coordinator keeps a training tracking system that shows the type, frequency and amount of training each person has completed and when each person is next due (14 NYCRR 633.8(b)(3)). Records are kept current. Employees must be able to confirm on interview that they received the training. Anyone overdue is not scheduled for unsupervised shifts until current, and the Training Coordinator reports overdue training to the Administrator weekly.

5. The one-time training of board members at 14 NYCRR 633.8(b)(5) applies only to not-for-profit corporations. If [AGENCY NAME] is organized as a not-for-profit corporation, the Administrator ensures the board completes it and keeps the record. Otherwise this step is not applicable and the Administrator notes that.

6. Within 30 days of admission, and as the plan changes, the program planning team identifies individuals who should receive self-protection training (14 NYCRR 633.8(a)(2), (b)(4)). The Residence Manager arranges the training in a form the person understands, which may include how to recognize abuse, say no, get help and use the complaint process. The team reviews the need at least yearly. Each decision is recorded in the plan of services.

7. At admission, and after any change, the Residence Manager gives each individual the rights and conduct rules in the individual's primary language or with communication support at no cost (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(8), (a)(15)). This includes the right to be free of abuse and the contact numbers for complaints (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(12)). The VPCR hotline number and complaint contacts are posted where individuals and staff can see them.

8. Staff are advised of individuals' rights at hire and each year (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(6)). Staff may not limit or withhold a right for convenience, as a threat, as retribution or as discipline (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(7)). Any rights limitation follows RIT-02.

9. Restraint: staff use only the techniques allowed by BEH-02 and only when trained. Any use of restraint is reported to the Residence Manager the same shift. Deliberate inappropriate use is treated as abuse or neglect and reported to the VPCR. Inappropriate use is a significant incident and is reported under REC-05.

10. Exploitation prevention: staff may not borrow from, sell to, accept gifts or loans from, hold or use the money, cards, or accounts of, or enter into a financial arrangement with, an individual (PER-07). The Residence Manager reconciles personal funds under REC-02. Any suspected theft or misuse is reported as REC-05 requires.

11. Supervision and risk reduction: the Residence Manager and the Program Director make unannounced visits to each residence, including some at night or on weekends, and check on staff conduct, staffing and the safety of individuals (PER-08). The Administrator reviews results monthly.

12. Reporting: any person with reasonable cause to suspect abuse, neglect or another reportable incident calls the VPCR immediately, and always within 24 hours of discovery, then follows REC-05. Telling a supervisor does not satisfy the duty to report. Staff who are unsure whether to report should report.

13. No retaliation: no one may discipline, threaten or treat unfairly an employee, volunteer, individual or family member for a good-faith report or complaint (PER-03, APP-02). The Administrator investigates any claim of retaliation.

14. When an allegation is made, the Residence Manager immediately protects the individual, separates the accused where needed, and follows REC-05. After a Category 2 finding is reported through the Staff Exclusion List check, the Administrator reviews it as a factor in the employment decision (PER-04).
15. The Administrator and the Training Coordinator review reports and training results at least yearly, update this policy and training content, and record the changes through POL-02.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures that training is completed, that safeguards are in place, and that abuse allegations are investigated and acted on.
Delivers and tracks all training in 14 NYCRR 633.8, keeps the records current, and reports overdue training.
Supervises staff on site, gives rights information to individuals, protects individuals when allegations are made, and arranges self-protection training.
Identifies individuals who need self-protection training and reviews the need each year.
Prevent abuse, neglect and exploitation, respect rights, report suspicion to the VPCR immediately, and complete training on time.

documentation: Signed mandated reporter statements
Training records and tracking report for each person (type, frequency, amount, dates)
Self-protection training decisions and records in the plan of services
Rights and complaint information acknowledgements
Unannounced visit logs
Board training record, if [AGENCY NAME] is a not-for-profit corporation

policies.category: Administration of records, incidents/abuse and medication (686.6(a)(2)(vi))
policies.title: Medication Administration, Staff Certification and Self-Administration Training
policies.applies_to: All staff who store, handle or administer medication, the nurse, and individuals who take part in self-administration training
policies.purpose: To make sure medication, including vitamins, is given safely by qualified, currently certified staff under medical or nursing supervision, and that individuals are taught to manage their own medication when able.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(vi)(f), medication administration, the current certification status of community residence staff to administer medications, and the self-administration of medication training program for individuals. [AGENCY NAME] follows 14 NYCRR 633.17. Staff may administer medication only if they hold a job description with direct care duties, have completed an OPWDD-approved medication course and practicum, and have been certified or recertified within the past year (14 NYCRR 633.17(a)(14)). Medical or nursing supervision of medication staff is required. The program planning team evaluates each individual's ability to self-administer, with input from an RN, physician or physician assistant, no later than 3 months after admission and at least annually. The residence keeps a separate administration record for each person. An RN, physician, physician assistant or pharmacist reviews each person's medication regimen annually. Medication is stored under lock. [AGENCY NAME] tracks the current certification status of every staff member who administers medication.

definitions.definition: A direct care employee who has completed the OPWDD-approved course and practicum and is currently certified or recertified within the year.
A separate record for each individual showing the individual's name, each medication, dose and route, and the date, time and signature of the staff member who gave it.
Medication available without a prescription, including vitamins and herbal products.
The individual takes or manages medication independently or with the level of staff support the planning team decides.
A physician, physician assistant or nurse practitioner who prescribes or directs medication.

procedures: 1. Eligibility: before assigning medication duties, the Residence Manager and the nurse confirm that the employee has a job description with direct care duties and has successfully completed the OPWDD-approved course and practicum. The nurse records the certification date in the certification roster. No one gives medication until the nurse confirms certification in writing.

2. Certification tracking: the nurse and Training Coordinator maintain a roster of every medication-certified staff member showing certification and recertification dates and the due date of the next recertification. The roster is checked weekly and posted in the staff area. The Residence Manager does not schedule an employee whose certification has lapsed to give medication. A lapsed employee does not administer until recertified.

3. Recertification: the Training Coordinator schedules recertification so that it is completed within the year, and the nurse verifies completion and updates the roster. Staff who do not recertify on time lose medication duties until they do.

4. Supervision: the RN or physician provides medical or nursing supervision of medication staff (HS-02). The nurse observes medication passes at least [FREQUENCY, e.g., quarterly] and documents results and any coaching. Medication problems found are corrected and retrained.

5. Orders: medication is given only from a written practitioner order and a pharmacy-labeled container. The staff member checks the person, medication, dose, route and time against the order each time. Staff do not change a dose or time without a new written order.

6. Administration record: the staff member signs the person's own record at the time the medication is given, showing name, medication, dose, route, date and time. No pre-charting, no documenting for another person's pass, and no blank spaces. If a dose is refused or missed, the staff member records that with the reason and follows the nurse's instructions.

7. Storage: all medication is kept locked. In supervised residences, controlled substances are double-locked. In supportive residences, locked storage and any approved arrangement for the individual are followed as set by the nurse. Medication kept in a food refrigerator is placed in a separate locked container. Keys are held only by on-duty certified staff.

8. Counts: staff count controlled substances at each shift change, and two staff sign the count book. A discrepancy is reported to the Residence Manager and nurse immediately and followed under REC-05 if loss or theft is suspected.

9. OTC medication: staff give OTC medication only under written practitioner approval that is renewed at least annually. Without practitioner direction, OTC medication may be given for no more than 2 days. If symptoms continue after 2 days, the staff member contacts the practitioner or nurse.

10. Adverse reaction: on any significant adverse reaction, staff suspend the medication and tell the practitioner immediately. If the reaction is serious or life-threatening, they call 911 and follow EMR-01. They notify the nurse and Residence Manager and document the event.

11. Medication errors: staff report any error, such as wrong person, dose, route, time or omission, to the nurse or practitioner immediately for direction, document it, and give an incident report to the Residence Manager the same shift. The nurse reviews errors each month for patterns. An error that results in harm or fits a reportable category goes through REC-05.

12. Annual regimen review: an RN, physician, physician assistant or pharmacist reviews each individual's complete medication regimen at least annually and documents the review. The nurse tracks due dates and shares recommendations with the practitioner.

13. Self-administration evaluation: no later than 3 months after admission, the program planning team evaluates the individual's ability to self-administer, with input from an RN, physician or physician assistant. The individual takes part in the evaluation. The team records the result and the support level in the plan of services (REC-01).

14. Self-administration training: when the team finds the individual can learn, the nurse and the team write a training program with steps, teaching methods and staff responsibilities, and staff teach it. Progress is recorded at least monthly. Individuals who self-administer keep medication in a locked space they can reach, and staff check administration as the plan directs.
15. Annual review: the program planning team reviews each individual's self-administration status and training at least annually, and sooner when health or abilities change. The review is recorded.

16. Disposal: discontinued, expired and refused medication is removed from active storage and disposed of under the nurse-approved written procedure that follows 14 NYCRR 633.17. Two staff witness and sign each disposal, and controlled substances are handled with the nurse. Medication is never given to another person.

17. Staff training: orientation includes medication safety and the rights of the individual to be free from unnecessary medication (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(4); 14 NYCRR 633.8). Medication is never used as discipline, for staff convenience or as a substitute for positive behavior supports (BEH-01).
18. The Administrator reviews the certification roster, error trends and audit results each quarter and reports them for quality review (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures nursing and medical supervision, adequate trained staff and a working certification-tracking system.
Supervises medication staff, maintains the certification roster, reviews errors, coordinates regimen reviews and self-administration evaluations and approves storage and disposal procedures.
Assigns medication duties only to currently certified staff, checks records and storage, and reports errors.
Give medication accurately, document each dose, safeguard storage and report errors and reactions immediately.
Evaluates and reviews self-administration ability and approves training programs.
Prescribes and approves orders and OTC use, and reviews the regimen when asked.

documentation: Medication certification roster with certification and recertification dates
Course and practicum completion records
Separate administration record for each individual
Controlled substance count records
OTC medication approvals (renewed at least annually)
Medication error and adverse reaction reports
Annual medication regimen review record
Self-administration evaluation, training program, progress notes and annual review
Medication disposal records
Nurse observation and supervision notes

policies.category: Administration of records, incidents/abuse and medication (686.6(a)(2)(vi))
policies.title: Individual Records, Retention and Access
policies.applies_to: All staff who create, use, store or release individuals' records, and all individuals and representatives who ask to see them
policies.purpose: To make sure a complete, accurate record is kept for each individual, retained for the required period, protected, and made available to the individual as the law requires.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(vi)(c), confidentiality and protection of individuals' records, as it applies to the content, retention, access and protection of the record. [AGENCY NAME] keeps one record for each individual. Individuals may request access in writing (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(10)). Requests for clinical record access follow Mental Hygiene Law 33.16. A denial may be reviewed by the OPWDD Clinical Record Access Review Committee. Individuals also have the right of access that 45 CFR 164.524 gives, to the extent it applies. Personal funds records are retained for 4 years. For all other records the Compliance Officer is confirming the retention period required by OPWDD and OMIG. Until that is confirmed in writing, [AGENCY NAME]'s own standard is to retain all other records for at least 6 years after the individual leaves the residence or the record is last used, whichever is later. Service documentation must match the rate code billed. OMIG disallows a claim when the documentation does not match the rate code (OMIG Audit Protocol). The Compliance Officer will confirm in writing whether additional Part 686 recordkeeping requirements apply before they are relied on. Confidentiality safeguards are in REC-03.

definitions.definition: All documents, paper or electronic, that [AGENCY NAME] keeps about one individual, including admission, plan, service, health, rights and funds information.
The part of the record containing the individual's evaluations, diagnosis, treatment, health and service information, as covered by Mental Hygiene Law 33.16.
A written instruction not to destroy records because of an audit, investigation, appeal or lawsuit.
A person legally authorized to act for the individual, such as a health care proxy agent or guardian (DEC-02).

procedures: 1. Contents: the Residence Manager makes sure each individual's record contains: the referral and admission review and approval documents (ADM-01, ADM-02); signed rights, conduct rules and charges disclosure acknowledgements (ADM-03, RIT-01); the plan of services with every review, daily notes and service documentation (REC-01); health records, nursing notes, medication administration records and the self-administration evaluation (REC-07, HS-02); rights modifications and due process records (RIT-02); behavior support plans, if any (BEH-01); consent and health care proxy documents (DEC-02); the individual protective oversight assessment (IRA-02); the personal funds ledger and receipts (REC-02); authorizations and the disclosure log (REC-03); and discharge records (DIS-02).
2. Incident and investigation files are kept in a separate secure file. The record shows only what is needed for care, with a cross-reference to the incident file (REC-05).

3. Entries: staff write entries at the time of service or as soon after as possible, in permanent ink or the approved electronic system. Each entry has the date, time, staff signature and title. Corrections are made by a single line through the error with initials and date. Late entries are labeled as late. Entries must be factual and must not be altered or backdated.

4. Billing match: staff document each service so the note supports the rate code and service billed (GOV-03). The Compliance Officer samples notes each month against billing. Gaps are corrected before billing is submitted, or the claim is held (OMIG Audit Protocol).

5. Storage: active records are kept in the locked record area at [ADDRESS] or on the approved secure system. Records are never left unattended in common areas. Records move between the residence and office only in a closed container.
6. Access by staff: staff may see a record only as REC-03 permits. The Residence Manager keeps a list of staff approved for access.

7. Request for access: an individual or authorized representative may ask to see or get a copy of the record. Staff help the person put the request in writing (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(10)), including with communication support, and give the request to the Privacy Officer the same day. The Privacy Officer records the date received.

8. Response: the Privacy Officer responds to each written request within the shortest timeframe required by Mental Hygiene Law 33.16 or 45 CFR 164.524, and in no case later than 30 days. The Privacy Officer confirms the requester's identity and authority. The individual may inspect the record with a staff member present to explain it, or may receive copies. Any fee is limited to what the law allows. No one is refused access because of inability to pay.

9. Denial: if part of a request is denied, the Privacy Officer gives the person a written notice that states the reason, the part denied and the right to ask for review by the OPWDD Clinical Record Access Review Committee (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(10)). The Privacy Officer helps the person file the request for review and gives the committee what it asks for. A copy of the notice is kept in the record.

10. Corrections: an individual may ask in writing to add a statement or correction to the record. The Privacy Officer reviews it with the clinical staff. The statement is added and the original is not removed.

11. Retention: personal funds records are kept for 4 years. All other records are kept at least 6 years, under [AGENCY NAME]'s standard described above, until the Compliance Officer confirms the OPWDD and OMIG period in writing. If that period is longer, the longer period applies. Personnel and training records are kept under PER-06.

12. Legal hold: the Administrator issues a written legal hold when an audit, investigation, appeal or lawsuit is pending or reasonably expected. Records under a hold are not destroyed until the Administrator lifts the hold in writing.

13. Discharge and transfer: when an individual leaves, the Residence Manager closes the record, sends the information needed for continued care with the individual's authorization (DIS-02, REC-03), and retains the original for the retention period.

14. Destruction: after the retention period ends and no hold applies, the Administrator approves destruction in writing. Paper is shredded and electronic records are securely deleted. The Residence Manager logs the date, method and records destroyed.
15. Electronic records are backed up at least daily and are encrypted. Access is by unique log-in. The Privacy Officer checks backup and recovery quarterly.
16. Closure or transfer of the agency: the Administrator makes a written plan for custody of all records, tells OPWDD, and keeps records available for the retention period.
17. The Compliance Officer audits a sample of records each quarter for completeness, timeliness, signatures and billing match. The results go to the Administrator and the quality review (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures that systems, storage and staff are in place, approves destruction, and issues legal holds.
Handles access requests and denials, helps individuals request committee review, and enforces safeguards.
Confirms retention periods and any Part 686 recordkeeping requirements, and audits records and billing match.
Keeps each record complete and current, controls the on-site record area, and assists individuals with requests.
Document accurately and on time, protect records, and forward access requests the same day.

documentation: Complete individual record with the contents listed in step 1
Written access requests, response dates, and denial notices
Requests for review by the OPWDD Clinical Record Access Review Committee
Record audit reports
Legal hold notices
Record destruction log
Written confirmation of retention periods from the Compliance Officer
Records custody plan

policies.title: Medical Emergencies and Change of Condition
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, supervisors, substitutes, nursing staff, the Program Director and any volunteer or contractor working in the residence, and every individual receiving services in the IRA.
policies.purpose: To make sure every individual receives immediate, competent and dignified response to a medical emergency or a change in health condition, and that staff know what to do and are trained and re-familiarized with these actions.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(vii), which requires written policies and procedures on medical emergencies, other potential emergencies, evacuation procedures that meet the special needs of persons with developmental disabilities, and disasters, the necessary staff actions in these situations, and the means to familiarize staff with them. This policy covers medical emergencies and other potential emergencies involving an individual's health, and the staff actions and staff familiarization that go with them. EMR-02 covers fire, evacuation and disasters, and IRA-04 covers the facility evacuation plan. [AGENCY NAME] will call 911 without delay whenever an individual's life or health may be in immediate danger. Staff do not wait for a supervisor or nurse approval before calling 911. Staff provide first aid and CPR only within their training and certification. A staff member stays with the individual until emergency responders take over, and then goes with the individual or arranges for another trained staff member to do so. If a significant adverse reaction to a medication occurs, staff suspend the medication and notify the prescribing or treating practitioner immediately, as required by 14 NYCRR 633.17 (C16). A health care proxy and any do-not-resuscitate order are honored and handled under the OPWDD regulations that govern them and DEC-02. Treatment beyond first aid by a physician, dentist, physician assistant or nurse practitioner is at least a minor notable occurrence and is reported under REC-05. Staff are familiarized with these actions at orientation, annually and through practice scenarios.

definitions.definition: A sudden illness, injury or change in condition that threatens life, limb or function, or that a reasonable person would believe needs immediate emergency medical care (for example unresponsiveness, difficulty breathing, choking, a seizure that does not stop as set out in the individual's protocol, chest pain, uncontrolled bleeding, suspected stroke, severe allergic reaction, serious fall or head injury).

Any noticeable difference from the individual's usual physical, behavioral, mental or functional status, such as new pain, fever, reduced eating or drinking, new confusion, new skin problem or loss of mobility, even if it is not an emergency.
An unexpected or harmful response to a medication that threatens health or function, such as rash with swelling, breathing difficulty, severe vomiting, over-sedation or a sudden change in alertness.

A current one-to-two page summary for each individual with name, photo, diagnoses, allergies, medications, practitioners, health care proxy and DNR status, communication needs, guardian or correspondent contacts and insurance information.

procedures: Any staff member who sees or suspects a medical emergency calls 911 immediately, gives the address of [ADDRESS], the individual's name, what happened and the callback number [PHONE], and follows the dispatcher's instructions.

While waiting for responders, staff trained in first aid and CPR provide it within their training. Untrained staff stay with the individual, keep the person safe and comfortable, and send another staff member to meet responders at the door.

Staff keep the other individuals in the home supervised and calm, and move them away from the emergency when needed. A second staff member or the on-call supervisor is called in if supervision cannot be maintained.

Staff hand the emergency information packet and current medication administration record to responders. The packet is kept in a marked, known location and a copy goes in the staff go-bag for every outing.

Staff tell responders about any health care proxy or do-not-resuscitate order on file and show the physician-signed order. They follow the individual's valid orders and the OPWDD regulations that govern them, as set out in DEC-02.

A staff member who knows the individual goes with the person to the hospital or arranges for the next available trained staff member to go. Staff stay to help with communication, comfort, medication and history until a family member, health care proxy or other staff member takes over, or the individual is discharged or admitted.

Staff notify the agency nurse and the supervisor on call right away, and the Program Director as soon as the situation is safe. The nurse gives clinical direction and follows the individual through treatment.

Staff notify the individual's family, guardian, health care proxy or other correspondent as soon as possible, unless the individual has said he or she does not want this or the law does not allow it. The notice is documented with the time and the name of the person reached.

If the individual had a significant adverse medication reaction, staff suspend the medication, tell the practitioner immediately, follow the practitioner's directions, record the event on the medication record and tell the nurse, as required by 14 NYCRR 633.17.

For a change of condition that is not an emergency, staff tell the nurse or supervisor on the same shift, record observations (what, when, vital signs if trained, eating, drinking, behavior) and follow the nurse's direction, including a call to the practitioner. The nurse documents the follow-up.

Every medical emergency, hospital transfer and treatment beyond first aid by a physician, dentist, physician assistant or nurse practitioner is reported and recorded under REC-05. The supervisor decides with the Program Director whether the event is a minor notable occurrence, a reportable incident or a serious notable occurrence, and makes the required reports on time.

If the event may involve abuse, neglect or a possible criminal act, the person involved is protected, evidence is kept, and REC-06 and REC-05 are followed, including reports to the Justice Center and OPWDD.

After the event, the Program Director and nurse review the response within 7 days, confirm that the individual's plan, protocols, medication orders and the emergency information packet are updated, and record corrective actions.

Staff are familiarized with this policy before working alone, at orientation (PER-02), annually, and when the policy or an individual's needs change. Staff sign an acknowledgment, and the Program Director keeps the sign-in sheet.

At least twice a year the nurse or Program Director runs a practice scenario on each shift (for example a choking event or a seizure that does not stop), debriefs staff and records what was learned. Emergency numbers, the address and the location of the emergency information packet and first aid kit are posted where staff can see them.

responsibilities.duty: Call 911 for a medical emergency, give first aid and CPR within training, stay with the individual, hand over the emergency packet, notify the nurse and supervisor, and document.
Support staff during the emergency, make notifications, ensure supervision of the other individuals, classify and report the event under REC-05, and keep emergency packets current.
Give clinical direction, coordinate with practitioners, follow up on change of condition and medication reactions, and help train staff.
Make sure staff are familiarized with this policy, review each emergency, make sure required reports are made and ensure corrective action.

documentation: Incident or notable occurrence report for every emergency and any treatment beyond first aid (REC-05).
Progress note for the individual, with times, observations, actions and who was notified.
Medication administration record entry and practitioner contact record for any adverse reaction.
Current emergency information packet for each individual, with date of last review.
Staff acknowledgment forms, orientation records and practice scenario debrief records.
Post-event review record with corrective actions.

policies.title: Emergency Preparedness, Disasters, Fire Drills and Evacuation
policies.applies_to: All staff, substitutes, volunteers, the Program Director, nursing staff and every individual in the IRA, including visitors present during a drill or emergency.
policies.purpose: To protect individuals during fires, evacuations, utility failures, severe weather and other disasters by using evacuation procedures that fit each person's needs, by testing them through drills, and by keeping life safety equipment in working order.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(vii), which covers other potential emergencies, evacuation procedures to meet the special needs of persons with developmental disabilities, disasters, the necessary staff actions, and the means to familiarize staff. It also supplies the emergencies and disasters content (item (iii)) of the written policy and procedure manual required by 14 NYCRR 686.6(b)(3)(i)-(viii). [AGENCY NAME] writes evacuation procedures that meet the special needs of each individual, and the evacuation ability of each person is assessed and recorded. If occupants cannot evacuate in 3 minutes or less, the additional requirements of 14 NYCRR 635-7.2(a)(1)(iii) apply, as stated in 14 NYCRR 686.16 (C3). The residence meets the building code and Life Safety Code requirements that 14 NYCRR 686.16 incorporates for its size: for 8 or fewer persons, the 635-7.1(h)(1)(ii) building code (in New York City, 635-7.1(i)(1)(ii)) and 635-7.4(b)(3); for 9 or more persons, 635-7.1, 635-7.2 and 635-7.3. For a residence with 9 or more beds, all heat and smoke-detecting alarm devices are tested quarterly and documented (635-7.3(e)(i)(1)). For a residence with 8 or fewer beds, fire alarms must be audible in sleeping areas with doors closed. Evacuation and fire drills are held at no less than the minimum frequencies in OPWDD ADM #2012-02, and are varied only for the reasons the ADM allows, without lowering the minimum number of full evacuation drills. If the home is certified under the Health Care chapters of the Life Safety Code, defend-in-place is not used for non-fire evacuations. Facility evacuation planning, staff and resident training and evaluation are further described in IRA-04.

definitions.definition: A documented assessment of how quickly and with what help each individual can leave the residence to a point of safety, including mobility, hearing, vision, response to alarms, behavior in an emergency and need for staff assistance.
A practice exit from the residence to a point of safety under conditions that simulate an emergency. Under OPWDD ADM #2012-02 these terms are generally procedurally synonymous.

A strategy in which occupants stay in a protected area rather than leave the building. It is not permitted for non-fire evacuations in homes certified under the Health Care chapters of the Life Safety Code.

An event that threatens the safety of individuals or disrupts the home, such as severe weather, flood, extended power or heat loss, water failure, gas leak, loss of the building, community-wide emergency or public health emergency.
A pre-designated location outside the residence where individuals gather after evacuation, and a designated alternate site if the home cannot be re-entered.

procedures: Before admission and at least annually, the Program Director and nurse assess each individual's evacuation ability (including whether the person can leave in 3 minutes or less), communication and sensory needs, and record it in the individual's plan. Any person who cannot evacuate in 3 minutes or less is identified and the Program Director applies the additional requirements of 635-7.2(a)(1)(iii).

The Program Director writes the facility evacuation plan with floor plan, exit routes, alternate routes, point of safety, alternate shelter [ALTERNATE SHELTER LOCATION], assignment of staff roles, individual assistance needs and emergency contacts. It is posted and reviewed at least annually and after any drill failure, incident or change in occupants. See IRA-04.

For a residence with 8 or fewer beds, each individual's ISP includes a current fire-evacuation evaluation, which is updated when the person's needs change and reviewed at least annually. The Program Director confirms this at each plan review.

The Program Director sets the drill schedule so that the minimum number and spacing of drills in OPWDD ADM #2012-02 is met: [DRILL MINIMUMS PER OPWDD ADM #2012-02 — Administrator to insert the frequency from the current ADM text before adoption]. Drills vary by time of day, shift and exit route, but the minimum number of full evacuation drills is always met.

At each drill, staff sound the alarm, evacuate every individual with the help each needs, account for everyone at the point of safety, record time to evacuate and note problems. Individuals are taught the drill in language and format they understand.

The supervisor completes the drill record the same day, including date, time, shift, staff present, individuals evacuated, evacuation time, the individuals who needed assistance, problems and corrective action. The Program Director reviews each record within 7 days.

If a drill shows that any individual cannot evacuate safely or within the time the plan assumes, the Program Director takes corrective action immediately (more staff, a different route, equipment, training) and repeats a drill to confirm the fix.

For a residence with 9 or more beds, the Program Director makes sure all heat and smoke-detecting alarm devices are tested quarterly and documented as required by 635-7.3(e)(i)(1). All residences also have the alarm system maintained under the code tier that applies.

For a residence with 8 or fewer beds, the Program Director or maintenance designee checks at least quarterly, and whenever bedroom doors or alarms change, that fire alarms are audible in all sleeping areas with doors closed, and records the check. Any alarm that is not audible is corrected before the next shift and staffing is adjusted until it is fixed.

Maintenance staff inspect fire extinguishers, exits, emergency lighting, smoke and heat alarms and sprinklers (if present) on the schedule required by the applicable code, keep exits clear and unlocked in a way that allows exit, and record defects and repairs.

In a non-fire emergency evacuation (for example a gas leak or flood), staff evacuate and do not shelter in place if the home is certified under the Health Care chapters of the Life Safety Code. Otherwise the supervisor decides with the Program Director whether to evacuate or shelter, based on the hazard.

For a disaster (severe weather, power loss, water loss, extreme heat or cold, public health emergency), staff follow the disaster section of the plan: call 911 when needed, move individuals to a safe area, check on individuals' medications, oxygen and medical equipment, keep a count, and contact the Program Director immediately. The Program Director decides on temporary relocation and notifies OPWDD, families and correspondents.

When an evacuation or disaster occurs, the Program Director makes sure each individual's medication, emergency packet, communication supports, mobility aids and personal items go with the person, and that staffing at the shelter site meets the individuals' protective oversight needs.
Every real emergency, evacuation, alarm activation, fire or injury is reported and recorded under REC-05, and a post-event review is completed within 7 days.

Staff are trained on this policy and the evacuation plan before working alone, and are retrained annually and when the plan changes. Training on fire safety is part of PER-02 and includes safety and security procedures. Sign-in sheets are kept.
The Program Director reviews drill results, alarm tests, plan changes and incidents at least quarterly and brings trends to the quality improvement review under GOV-02.

responsibilities.duty: Know the evacuation plan and each individual's assistance needs, take part in drills, evacuate and account for everyone, and report defects.
Lead drills and real evacuations, complete drill records, check alarms and exits and report problems to the Program Director.
Write and review the evacuation plan, assess evacuation ability, ensure drill minimums under ADM #2012-02 are met, correct failures, and make required reports.
Advise on medical equipment, mobility and medication needs during evacuation and disasters.
Test and maintain alarms, extinguishers, exits and lighting, and keep records.

documentation: Facility evacuation plan with review dates.
Individual evacuation ability assessments and, for 8 or fewer beds, the current fire-evacuation evaluation in each ISP.
Drill records with date, shift, time, participants, evacuation time and corrective action.
Quarterly alarm test records (9 or more beds) and audibility checks (8 or fewer beds).
Fire equipment inspection and repair logs.
Staff training records and sign-in sheets.
Incident reports and post-event reviews.

policies.title: Death of an Individual
policies.applies_to: All staff, supervisors, nursing staff, the Program Director, the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) or designee, and any contractor or volunteer who learns of the death of an individual receiving services.
policies.purpose: To make sure that the death of any individual is handled with dignity and respect for the individual's wishes and family, is reported immediately to the right authorities, and is reviewed so that lessons are learned.
policies.policy: Every death of an individual who resides in an OPWDD-certified residence is a serious notable occurrence, regardless of cause (14 NYCRR 624.4). [AGENCY NAME] reports every death immediately to the CEO or designee and to OPWDD under 14 NYCRR 624.5. If the death is also a reportable incident (for example, suspected abuse or neglect), it is reported both ways: to the Justice Center Vulnerable Persons' Central Register at 1-855-373-2122 and to OPWDD (C35). All employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors must report. The agency notifies the individual's family or correspondent as required by Jonathan's Law and in line with the individual's wishes or health care proxy, within the timeframes stated in that law and in 14 NYCRR 624.5. The agency updates OPWDD at least monthly until the matter is closed. Staff preserve the scene and records, and cooperate fully with emergency responders, the medical examiner or coroner when involved, and any investigation. Staff treat the individual and the people in the home with dignity, and the agency supports housemates, staff and the family. The death is reviewed under GOV-02.

definitions.definition: Under 14 NYCRR 624.4, the death of any person receiving services regardless of cause, including every death of a resident of an OPWDD-certified residence, and sensitive situations as defined by agency policy.
An incident that must be reported to the Justice Center VPCR and OPWDD, such as abuse, neglect or a significant incident. A death can be both a serious notable occurrence and a reportable incident.
A family member, guardian, health care proxy, advocate or other person who the individual has chosen or the law identifies as entitled to be told about the individual's care.
The OPWDD incident reporting and management application used to report, update and close incidents and serious notable occurrences.

procedures: Any staff member who finds an individual unresponsive or not breathing calls 911 immediately and starts CPR if trained and if no valid DNR order or other lawful direction prevents it (see EMR-01 and DEC-02), and continues until responders take over.
The staff member informs the supervisor on duty at once. The supervisor calls the nurse on call and the Program Director immediately.

When death is confirmed or declared, staff keep the scene as undisturbed as possible, except for care needed by responders, and do not remove or discard medications, equipment, food, linens or documents related to the death.

The supervisor ensures other individuals in the home are told in a caring way that fits their understanding, supervised, supported and offered continued routines. Staff note any person who is distressed and tell the nurse and Program Director.
The Program Director or designee notifies the CEO or designee immediately and reports the death to OPWDD immediately through IRMA or the OPWDD reporting process, as required by 14 NYCRR 624.5.

If there is any suspicion of abuse, neglect, exploitation, a possible criminal act or an unexplained death, the Program Director also reports at once to the Justice Center VPCR at 1-855-373-2122 and records the report both ways, as required by 14 NYCRR 624.4 and C35. Staff follow REC-06.

The Program Director or designee notifies the individual's family, guardian, health care proxy or other correspondent as soon as possible, and in any case within the timeframes of Jonathan's Law and 14 NYCRR 624.5, in line with the individual's expressed wishes and with respect for the family's needs. The call is made by a person with authority, in person or by phone, and not by text or email. The notification is recorded with date, time and the name of the person notified.

The Program Director arranges for release of the body in line with the law and the family's or health care proxy's wishes. Where the medical examiner or coroner takes jurisdiction, staff cooperate and give the health information requested.

Staff identify and secure the individual's personal property, funds, medications, medical equipment and records. The Program Director inventories them with a second staff member, records the inventory, and releases property only to the legally authorized person under REC-02 and REC-08. Controlled substances and other medications are handled under REC-07.

The Program Director notifies the individual's service coordinator and care manager, and gives notice required by OPWDD for the bed to be reported as vacant, and the billing office stops service claims from the date of death under GOV-03.

The nurse and Program Director pull together the individual's recent health history, medication records, incident reports, plans and protocols, so that the records are complete for any review or investigation. No record is changed, backdated or removed. Late entries are clearly marked as late.
The Program Director updates IRMA at least monthly until closure and makes sure all questions from OPWDD, the Justice Center, the medical examiner or others are answered on time.

The agency supports housemates and staff after the death: grief counseling resources, time to talk, and options to take part in memorial or funeral events when the family agrees. Staff supervisors check on each staff member who was present.

The agency's mortality review under GOV-02 starts within the timeframe set in that policy. The review looks at care, supervision, protocols, emergency response and any recommendations, and the Program Director records corrective actions and tracks them to completion.
The Program Director keeps the record of the death, reports, notifications, inventory and review in the individual's closed record and in the incident file, and keeps them for the period in REC-08.

responsibilities.duty: Call 911, give CPR where appropriate, notify the supervisor, preserve the scene and report as a mandated reporter.
Call the nurse and Program Director, support other individuals, preserve records and property and document events.
Make immediate reports to the CEO or designee, OPWDD and (when also reportable) the Justice Center, notify correspondents, update IRMA monthly and lead the post-death review.
Receive the immediate notice, make sure reports are filed and oversee investigation and review.
Provide the health record, assist with the medical examiner and family, and take part in mortality review.

documentation: IRMA report and monthly updates until closure.
Justice Center VPCR report and number if the death is also a reportable incident.
Notification log for family, guardian, health care proxy, service coordinator and others.
Incident report, staff statements and timeline.
Property, funds and medication inventory and release forms.
Mortality review report and corrective action tracking.
Closed individual record.

policies.title: Health and Safety Program
policies.applies_to: All staff, supervisors, substitutes, volunteers, contractors, the Program Director and every individual in the IRA.
policies.purpose: To give every individual a safe, sanitary, hazard-free home and to protect staff, by finding, reporting and correcting hazards, managing hazardous materials and smoking, training staff and reviewing the program regularly.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(viii) (health and safety issues). It also supplies the health and safety content (item (iv)) of the written policy and procedure manual required by 14 NYCRR 686.6(b)(3)(i)-(viii). Individuals have the right to a safe and sanitary environment (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(4)), and [AGENCY NAME] will not limit this or other rights for staff convenience, as a threat, as retribution or for discipline (633.4(a)(7)). The residence meets the building code, Life Safety Code and environmental requirements in 14 NYCRR 635-7 that apply to it (C10). The agency runs a written health and safety program that includes regular safety inspections, hazard reporting and correction, safe storage and use of chemicals and hazardous materials, a smoking policy that follows the OPWDD smoking regulation, safe water temperature and food handling, pest control, protection against infectious disease and blood-borne pathogen exposure (29 CFR 1910.1030), and training of all staff on health and safety. Staff are advised of individuals' rights and of this policy at orientation (633.4(a)(6)). The program is reviewed after incidents and in quality improvement under GOV-02.

definitions.definition: Any condition, object or practice that can cause injury, illness, fire or property damage, such as a broken stair, blocked exit, spill, unsafe cord, unsecured chemical or hot water above the safe limit.
Cleaning products, disinfectants, pesticides, flammable liquids, oxygen, sharps, biohazard waste or any substance that can cause harm if misused, swallowed, inhaled or touched.
Contact with blood or other body fluids in a way that can pass infection, such as a needle stick or splash to eyes or mouth, handled under HS-04 and the bloodborne pathogens rules.
A documented walk-through of the home, grounds and vehicle using a checklist.

procedures: The Program Director names a health and safety lead for the residence ([HEALTH AND SAFETY LEAD NAME]) and sets a written schedule for monthly home safety inspections and a more detailed annual review with the nurse.

At each monthly inspection the lead walks the whole home and grounds with a checklist covering exits and egress, smoke and heat alarms, extinguishers, lighting, stairs and railings, floors, electrical cords and outlets, heating and cooling, water temperature, kitchen, bathrooms, bedrooms, storage areas, medication storage, hazardous materials, pest signs, outdoor areas, and the vehicle if it is used by the home. The lead signs and dates the checklist.

Any staff member who sees a hazard reports it right away to the supervisor, makes the area safe if this can be done safely (for example, a wet floor sign or removing an object), and records it in the hazard log. Staff do not wait for the monthly inspection.

The supervisor ranks the hazard: an immediate danger is fixed or the area is closed on the same shift, and individuals are moved if necessary. Other hazards are assigned to a named person with a due date no later than 14 days (shorter if the risk is higher). The Program Director follows each item to closure and records the date fixed.

Hazardous materials are kept in original or properly labeled containers, in locked or inaccessible storage when an individual may not use them safely, away from food and medications. Safety data sheets are kept in the home and staff are trained to read them. Staff never mix cleaning products.

Water temperature at taps and showers used by individuals is checked at least monthly and after any plumbing work, and kept within a safe range recorded in the checklist. Individuals who cannot judge water temperature safely have supports in their plan.

Smoking: [AGENCY NAME] follows the OPWDD smoking regulation. Smoking is not allowed inside the residence or in agency vehicles. Any permitted smoking is only in a designated outdoor area away from entrances, windows and combustible materials. Individuals who smoke have their smoking supports and any safety limits written in their plan and reviewed by the planning team, with attention to the individual's rights. Staff do not smoke in view of individuals while on duty. Oxygen use and fire risks are covered in each individual's plan.

Staff follow standard precautions and the bloodborne pathogens rules (29 CFR 1910.1030): gloves and personal protective equipment are available in the home, sharps and biohazard waste are disposed of safely, and exposure is reported at once to the supervisor and nurse. The agency offers hepatitis B vaccine to staff at risk and keeps an exposure control plan. See HS-04 and PER-05.

All staff, including substitutes, are trained on health and safety at orientation and every year, including fire and safety and security procedures, hazard reporting, hazardous materials, infection control, emergency response, safe lifting and handling, and the rights of individuals to a safe and sanitary environment. Training is recorded under PER-02.

The Program Director makes sure the home meets the code requirements of 14 NYCRR 635-7 that apply to its size and tracks fire, building and sanitation inspections and corrections (see HS-07 and EMR-02).

Individuals are taught, in ways that suit them, how to stay safe at home and in the community, including fire safety, safe use of appliances, stranger safety and how to ask for help. This is built into their plan.
Each individual may report a safety concern, and the concern is handled under APP-02 without reprisal. Staff may raise safety concerns without threat of job loss under PER-03.
After any incident, injury, near miss, illness cluster or failed inspection, the Program Director reviews the health and safety program within 7 days, records changes, and informs staff.

At least quarterly, the Program Director summarizes hazards found, time to correct, injuries, incidents and drill results and brings the summary to quality improvement review under GOV-02. The plan is updated at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Spot and report hazards, keep the home clean and safe, follow safety procedures and use protective equipment.
Complete monthly inspections, run the hazard log, assign and track corrections.
Own the health and safety program, make sure hazards are fixed, ensure staff training and review the program after incidents.
Advise on infection control, medical equipment, oxygen and individual health and safety needs.
Give the resources needed to fix hazards and receive quarterly summaries.

documentation: Monthly home safety inspection checklists.
Hazard log with dates reported and corrected.
Water temperature, pest control and maintenance records.
Safety data sheets and hazardous material inventory.
Staff health and safety training records.
Individual safety and smoking supports in the plan.
Post-incident program review notes and quarterly summaries.

policies.title: Nursing Oversight and Health Care Coordination
policies.applies_to: Agency nurses, the Program Director, supervisors, direct support staff who administer medications or support health care, and every individual in the IRA.
policies.purpose: To make sure each individual's health needs are assessed, that medication-administering staff are supervised by a nurse or physician, and that routine and specialty care and practitioner orders are coordinated and followed.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(viii) (health and safety issues) as it relates to health care. Medical or nursing supervision of staff who administer medication is required (14 NYCRR 633.17(a)(15)), and [AGENCY NAME] provides it through a licensed nurse and, where needed, a physician. Only staff who hold a job description with direct care duties, have completed an OPWDD-approved medication course and practicum, and have been certified or recertified within the year administer medications (633.17(a)(14)(iii)(c)); see REC-07. A registered nurse, physician, physician assistant or pharmacist reviews each individual's medication regimen at least annually (633.17(a)(18)). A program planning team evaluates each individual's ability to self-administer medication, with input from an RN, physician or PA, no later than 3 months after admission and at least annually (633.17(a)(16)). The agency sets nursing hours and nursing duties from the health needs of the individuals served. The required nursing hours have not been verified by the agency's regional office, so the Program Director confirms the nursing plan with the OPWDD regional office before admission and when needs change. Individuals choose their own physician and dentist, and staff coordinate routine and specialty care and follow up on all practitioner orders.

definitions.definition: Supervision by a licensed nurse of medication administration, health monitoring, health-related training of staff and coordination of health care.
A physician, dentist, physician assistant or nurse practitioner who is licensed to diagnose and treat and who gives orders.
An annual review of all of an individual's medications, including over-the-counter products and vitamins, by an RN, physician, PA or pharmacist.
The individual, family or correspondents, clinical staff, direct support staff and others who make decisions about the individual's plan.

procedures: The Program Director names a licensed nurse ([AGENCY NURSE NAME]) as the nursing supervisor for the residence and records the nurse's license number, hours and on-call arrangements. The nurse's hours are set from the health needs of the individuals and the number of staff who give medication, and the Program Director confirms the plan with the OPWDD regional office.

Before admission and after any significant health change, the nurse completes a health assessment of the individual, reviews the medical history, medications, allergies, diet, mobility, seizure and choking risks, immunizations and screening, and writes health care instructions for staff. The results go into the plan (REC-01).

Within 30 days of admission, the nurse and Program Director make sure the individual has chosen or been helped to choose a primary physician and dentist, that records are requested, and that the individual and correspondents know who they are.

The nurse supervises medication administration: observes staff medication passes at least [NURSING OBSERVATION FREQUENCY] and reviews medication records at least monthly, checking the separate administration record for each person (name, medication, dose, route, date, time and staff signature).

The nurse confirms before each staff member gives medications that the person has an OPWDD-approved course and practicum on file and a current certification or recertification within the past year, and tells the Program Director if any is lapsed. A lapsed staff member does not give medication until recertified. See REC-07.

The nurse arranges or performs an annual medication regimen review for each individual by an RN, physician, PA or pharmacist, records the findings and sends recommendations to the prescriber. The nurse follows up until the prescriber responds.

No later than 3 months after admission, and at least annually, the program planning team evaluates each individual's ability to self-administer medication with input from the RN, physician or PA, and records the outcome and any training plan. See REC-07.

The nurse makes sure that over-the-counter medications are used only with written practitioner approval renewed at least annually, and that staff do not give them for more than 2 days without practitioner direction.

The nurse is told immediately of any significant adverse reaction to a medication. Staff suspend the medication and notify the practitioner immediately, and the nurse follows up on the practitioner's direction and records it. See EMR-01.

Staff schedule routine care (physical exams, dental visits, vision and hearing screening, immunizations, age- and sex-appropriate screening, and annual labs) with the individual's practitioners and keep a health calendar. The nurse reviews the calendar monthly and the Program Director reviews overdue items.

Staff schedule specialty care when ordered and send a staff member who knows the individual, with the emergency information packet, a list of questions and a form to record the practitioner's findings, orders and next visit. The nurse reviews each visit summary within 2 business days.

Practitioner orders are written into the home's order record or medication record by the nurse or by staff trained and directed by the nurse. The nurse verifies telephone orders, gets written confirmation and checks that the order has been carried out. Orders for treatments, therapies, diets and equipment are followed up until completed.

The nurse teaches staff about each individual's health conditions, including how to recognize a change of condition and when to call the nurse, practitioner or 911. Health teaching is recorded and repeated when needs change.
The nurse tells the individual and the people he or she chooses about health care decisions in plain language and with needed supports. Consent and health care proxy are handled under DEC-02.

The nurse reports to the Program Director at least monthly on health trends, medication variances, missed appointments, overdue orders and hospital visits, and the Program Director takes corrective action. These items go to quality improvement under GOV-02.

responsibilities.duty: Assess health needs, supervise medication staff, arrange the annual regimen review, coordinate practitioner follow-up and teach staff.
Set and confirm nursing hours with the regional office, make sure certification is current, and correct gaps.
Carry out health care instructions, give medications only if certified, report changes, and take individuals to appointments.
Evaluate individuals, write orders, respond to medication review recommendations.
Choose practitioners, take part in health decisions and in the planning team.

documentation: Nursing health assessments and health care instructions.
Medication administration records and nurse observation and review notes.
Staff medication course, practicum and annual certification records.
Annual medication regimen review and prescriber response.
Self-administration evaluations by the planning team.
Practitioner approval for over-the-counter medication.
Health calendar, appointment records and order follow-up log.
Monthly nursing report to the Program Director.

policies.title: Health Monitoring, Seizures and Choking Risk
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, supervisors, substitutes, nursing staff, the Program Director, and individuals with a known seizure disorder, choking or swallowing risk or other health condition that needs monitoring.
policies.purpose: To protect individuals from preventable harm by monitoring health, by writing and following individual protocols for seizures and choking, and by training staff to respond correctly and report accurately.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(viii) (health and safety issues) as it applies to health monitoring, seizures and choking. [AGENCY NAME] monitors each individual's health in line with the nurse's assessment, and writes an individual protocol for every person with a seizure disorder or a choking or swallowing risk. The protocol is part of the individual's plan and is available to all staff on every shift. Staff are trained on safety and security procedures and incident reporting (14 NYCRR 633.8) and on each protocol before they work alone with an individual. Choking with a known risk and other health events are classified and reported under the Part 624 incident categories as set out in REC-05; the Program Director confirms the current classification each year, because a choking event may be a reportable incident and not only a notable occurrence. Treatment beyond first aid by a physician, dentist, physician assistant or nurse practitioner is a minor notable occurrence under 14 NYCRR 624.4. A death is always a serious notable occurrence (EMR-03). Supervisors with oversight responsibility in an IRA must have first-aid training, which is kept current under IRA-03. A deliberate or inappropriate use of restraint during a seizure, choking or other health event is not permitted; see BEH-02.

definitions.definition: Planned observation and recording of an individual's health indicators, such as weight, vital signs, eating and drinking, bowel and bladder function, skin, sleep, pain, seizure activity and mood.

A written, individual set of steps for a person with epilepsy or seizures that includes seizure types, triggers, what to do, when to give any ordered rescue medication, when to call 911, how to record the seizure and how to protect the person afterwards.
A known or suspected difficulty with chewing or swallowing (dysphagia), pica or rapid eating that increases the chance of airway blockage or aspiration.

A written, individual set of steps for a person at risk of choking, including food texture and liquid consistency, positioning, pacing, supervision during meals, adaptive equipment and emergency response.
Under 14 NYCRR 624.4, among other things, an injury that needs treatment beyond first aid by a physician, dentist, physician assistant or nurse practitioner.

procedures: Before admission and at least annually, the nurse reviews each individual's health history and assesses seizure, choking and swallowing risk, with input from the physician, speech-language pathologist or dietitian when needed. The nurse sets the monitoring plan: what is checked, how often, by whom and what findings must be called in.

For each individual with a seizure disorder, the nurse and planning team write a seizure protocol with the neurologist's or practitioner's orders, including when to call 911, when and how to give any rescue medication ordered, how long to observe, how to record, and how to support the person after a seizure. Staff who give rescue medication hold the required training and certification. See REC-07.

For each individual with a choking or swallowing risk, the nurse and planning team write a choking protocol that follows the practitioner's, therapist's and dietitian's orders: texture and liquid, portion size, pace, position, supervision at meals and snacks, adaptive equipment, and what to do if the person chokes. The protocol is shared with the kitchen and food staff under HS-05.

The protocols are put in the plan under REC-01, kept in a known place in the home, and a one-page summary is posted where staff can see it without breaching the individual's privacy. Copies go with the individual on outings, to day programs and to appointments.

Before a staff member works alone with an individual with a protocol, the nurse or a trained supervisor teaches the protocol and watches the staff member show the steps. The training is signed and dated. Substitutes are trained before they take a shift.

All staff are trained at orientation and every year on safety and security procedures and incident reporting under 14 NYCRR 633.8, and on first aid and CPR as the agency requires. Supervisors with oversight responsibility keep first-aid training current as set out in IRA-03.

Staff carry out health monitoring as written, record each result on the day it is observed, and tell the nurse the same shift about any result outside the limits in the monitoring plan. The nurse reviews the record at least weekly and decides about further action.

During a seizure, staff follow the protocol: keep the person safe, note time and details, do not put anything in the mouth, do not hold the person down, give any ordered rescue medication, and call 911 when the protocol says or if the staff member is unsure. The nurse and supervisor are told immediately.

If an individual chokes, staff follow the choking protocol and first aid, call 911 as soon as the airway is not cleared or the person is in distress, and stay with the person. Staff then tell the nurse and supervisor immediately. Even if the person recovers, the nurse checks the person the same day for aspiration signs and decides whether a practitioner visit is needed.

After any seizure, choking event or other health event, the staff member records what happened in the progress note and in an incident report if required. The supervisor and Program Director decide the classification under Part 624, and the Program Director makes the required reports on time under REC-05.

Treatment beyond first aid by a physician, dentist, PA or NP is recorded as at least a minor notable occurrence under 14 NYCRR 624.4 and is reported under REC-05. If the event may involve neglect (for example, a protocol was not followed or supervision was missing), it is reported as a possible reportable incident to the Justice Center VPCR at 1-855-373-2122 and to OPWDD, as in REC-06.

Use of a hold, restraint or other restriction during a seizure, choking or other medical event is prohibited unless a practitioner has written a protective order that meets BEH-02. Deliberate inappropriate use of restraint is abuse or neglect, and inappropriate use is a significant incident, and both are reported.

The nurse reviews each protocol after any event, after any change in medication, diet or condition, after hospitalization and at least every 6 months. The planning team reviews it at the annual plan review. Staff are retrained after any change.

The nurse counts and trends seizures, choking events, aspiration, weight changes, falls and other health events each month and reports them to the Program Director, who reviews them and brings them to quality improvement under GOV-02.

responsibilities.duty: Know and follow each protocol, monitor and record health, respond to seizures and choking, call 911 when required and report promptly.
Make sure only trained staff work with at-risk individuals, keep first-aid training current, review records and report events.
Assess risk, write and review protocols with the team, train staff and review monitoring records.
Make sure training and protocols are in place, classify and report events correctly and use trends to improve care.
Approve protocols, review them at least annually and respect the individual's preferences within safety needs.

documentation: Health monitoring records and nurse review notes.
Individual seizure and choking protocols with review dates.
Staff protocol training records, first aid and CPR certificates, and annual training records.
Seizure logs, progress notes and incident reports.
Notable occurrence and reportable incident records and reports.
Monthly health trend report and quality improvement review notes.

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, contractors and individuals at every [AGENCY NAME] IRA site (supervised and supportive)
policies.purpose: To protect individuals and staff from infection and from exposure to blood and other body substances. The policy also sets out staff training and confidentiality of health information.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(viii) — Health and safety issues (infection prevention and control). [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written infection prevention and control program. It follows the OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) and uses standard precautions for every individual at all times. Every employee and volunteer is trained to prevent and manage significant-risk body substance exposure (14 NYCRR 633.8(a)(1)(viii)-(ix)). This training is part of the abuse-prevention and safety training required within 3 months of hire or start of volunteering and again each year (633.8(b)(1)-(2)). Employee TB screening and control follow OPWDD requirements and policy PER-05. An individual's HIV-related information is confidential under New York's HIV confidentiality law and is shared only as that law permits. An individual's infection status is never a reason to deny admission or services (see ADM-03 and RIT-03).
