definitions.definition: Infection control practices applied to all individuals regardless of known infection status. They include hand hygiene, gloves and other protective equipment, safe handling of sharps, and cleaning of contaminated surfaces.

Contact with blood or other body substances in a way that could transmit a bloodborne infection such as HIV or hepatitis. Examples are a needlestick, or splash to a mucous membrane or non-intact skin.
The written OSHA plan that identifies tasks with exposure risk and sets out protective measures, vaccination, training and post-exposure follow-up.

procedures: The Program Director [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and the agency nurse write an Exposure Control Plan that identifies job tasks with possible exposure to blood or body substances (for example personal care, first aid, wound care, laundry, cleaning, sharps handling and medication administration). The plan is kept at each site.
The Program Director reviews and updates the Exposure Control Plan at least annually, and whenever tasks, procedures or available safer devices change. The review is dated and signed.

Before staff are assigned unsupervised duties, and again every year, the agency trains them on preventing and managing significant-risk body substance exposure (633.8(a)(1)(viii)-(ix)). Training covers standard precautions, protective equipment, cleanup, sharps, and what to do after an exposure.

Training also covers safety and security procedures, including fire safety, as required in 633.8(b)(1)-(2). The Training Coordinator records each session in the training-monitoring record (see PER-02).

Each site stocks disposable gloves, face and eye protection, gowns or aprons, hand soap, alcohol-based hand rub, a spill cleanup kit, a sharps container, and leak-proof biohazard bags. The Residence Manager checks stock weekly and restocks the same day if supplies are short.

Staff perform hand hygiene before and after direct care, before preparing or serving food, before and after medication administration, after glove removal, after using the toilet, and whenever hands are visibly soiled.

Staff clean up blood or body fluid spills immediately with gloves and an EPA-registered disinfectant that is effective against bloodborne pathogens, used as the label directs. Contaminated waste goes in biohazard bags. Sharps go in puncture-resistant containers, which are never overfilled.

Soiled laundry is handled with gloves, bagged where it is soiled, and washed on the hot or disinfecting cycle. Kitchen and bathroom surfaces are cleaned and disinfected on the schedule posted at each site.

Staff support each individual to practice hand hygiene, personal hygiene, oral care, safe use of personal items such as razors and toothbrushes, and respiratory etiquette. Teaching is adapted to the person's abilities and recorded in the plan of services where it is a need (see REC-01).

The agency offers hepatitis B vaccination at no cost to employees with occupational exposure risk. Vaccination is offered within 10 working days of assignment unless the employee has already been vaccinated or declines in writing. The agency keeps a signed declination on file.

An employee with a possible exposure washes the area immediately, reports to the supervisor on duty at once, and is sent for medical evaluation as soon as possible. The supervisor completes an incident report (see REC-05) and notifies the Program Director.

The Program Director arranges confidential post-exposure evaluation and follow-up at no cost to the employee. Test results and medical records are kept in a separate confidential medical file, not in the personnel file (see PER-06).

The agency nurse monitors individuals for signs of infection (fever, cough, diarrhea, rash, wound changes) and for outbreaks. The nurse arranges prompt medical evaluation and keeps symptomatic individuals comfortable and, where advised, separated. The nurse reports any reportable condition to the local health department.

Employees with symptoms of a communicable illness do not work with individuals until cleared under PER-05 and the Program Director's direction. Employees notify their supervisor before the shift. Staff, volunteers and contractors with TB risk or symptoms follow the screening and medical clearance requirements in PER-05.

Staff keep HIV-related information about an individual or employee confidential. They record it only in the protected clinical record and disclose it only where New York's HIV confidentiality law permits (see REC-03 and REC-08).

The Program Director reviews infection-related incidents, exposures and outbreaks at least quarterly and reports trends to the quality improvement process (see GOV-02). Corrective actions are assigned and tracked to completion.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the Exposure Control Plan, ensures supplies, vaccination offers and training, and reviews exposure and infection data.
Monitors individuals' health, advises on isolation and cleaning, arranges medical follow-up, and reports reportable conditions.
Checks supplies weekly, supervises cleaning schedules and spill response, and reports exposures and illness.
Use standard precautions every shift, report exposures immediately, and keep HIV-related information confidential.
Schedules and records exposure-prevention and annual retraining.

documentation: Written Exposure Control Plan and dated annual review
Training attendance and content records (633.8(b)(3) monitoring record)
Hepatitis B vaccination offers, acceptances and signed declinations
Exposure incident reports and confidential post-exposure follow-up records in a separate medical file
Cleaning and disinfecting logs, and supply checklists
Quarterly infection and exposure trend review

policies.title: Food, Nutrition and Modified Diets
policies.applies_to: All individuals and all staff at every [AGENCY NAME] IRA site (supervised and supportive)
policies.purpose: To make sure each individual has a balanced, appealing diet of their own choosing, access to food at any time, and safe modified diets when a practitioner orders them.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(viii) — Health and safety issues (food and nutrition). Each individual has the right to a balanced diet (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(4)). Each individual also has access to food at any time, as required for HCBS settings (42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi); OPWDD Health and Safety Alert on access to food). Any restriction on food access is a rights modification. It is made only through the person-centered planning process, begins with the least restrictive option (all foods, all the time), and is justified under 14 NYCRR 636-1.4 and documented in the plan of services (see RIT-02). Food is never withheld or restricted for staff convenience, as a threat, as retribution or as discipline (633.4(a)(7)). In supervised IRAs, [AGENCY NAME] provides the supplies and services required under 14 NYCRR 635.9. It does not charge individuals for what it must provide, and it applies the room-and-board and personal-allowance rules in 635.9 and Social Services Law 131-o. Modified diets, choking-risk precautions and practitioner orders are written into the plan of services and carried out exactly as ordered.

definitions.definition: A diet ordered by a licensed practitioner because of a medical, dental, swallowing or nutritional need. Examples are texture-modified, pureed, thickened liquids, diabetic, low-sodium and allergen-free diets.

definitions.term: Access to food at any time
definitions.definition: The individual may get food and drink, including snacks and meals outside a set schedule, without needing staff permission, unless a justified and documented restriction applies.
A documented risk that an individual may aspirate or choke on food or liquids. It is addressed through a practitioner's assessment and a written mealtime plan (see HS-03).

procedures: At admission and at each plan review, staff ask each individual about food preferences, cultural and religious practices, dislikes, allergies and mealtime routines. The Residence Manager records them in the plan of services (see REC-01).
The agency nurse confirms any practitioner diet orders, allergies and swallowing or choking concerns before admission and at each change (see ADM-02 and HS-02). The nurse documents them in the plan.
Individuals take part in planning menus at least weekly, shopping, and preparing meals to the extent they choose and are able. Planning is recorded in the house meeting or plan notes (see DEC-01).

Menus include a balanced variety from all food groups, are posted where individuals can see them, and offer alternatives. The agency nurse or a registered dietitian [DIETITIAN/CONSULTANT NAME] reviews menus at least annually and when an individual's health needs change.

Food, drinks and snacks are kept available and visible at all times in the kitchen and refrigerator, in a manner each individual can reach and use. Staff do not lock the kitchen or refrigerator or set mealtimes that prevent access, unless a restriction has been approved as in step 7.
Staff support individuals to get food between meals, including at night, and record any request that could not be met and why.

If a team believes a food restriction is needed (for example for a medical condition), the team first tries the least restrictive option. It documents the assessed need, the less intrusive methods tried, the time limit, the data to be collected and a plan to end the restriction. It also records the individual's informed consent and the justification under 636-1.4, using the process in RIT-02. Staff do not start a restriction until it is approved and written into the plan.
The Program Director reviews each food restriction at least every [REVIEW INTERVAL] and at each plan review, and ends it as soon as it is no longer justified.

Staff follow every modified-diet order exactly as written, including texture, liquid consistency, portion, feeding position, supervision level and adaptive equipment. Mealtime instructions are posted discreetly where staff prepare and serve food and are included in staff training (see HS-03).

Staff stay with individuals who have a choking risk during meals and snacks as the plan directs. They use only the approved texture and equipment, and they respond to choking under the emergency procedures in EMR-01.

When an individual refuses food or drink, loses or gains weight noticeably, has difficulty swallowing, or shows a change in appetite, staff tell the nurse the same day. The nurse follows up with the practitioner and records the outcome.

Staff store, prepare and serve food safely: wash hands, keep refrigerators at 40°F or below and freezers at 0°F or below, label and date opened and leftover foods, separate raw from ready-to-eat foods, cook foods to safe temperatures, and clean surfaces and equipment after use. The Residence Manager checks refrigerator temperatures and food dates weekly.

The agency does not charge individuals for supplies and services it is required to provide under 635.9. Room-and-board and personal-allowance responsibilities are explained in writing before admission (see ADM-03 and REC-02). Individuals are not charged more than the maximum cost of care set in regulation.

Individuals are supported to buy and eat food of their own choosing, to eat out, and to share meals with friends and family, using their own funds under REC-02. Staff do not require individuals to eat at set tables or times.
The Residence Manager audits food access, menus, diet-order compliance and food safety monthly. The Program Director reviews audit results and any complaint about food through GOV-02 and APP-02.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures food access, supplies and funding comply with this policy and approves and reviews any food restriction.
Verifies diet orders, reviews menus and monitors weight, swallowing and nutrition concerns.
Posts menus, supervises food safety, checks access and diet-order compliance, and completes monthly audits.
Support choice and access to food, follow modified-diet and mealtime plans exactly, and report concerns the same day.
Considers least restrictive options and documents any restriction with justification under 636-1.4.

documentation: Food preferences, allergies, diet orders and mealtime plans in the plan of services
Posted menus and house-meeting menu-planning notes
Rights modification documentation for any food restriction (assessment, less intrusive methods, consent, time limit, data, review dates)
Weight and swallowing concern notes and nurse follow-up
Refrigerator temperature and food safety checklists
Monthly food access and diet compliance audits
Written disclosure of room-and-board and charges

policies.title: Transportation and Vehicle Safety
policies.applies_to: All drivers, escorts and staff who transport or accompany individuals in agency, staff or contracted vehicles
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals are transported safely, in accessible vehicles, by screened and trained drivers and escorts, with respect for their rights and choices.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(viii) — Health and safety issues (transportation and vehicle safety). Drivers and escorts are presumed to have regular and substantial unsupervised contact with individuals and must have a criminal history record check before they work (14 NYCRR 633.22(d)(2); see PER-04). Safety procedures, including safety and security training, are part of staff training (633.8; see PER-02). Transportation must meet each person's mobility, communication and health needs, consistent with the ADA. Individuals keep their rights to a safe environment, community access and freedom from abuse during transport (633.4(a)(4)). [AGENCY NAME] will confirm insurance and driver requirements with OPWDD before using vehicles. No specific OPWDD vehicle standard was identified for this manual. Until confirmed, the agency follows the safeguards in this policy and applicable New York law.

definitions.definition: An employee, volunteer or contractor who operates a vehicle that carries an individual.
A person who accompanies an individual in a vehicle to provide support and supervision.

A vehicle and procedures that allow safe boarding, securement and travel for the individual's mobility, sensory and health needs, for example a lift-equipped vehicle with proper wheelchair securement.

procedures: The Program Director [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] designates which vehicles the agency uses (agency-owned, leased, staff-owned or contracted transport) and records whether each is approved for individuals. Staff-owned vehicles are used only if the Program Director approves in writing and insurance is confirmed.

Before the agency first transports individuals, the Program Director contacts OPWDD and the agency's insurer to confirm required insurance coverage, driver and vehicle requirements. The responses are placed in the compliance file. Any new requirement is added to this policy through POL-02.

Before a person drives or escorts individuals, the agency completes the criminal history record check for drivers and escorts under 633.22(d)(2) through the process in PER-04. A provisional driver or escort is not allowed unsupervised physical contact, and is monitored as PER-04 requires.

Before a person drives, the Residence Manager verifies and copies a valid driver's license of the class needed, and confirms any required driving record review. The agency repeats the license check at least annually and removes a driver from duty if the license is suspended, revoked or restricted.

Staff who transport individuals complete orientation on safe driving, vehicle emergencies, wheelchair securement and lift operation where used, supervision during travel, and safety and security procedures, and are retrained annually (633.8; see PER-02). The Training Coordinator records the training.

The Residence Manager inspects each vehicle at least monthly (tires, brakes, lights, seat belts, lift, securement devices, first aid kit, fire extinguisher, emergency contacts). Vehicles are maintained and inspected according to the manufacturer's schedule and New York requirements. Defects are repaired before the vehicle is used for individuals.

The agency nurse and planning team identify each person's transport needs in the plan of services (mobility device, securement, seating, supervision, medical equipment, behavior supports, sensory needs and communication). The agency uses vehicles and equipment that meet these needs.

Everyone in the vehicle uses a seat belt or properly secured restraint system. Wheelchairs are secured with four-point tie-downs and the occupant uses a lap and shoulder belt, as the vehicle and chair manufacturers direct. Staff are trained to do this correctly. Drivers do not use handheld devices and do not drive impaired.

Before each trip, the driver or escort confirms who is traveling, the destination, the return plan, any medication or emergency supplies needed, and each person's emergency information. For medication taken on outings, only certified staff handle it (see REC-07).
Drivers do not leave an individual unattended in a vehicle unless the plan of services permits it. Staff supervise at the level the plan requires during boarding, travel and unloading.

Staff respect individuals' choices about where to go, who to travel with and when, and support community participation and employment travel (see COM-01). Staff also help individuals use public transit, para-transit or other transport as they choose.

If a vehicle breaks down or there is a crash, the driver secures the scene, calls 911 if anyone may be hurt, checks every person, contacts the on-call supervisor, and follows EMR-01. The driver records the event, and the supervisor completes the incident report under REC-05 and tells the Program Director and families or advocates as required.
If an individual leaves or goes missing during an outing, staff follow BEH-03. If an individual has a seizure, choking or medical episode, staff follow the individual's health plan and EMR-01.

Staff report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation during transport through REC-06. Behavior supports in vehicles follow the plan and BEH-01. Physical restraint is not used during transport except as BEH-02 permits.
Drivers and escorts do not charge individuals for transport the agency must provide. Where an individual pays for their own transport, it is recorded under REC-02.
The Program Director reviews vehicle incidents, inspections, driver files and complaints at least quarterly through GOV-02.

responsibilities.duty: Approves vehicles and drivers, confirms insurance and OPWDD requirements, and reviews incidents and inspections.
Verifies licenses, inspects vehicles, assigns drivers and escorts to trips, and keeps trip and maintenance records.
Drive safely, use securement correctly, supervise as planned, and report incidents and concerns.
Identifies health-related transport needs and emergency supplies.
Provides and tracks driver and escort training.

documentation: Criminal history check approvals for drivers and escorts
Driver license verification and annual re-checks
Insurance confirmation and OPWDD requirement correspondence
Vehicle inspection, maintenance and repair records
Transport needs in the plan of services
Training records for transport safety and securement
Incident reports and quarterly transportation review

policies.title: Residential Environment and Accessibility
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] IRA sites, grounds and furnishings, supervised and supportive
policies.purpose: To make sure each IRA site is a safe, sanitary, accessible and homelike residence that meets the building, fire and life safety requirements OPWDD applies to its size.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(viii) — Health and safety issues (residential environment and accessibility). Each IRA meets 14 NYCRR 686.16, which sets the building and life safety tier by number of residents. An IRA of eight or fewer persons must meet the 635-7.1(h)(1)(ii) building code (in New York City, 635-7.1(i)(1)(ii)) and 635-7.4(b)(3). If the occupants cannot evacuate in 3 minutes or less, 635-7.2(a)(1)(iii) also applies. An IRA of nine or more persons must meet 635-7.1, 635-7.2 and 635-7.3 (686.16(a)(2)-(3)). Uniform Code enforcement for OPWDD IRAs runs through 635-7.4(a)(3). In an IRA of eight or fewer, fire alarms must be audible in sleeping areas with doors closed (686.16(b)). Site selection under Mental Hygiene Law 41.34 applies to 4-14 bed IRAs with onsite supervision and to 1-3 bed IRAs with 24-hour supervision (686.16(a)(7)). The residence is safe, sanitary, physically accessible to the people who live there, and homelike. Individuals can furnish and decorate their own rooms.

definitions.definition: An IRA certified for 8 or fewer persons. It follows the building code in 635-7.1(h)(1)(ii) (NYC: 635-7.1(i)(1)(ii)) and 635-7.4(b)(3).
An IRA certified for 9 or more persons. It must meet the physical plant, Life Safety Code and safety and welfare requirements in 635-7.1, 635-7.2 and 635-7.3.
The home, grounds and features can be entered, used and exited safely by each resident, including those with mobility, vision or hearing limitations.
The local building authority's document confirming lawful use of the building. In New York City it is issued by the Department of Buildings.

procedures: Before a site is proposed, the Program Director [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms the number of beds planned, whether the model is onsite supervision or 24-hour supervision, and which building and life safety tier applies under 686.16(a)(2)-(3). The determination is written and kept in the site file.

For a site of 4-14 beds with onsite supervision, or 1-3 beds with 24-hour supervision, the Program Director completes the MHL 41.34 site-selection process as applied by 686.16(a)(7) before the site is certified, and keeps the notices and responses in the site file. Counsel and the OPWDD regional office are consulted on timing and content.

For an eight-or-fewer site, the Program Director has a qualified professional confirm that the building meets the 635-7.1(h)(1)(ii) code (NYC: 635-7.1(i)(1)(ii)) and 635-7.4(b)(3). The professional also confirms whether occupants can evacuate in 3 minutes or less, and if they cannot, that 635-7.2(a)(1)(iii) is also met.
For a nine-or-more site, the Program Director confirms compliance with 635-7.1, 635-7.2 and 635-7.3 and documents it.

The Program Director confirms with the local code enforcement official and OPWDD that the building has the required approvals, and that Uniform Code enforcement under 635-7.4(a)(3) is understood. In New York City, the Program Director also asks the Department of Buildings whether the 1994 notice (TPPN #9/94), which tied the final Certificate of Occupancy for IRAs to the IRA license, still applies, and files the answer. The status of that notice is not assumed.

For an eight-or-fewer IRA, the agency verifies that fire alarms can be heard in all sleeping areas with bedroom doors closed. The agency tests this at least [TEST INTERVAL] and after any alarm work, and records the result.
For a nine-or-more IRA, the agency tests all heat and smoke-detecting alarm devices at least quarterly and records the results (635-7.3(e)(i)(1)).

Each site has a written facility evacuation plan and a current fire-evacuation evaluation for each individual in each plan of services, as required by 686.16(b). Staff and individual training and evaluation follow IRA-04 and EMR-02.

The Residence Manager inspects the site at least monthly using a checklist. It covers exits and egress paths, smoke and carbon monoxide devices, extinguishers, lighting, heat and hot water temperatures, plumbing, electrical equipment, pest control, cleanliness, bedroom privacy, storage and secure storage of medications and hazardous materials.

The Residence Manager promptly repairs hazards, or removes the hazard from use and tells the Program Director the same day for serious hazards. Work orders show who fixed the item and the date. Individuals are moved if a hazard cannot be fixed safely and quickly, and the move follows individual rights procedures.

At admission and each annual review, the planning team assesses each person's physical access needs (mobility device, vision, hearing, sensory and cognitive needs). The team identifies adaptations such as ramps, grab bars, wide doorways, roll-in showers, visual alarms and adaptive equipment, and records them in the plan of services. The agency makes the modifications and keeps them working, and confirms the setting is physically accessible under HCBS settings requirements (see RIT-01).

The home looks and feels like other homes in the neighborhood. Each person has their own bedroom space of their choosing as far as the certification allows. Individuals choose furnishings, décor and personal items and have lockable space and storage. Staff knock and wait before entering bedrooms and bathrooms (see RIT-01).

The agency makes the program's reasonable accommodations for individuals, staff and visitors with disabilities in line with the ADA, and checks accessible routes to entrances, parking and community access (see RIT-03).

The Program Director reviews inspection results, work orders and incidents quarterly through GOV-02 and keeps the site's certification documents, fire-safety approvals, Certificate of Occupancy and site-selection file current. The Program Director updates them whenever bed capacity, program model, alterations or use changes, and notifies OPWDD as required (see GOV-01).

responsibilities.duty: Determines the applicable code tier, completes site selection and approvals, funds repairs and keeps certification documents current.
Conducts monthly inspections, tests alarms, arranges repairs and maintains accessibility features.
Report hazards immediately, keep egress clear and support individuals' use of their homes.
Assess each person's access needs and record adaptations in the plan.

responsibilities.role: Qualified building or fire safety professional
responsibilities.duty: Confirms code compliance and evacuation evaluation for the site.

documentation: Site file with tier determination, MHL 41.34 site-selection records and local code or Certificate of Occupancy documents
NYC DOB inquiry and response on TPPN #9/94 (NYC sites)
Alarm audibility tests and, for 9+ bed sites, quarterly alarm test logs
Facility evacuation plan and individual fire-evacuation evaluations
Monthly environmental inspection checklists and work orders
Accessibility assessments and modifications in the plan of services
Quarterly environmental review

policies.title: Recruitment, Hiring, Residence Manager Qualifications and Job Performance Evaluation
policies.applies_to: All applicants and employees of [AGENCY NAME], including residence managers, supervisors and direct support staff
federal: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act
policies.purpose: To hire qualified, screened staff fairly, to set clear qualifications, job descriptions and duties, and to evaluate job performance regularly.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(ix) — Personnel policies and procedures. It also meets 686.6(a)(2)(ix)(a): the recruitment and hiring process; qualifications, education and skills required; job descriptions; description of duties and responsibilities; and job performance evaluations. It meets 686.6(b)(1): written criteria for a residence manager. [AGENCY NAME] has written criteria that require the residence manager to have, at a minimum, a high school diploma or its equivalent and at least one year of experience working with persons with developmental disabilities. No one is placed in the residence manager position without meeting both. Applicants are screened under the criminal history record check requirements of 14 NYCRR 633.22 (see PER-04) and under OPWDD's other requirements for reviewing applicants' backgrounds and for supervision, which the Program Director confirms against current regulation. The agency recruits and hires without discrimination, consistent with Title VII and the ADA (see PER-03).

definitions.definition: The employee responsible for the day-to-day operation of an IRA site, including supervising direct support staff and coordinating individuals' services.
An employee with direct care duties who supports individuals' daily living, health, safety, community participation and goals.
A prospective employee or operator who must have a criminal history record check because of regular and substantial unsupervised contact with individuals (633.22(d)(2)).
Temporary approval to begin work before the check is complete. It is allowed only without unsupervised physical contact, with monitoring by a trained employee and an attestation (633.22(f)).

procedures: The Program Director [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] writes a job description for each position (residence manager, supervisor, DSP, nurse, driver and others). Each lists title, reports-to, qualifications, education, skills and licenses required, duties and responsibilities, work location, physical requirements and essential functions. Job descriptions are reviewed at least every [REVIEW INTERVAL] and when duties change.

The residence manager job description requires a high school diploma or equivalent and at least one year of experience working with persons with developmental disabilities (686.6(b)(1)). Experience may be paid or unpaid work directly with people with developmental disabilities. The agency verifies it through application, references and employer contact, and records the verification.

The job description for a DSP states that the job has direct care duties. It also states any requirement to complete medication certification (see PER-02 and REC-07), first aid and CPR, and driver duties if applicable.
Positions are advertised with an equal opportunity statement. The posting states required qualifications, duties and any physical requirements, without discriminatory language (see PER-03).

Applicants submit a written application listing work history, education, references and certifications, and consent to checks. The hiring manager interviews applicants using job-related questions, the same core questions for each applicant for the position.

The Program Director identifies in writing which positions are subject parties for criminal history checks, using 633.22(d)(2) as the baseline. It includes direct care staff in residential facilities, residential habilitation staff, supervisors of direct care staff, drivers and escorts, clinicians, care managers, and anyone assigned to a certified site, as well as operators with an ownership interest.

The Program Director designates the authorized parties for criminal history checks and submits their names, positions and contact information to the Justice Center (633.22(c)(1)). The agency updates the Justice Center when they change. The authorized parties run the check process under PER-04 (633.22(e)).

No applicant covered by 633.22 is offered unsupervised work until the check result is received and reviewed under PER-04. If a provisional start is used, the applicant has no unsupervised physical contact, a trained employee monitors them, and the agency completes the required attestation (633.22(f)). The provisional person is not counted toward staffing coverage in PER-08 unless the plan permits.

The agency also reviews applicant backgrounds as OPWDD's applicant-screening regulations require, including reference and employment history checks and registry checks (see PER-04). The Program Director pulls and confirms the current text of those requirements and records it in the compliance file. A candidate whose screening is not complete is not hired.

The agency makes any conditional offer in writing, subject to completion of checks, health screening (see PER-05) and verification of qualifications. Each new hire receives the job description, this policy's performance evaluation process, and the manual's conduct rules, and signs for receipt.

Supervisory staffing and supervision of direct care staff follow OPWDD supervision requirements and PER-08. The Program Director confirms current requirements and makes sure each supervisor meets them. IRA supervisor and substitute qualifications are also covered in IRA-03.
The agency creates the personnel record at hire and keeps application, verification of qualifications, check results, offer letter, job description and training records in it (see PER-06).

Each new employee has a first performance review at the end of a [PROBATIONARY PERIOD] probationary period and at least annually thereafter. The supervisor evaluates performance against the job description, including individual-centered support, rights, documentation, attendance, training completion and conduct, using the agency form.

The supervisor meets with the employee, reviews the written evaluation, sets goals and training needs, and gives the employee a chance to comment in writing. The employee and supervisor sign, and the original goes in the personnel record.

Performance problems are addressed promptly through coaching, written warnings, retraining or other action under PER-07. Evaluation results inform training plans under PER-02. The Program Director evaluates the residence manager at least annually.

If the agency learns after hire that an employee has a later conviction or pending charge, the Program Director follows the written procedure in PER-04 required by 633.22(c)(2). When a person stops being a subject party, the authorized party notifies the Justice Center as 633.22(c)(2) requires.

responsibilities.duty: Approves job descriptions and criteria, designates authorized parties, makes hiring decisions and evaluates the residence manager.

responsibilities.role: Authorized party for criminal history checks
responsibilities.duty: Submits and tracks checks, receives results and keeps them confidential under PER-04.
Interview, verify qualifications with the Program Director, supervise provisional staff and complete performance evaluations.
Maintain personnel records, postings and signed acknowledgments.
Provide accurate information, meet job requirements and take part in evaluations.

documentation: Job descriptions with duties, qualifications and skills for each position
Written residence manager criteria and verification of diploma/equivalent and one year of experience
Applications, interview notes, references and offer letters
List of authorized parties and Justice Center submission
Criminal history check approvals and provisional approval attestations and monitoring records
Performance evaluations with signatures and employee comments
Signed acknowledgments of job description and policies

policies.title: Direct Support Professional Orientation, Training and In-Service
policies.applies_to: All employees and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], especially direct support professionals and medication-certified staff
policies.purpose: To make sure every staff member and volunteer is oriented, trained and retrained to support individuals safely, protect them from abuse, and carry out their duties competently.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(ix) — Personnel policies and procedures. It also meets 686.6(a)(2)(ix)(b), staff training programs that include at a minimum: (1) coordination of staff development and training that is consistent with individuals' and staff needs and agency policies; (2) orientation procedures; (3) in-service training; and (4) the use of community training resources. Within 3 months of hire or start of volunteering, each employee and volunteer is trained on human growth and development, characteristics of persons served, promoting positive relationships, abuse prevention, identification and reporting, laws and policies on protection from abuse, incident reporting, and safety and security procedures including fire safety (14 NYCRR 633.8(b)(1)). Each person is retrained annually on positive relationships, abuse prevention and reporting, laws and policies, incident reporting, and safety and security including fire safety (633.8(b)(2)). Training on preventing and managing significant-risk body substance exposure (HIV) is also provided (633.8(a)(1)(viii)-(ix)). Staff who administer medication complete an OPWDD-approved course and practicum and are certified or recertified within the year (14 NYCRR 633.17(a)(14)(iii)(c)). The temporary training flexibility in 14 NYCRR 633.27 is expired. [AGENCY NAME] does not rely on it and requires full training.

definitions.definition: Initial training and shadowing a new employee or volunteer completes to learn the agency, the site, the individuals and the job before and during the first weeks of work.
Ongoing training during employment, including required annual retraining and training based on individual and staff needs.
Employees who hold a job description with direct care duties and have completed an OPWDD-approved medication course and practicum and are certified or recertified within the year.
The agency's system for tracking the type, frequency and amount of training each person completes, with current records (633.8(b)(3)).

procedures: The Program Director [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] appoints a Training Coordinator who is responsible for the annual training plan, the training schedule and the training records. The plan is reviewed and approved each year.

The Training Coordinator builds the annual training plan by reviewing individuals' plans of services and support needs, incident and quality data (GOV-02), supervisory feedback, performance evaluations (PER-01) and each staff member's requests. This coordinates staff development and training consistent with individuals' and staff needs and agency policies (686.6(a)(2)(ix)(b)(1)).

On or before the first day, each new employee and volunteer receives orientation (686.6(a)(2)(ix)(b)(2)). It covers the agency mission, policies and this manual, individual rights, confidentiality, emergency and evacuation procedures, incident reporting, the site and individuals' plans, and mandated reporting under REC-06.

A new DSP does not work alone or unsupervised with individuals until orientation on rights, abuse reporting, emergency and evacuation procedures, and the specific needs and plans of the individuals is complete. The new employee shadows an experienced staff member for at least [SHADOW HOURS] before being counted in staffing.

Within 3 months of hire or start of volunteering, the Training Coordinator completes training on every topic in 633.8(b)(1): human growth and development, characteristics of persons served, promoting positive relationships, abuse prevention/identification/reporting/processing, laws and policies on protection from abuse, incident reporting, and safety and security procedures including fire safety.

The Training Coordinator also trains each employee and volunteer on preventing and managing significant-risk body substance exposure, as in HS-04 (633.8(a)(1)(viii)-(ix)). Training in first aid and emergency procedures follows IRA-03 and EMR-01.

Each employee and volunteer completes annual retraining, due before the anniversary of the previous training, on positive relationships, abuse prevention and reporting, laws and policies, incident reporting, and safety and security including fire safety (633.8(b)(2)).

Staff who will administer medication must hold a job description with direct care duties and complete an OPWDD-approved medication course and practicum. They are certified before administering medication and recertified within the year, and medical or nursing supervision is in place (633.17). The agency nurse verifies certification dates, and staff whose certification lapses do not administer medication until recertified. Details are in REC-07.

Training specific to individuals' needs is given before staff support those individuals. Topics include communication methods, behavior support plans (BEH-01), seizure and choking protocols (HS-03), modified diets (HS-05), mobility and transfer techniques, and technology supports (IRA-01).

The Training Coordinator schedules in-service training during the year to meet the annual plan and any need found through incidents, audits or evaluations (686.6(a)(2)(ix)(b)(3)). Each in-service is documented with date, topic, trainer, length and attendees.

The agency uses community training resources where they fit the need (686.6(a)(2)(ix)(b)(4)). Examples are OPWDD and Justice Center training, local health department, Red Cross or American Heart Association first aid and CPR, other approved trainers, self-advocacy organizations, and training by people receiving services. The Training Coordinator records the provider, topic and attendance.

The agency also trains individuals on their safety and self-protection where their program planning team identifies a need, and includes them in fire safety and evacuation training under 633.8(a)(2), (b)(4) and IRA-04.

The Training Coordinator maintains a training-monitoring mechanism that tracks the type, frequency and amount of training for each employee and volunteer. Records are current and available for review, and employees can confirm on interview that they have received training (633.8(b)(3)).

The Training Coordinator checks the tracking system monthly and gives the Program Director a list of anyone whose training is overdue or due within 60 days. Overdue staff are scheduled immediately, and the Program Director decides whether duties are limited until training is complete.

The agency confirms whether the one-time board training in 633.8(b)(5) applies to its corporate form. It applies only to not-for-profit corporations. If it applies, the Program Director records completion.

The Training Coordinator evaluates training effectiveness through quizzes, skills demonstration and supervisor observation, and revises the plan each year. Training content, sign-in sheets and tests are kept in the personnel and training files (see PER-06).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the annual training plan and resources, enforces timely completion and limits duties when training is overdue.
Plans, schedules, delivers or arranges training, and keeps the monitoring mechanism and records current.
Supervises medication staff, verifies medication certifications and teaches health-related content.
Give site orientation and shadowing, observe skills, and release staff for training.
Complete required training on time and apply it in daily work.

documentation: Annual training plan
Orientation checklist and shadowing records
633.8 training records (initial within 3 months and annual retraining) with sign-in, topics and trainer
HIV and body substance exposure training records
Medication course, practicum and certification/recertification records
Training-monitoring tracker and monthly overdue report
Records of community training resources used and of individuals' safety training

policies.title: Staff Concerns Without Threat of Job Loss and Nondiscrimination in Employment
policies.applies_to: All employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors of [AGENCY NAME], and all applicants for hiring or promotion, at every OPWDD-certified IRA site operated by the agency.
federal: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act
policies.purpose: To give every staff member a safe, known way to raise matters of concern, including concerns about the care or safety of the people we support, without risk of losing their job. To ensure hiring and promotion are free of discrimination. To tell staff that every reportable incident is investigated.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(ix) (personnel policies and procedures), 686.6(a)(2)(ix)(c) (the means whereby matters of concern to staff can be made known without threat of job loss) and 686.6(a)(2)(ix)(d) (the prohibition of discrimination in hiring and promotion based on race, religion, color, gender, national origin, age or disability).

[AGENCY NAME] provides several ways for staff to raise matters of concern: their supervisor or Residence Manager, the Program Director, a designated Staff Concerns Contact outside the direct supervisory chain, and a confidential written route. No employee will be discharged, demoted, disciplined, threatened, have hours or schedule reduced, or be treated less favorably because that employee raised a concern in good faith, reported an incident, or took part in an investigation. Retaliation is itself misconduct and is grounds for discipline up to termination.

Employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors who have reasonable cause to suspect abuse or neglect may report directly to the NYS Justice Center Vulnerable Persons' Central Register (VPCR) hotline, 24 hours a day, at 1-855-373-2122 (Relay: dial 711 and give the number). They do not need a supervisor's permission and do not have to notify a supervisor first. Mandated reporter duties are in REC-06.

Under 14 NYCRR 624.5, all employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors must report incidents. Minor notable occurrences go to the CEO or designee within 48 hours. Reportable incidents and serious notable occurrences go to the CEO or designee immediately, and the agency reports them to OPWDD immediately. Every reportable incident is investigated. The investigation continues to a substantiated or unsubstantiated finding even if the employee involved leaves the agency. Staff are notified of this in writing.

[AGENCY NAME] prohibits discrimination in hiring and promotion based on race, religion, color, gender, national origin, age or disability. The agency complies with Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and applicable New York State law. Hiring and promotion decisions rest on job-related qualifications, skills, performance and the requirements in the job description.

definitions.definition: Any worry a staff member has about the care, safety, rights or treatment of individuals, working conditions, agency practices, or possible discrimination or retaliation.
Any adverse action, threat, or less favorable treatment taken because a person raised a concern, made a report, or took part in a review or investigation.
The NYS Justice Center's 24-hour Vulnerable Persons' Central Register hotline, 1-855-373-2122, used to report abuse and neglect.
A person designated by the Administrator, outside the direct supervisory chain of site staff, who receives and tracks staff concerns.
An incident, including abuse or neglect, that must be reported and investigated under 14 NYCRR 624.5 and the Justice Center process; see REC-05 and REC-06.

procedures: On or before the first day of work, the Administrator or Residence Manager gives each new employee, intern, volunteer, consultant and contractor a written copy of this policy, including the VPCR hotline number (1-855-373-2122; Relay 711) and the names and contact details of the Staff Concerns Contact and Program Director. The person signs an acknowledgment that goes in the personnel file (PER-06).

The Administrator posts at each site, in a staff area, the VPCR number, the Staff Concerns Contact [NAME] and [PHONE], the Program Director's contact information, and a statement that concerns may be raised without threat of job loss.

Staff may raise a concern verbally or in writing with their supervisor, the Residence Manager, the Program Director, the Staff Concerns Contact, or through the confidential written route [EMAIL OR SEALED-BOX LOCATION]. Staff may raise a concern anonymously, though the agency may be less able to respond fully.

Any staff member who suspects abuse or neglect may call the VPCR hotline directly at any time. Supervisors may not require staff to notify them first, ask staff to hold a report, or discourage a report. Staff also follow REC-05 and REC-06 for internal notification.

Whoever receives a concern records it in the Staff Concerns Log within 1 business day, with the date, a summary, who received it and whether it involves a possible reportable incident. Information that identifies the reporter is limited to those who need it to respond.

If the concern describes a possible reportable incident or notable occurrence, the receiver notifies the CEO or designee immediately and the Administrator follows REC-05, including immediate OPWDD notification of reportable incidents and serious notable occurrences. Minor notable occurrences reach the CEO or designee within 48 hours.

The Staff Concerns Contact acknowledges every non-anonymous concern within 2 business days and gives a written or verbal response on the outcome or action taken within 10 business days. If more time is needed, the contact tells the staff member and gives a new date.
The Administrator assigns each concern to someone who is not the subject of it. If the concern is about the Administrator, it goes to the chair of the governing body [GOVERNING BODY CHAIR NAME].
Supervisors are told in writing at hire or promotion, and annually, that retaliation is prohibited. Anyone who retaliates is subject to discipline up to termination.

Before any termination, demotion, discipline or schedule or hours change for an employee who raised a concern or took part in an investigation within the prior 6 months, the Administrator and a second reviewer, such as the governing body chair, review the action. They document that it is based on legitimate, non-retaliatory reasons.

An employee who believes they have been retaliated against reports it to the Staff Concerns Contact, the Program Director or the governing body chair. The complaint is logged, reviewed within 10 business days and documented to a conclusion. Corrective action is taken when retaliation is found.

At hire, annually and when an incident occurs, the agency notifies employees in writing that every reportable incident is investigated and that the investigation continues to a substantiated or unsubstantiated finding even if the employee leaves. The notice is included in orientation (PER-02) and the signed acknowledgment.

The Administrator ensures job postings state that [AGENCY NAME] is an equal opportunity employer and does not discriminate in hiring or promotion based on race, religion, color, gender, national origin, age or disability.

Interviewers use the written qualifications in the job description and the same job-related questions for all applicants for a position. They record the reasons for the hiring or promotion decision in the applicant or personnel file. Questions about protected characteristics are not asked.

When an applicant or employee with a disability or a sincerely held religious practice requests an accommodation, the Administrator discusses it with the person, considers reasonable accommodations under the ADA and Title VII, and documents the request and outcome in a confidential file.
Complaints of discrimination are handled through the same channels as other concerns, investigated promptly and documented, with corrective action where found.

Each quarter the Administrator summarizes the Staff Concerns Log by type and outcome, without names, for the governing body and the quality improvement review (GOV-02). Trends in retaliation or discrimination complaints trigger corrective action.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures this policy is distributed, posted and followed. Assigns concern reviews, approves actions affecting employees who raised concerns, and reports trends to the governing body.
Receives and logs concerns, acknowledges and responds within the stated times, and protects the identity of reporters to the extent possible.
Welcome concerns, never discourage or delay a VPCR report, forward possible reportable incidents immediately, and never retaliate.

responsibilities.role: All staff, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors
responsibilities.duty: Raise concerns, report incidents as required, report suspected abuse or neglect to the VPCR, and cooperate with investigations.
Receives concerns about the Administrator and the quarterly summary, and oversees corrective action.

documentation: Signed acknowledgment of this policy and the investigation notice in each personnel file (PER-06)
Staff Concerns Log with dates, receiver, summary, response and closure
Written responses to staff concerns
Second-review record for any adverse action involving an employee who raised a concern
Retaliation and discrimination complaint files and outcomes
Interview and promotion decision records
Accommodation request records, kept confidentially
Quarterly de-identified summary to the governing body

policies.title: Criminal History Checks, Background Checks and Employee Registries
policies.applies_to: All applicants, employees, volunteers and operators of [AGENCY NAME] who are subject parties under the Justice Center criminal history check program, and the Authorized Parties and hiring managers who administer it.
policies.purpose: To ensure no person with regular and substantial unsupervised contact with individuals is allowed that contact before required background checks are complete. To ensure provisional staff are properly limited and monitored, and that registry and check results are weighed and documented.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(ix) (personnel policies and procedures) and 686.6(a)(2)(ix)(a) (the recruitment and hiring process, including qualifications and the screening of applicants). It is the written policy required by 14 NYCRR 633.22(c)(2) and is part of the agency's hiring process described in PER-01.

[AGENCY NAME] designates Authorized Parties and submits their name, position and contact information to the NYS Justice Center (633.22(c)(1)). The agency requires a criminal history record check for every prospective employee and every operator (a natural person with an ownership interest) who will have regular and substantial unsupervised contact with individuals (633.22(d)(2)). That contact is presumed for direct care staff in the IRA, residential habilitation staff, supervisors of direct care staff, drivers and escorts, clinicians, care managers, and anyone assigned to the certified site. Checks are also required on a change in ownership. Volunteers are checked under Mental Hygiene Law 16.34. Requests are submitted through OPWDD under the Justice Center Criminal Background Check (CBC) program, and applicants are fingerprinted through IdentoGO. The process follows Part 701 (633.22(e)).

Provisional approval is permitted only when the person has no unsupervised physical contact with individuals, is monitored by a trained employee, and an attestation is completed (633.22(f)). A final Category 2 finding reported through the Staff Exclusion List check is not an automatic bar to employment, but it must be weighed in the hiring decision, and the decision and its reasons must be documented.

definitions.definition: A person designated by the agency and registered with the Justice Center to register applicants for fingerprinting and receive results.
A prospective employee, volunteer or operator who must have a criminal history record check because of regular and substantial unsupervised contact.

Contact with individuals that is not directly observed by another employee who has completed the check. It is presumed for direct care staff, supervisors, drivers, escorts, clinicians and anyone assigned to the certified site.
Temporary approval to work or volunteer before the check is complete, allowed only without unsupervised physical contact, with monitoring and an attestation.
The registry of persons with final Category 1 findings. SEL checks also report final Category 2 findings to OPWDD providers.
A final Justice Center finding that is not an automatic bar to employment but must be weighed in the hiring decision.

procedures: The Administrator designates at least two Authorized Parties, with a backup if one is absent. Before they act, the Administrator submits each one's name, position and contact information to the Justice Center. The Administrator updates the Justice Center whenever the list changes. The current list is kept at [ADDRESS].

During recruitment (PER-01), the hiring manager tells every applicant in writing that employment is conditioned on a satisfactory criminal history check, a Staff Exclusion List check and required reference checks.

Before any offer takes effect, the Authorized Party determines whether the position is a subject-party position. Direct care, residential habilitation, supervisory, driver, escort, clinician, care manager and site-assigned positions are treated as subject. Any doubt is resolved in favor of requiring the check.

The Authorized Party registers the applicant through the Justice Center CBC program, submitting the request through OPWDD under MHL 16.34. The applicant is given instructions to be fingerprinted through IdentoGO.

The Authorized Party checks the Staff Exclusion List and reviews any final Category 2 finding or other registry result for each applicant before the person works with individuals. The date and result are written on the Background Check Record.

Volunteers and any operators with an ownership interest who will have regular and substantial unsupervised contact go through the same process. On a change in ownership the Administrator ensures the required checks are requested.
No person works with individuals unsupervised until the Authorized Party records that the criminal history check is complete and acceptable.

If a start date must precede the result, the Administrator may grant provisional approval only if the person has no unsupervised physical contact with individuals. The person is never alone with an individual, including during transport, bathing, toileting, overnight shifts or community outings.

For each provisionally approved person, the Administrator names a trained employee who monitors the person at all times when with individuals. The monitor and the Administrator sign the attestation before the first shift. The monitoring assignment is written on the schedule (PER-08).
When the result arrives, the Authorized Party notifies the Administrator the same business day. Provisional approval ends immediately if the result is not acceptable.

Where a result shows a conviction, pending charge, or a final Category 2 finding, the Administrator and a second reviewer assess it in writing. They consider the nature and seriousness of the matter, its relationship to the duties of the position, time elapsed, any rehabilitation and the risk to individuals. The written decision is signed and placed in the confidential background file.
A final Category 2 finding does not bar hiring automatically. It is weighed as one factor and the reasoning is documented. The agency does not hire someone it is legally barred from hiring.
Background check results are kept in a confidential background file separate from the general personnel file (PER-06) and are shared only with those who need them to make employment decisions.

Employees must tell the Administrator within 1 business day if they are charged with or convicted of a crime. The Administrator reviews the matter with the Authorized Party, decides whether to restrict duties, suspend or end employment, and documents the decision.
The Administrator may remove an employee from unsupervised contact immediately while a later conviction, pending charge or new registry finding is reviewed.

When a person stops being a subject party, for example on resignation, termination or end of volunteering, the Authorized Party notifies the Justice Center within [NUMBER OF DAYS AS REQUIRED BY JUSTICE CENTER] and records the date.

Annually, the Administrator audits all personnel files for subject parties, confirming the check dates, SEL results, provisional approvals and attestations, and reports gaps to the governing body (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Designates and registers Authorized Parties, approves provisional status, makes or co-signs decisions on adverse results and ensures no unsupervised contact before clearance.
Register applicants, receive results, check the Staff Exclusion List, keep the Background Check Record and notify the Justice Center when a person ceases to be a subject party.
Tell applicants about the checks, ensure provisional staff are monitored, and never allow unsupervised contact before clearance.
Stays with the provisional staff member throughout contact with individuals and signs the attestation.
Complete fingerprinting as instructed and report new charges or convictions within 1 business day.

documentation: Authorized Party designation and Justice Center submission record
Background Check Record per person, with request, result and Staff Exclusion List check dates
Provisional approval, monitor assignment and attestation
Written decision on any conviction, pending charge or final Category 2 finding
Record of notices to the Justice Center when a party ceases to be a subject party
Self-reports of charges or convictions
Annual audit of background checks

policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All employees, interns and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME] who work at or visit the IRA site and may have contact with individuals, and the Nurse and Administrator who manage the program.
policies.purpose: To protect individuals and staff from tuberculosis and other communicable disease and from exposure to blood and body substances. To keep employee health information confidential and separate from personnel files.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(ix) (personnel policies and procedures), which includes policies on employee health.

[AGENCY NAME] follows OPWDD's tuberculosis (TB) control requirements for certified residential facilities. Under the agency's TB control procedure, maintained by the Nurse, each employee is screened for TB at hire before contact with individuals, and again at the times and by the methods those requirements specify. Anyone with symptoms or a positive result is evaluated and may not work with individuals until cleared in writing by a licensed health practitioner.

Employee health records, including TB screening and exposure follow-up, are kept in a confidential employee health file separate from the personnel file. They are shared only with those who need to know for health and safety purposes or as required by law. The agency complies with the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard (29 CFR 1910.1030), including vaccination offers and post-exposure follow-up.

Training on preventing and managing significant-risk body substance exposure (including HIV) is part of required staff training under 14 NYCRR 633.8(a)(1)(viii)-(ix), and exposure follow-up is covered under that training (see PER-02).

definitions.definition: A health practitioner's evaluation, including testing and symptom review, done by the methods and at the times OPWDD's TB control requirements specify.
A confidential file, separate from the personnel file, holding screening results, clearances, vaccination records and exposure follow-up records.
Contact with blood or other body substances that carries a risk of transmitting infection such as HIV or hepatitis, such as a needlestick or splash to mucous membranes.
Written confirmation from a licensed health practitioner that an employee may work with individuals.

procedures: The Administrator informs applicants in the job offer that employment depends on completing TB screening before contact with individuals, and explains the procedure.

Before the first shift involving contact with individuals, the new employee completes TB screening through a licensed health practitioner or the local health department, per the agency's TB control procedure. The result is delivered to the Nurse.
The Nurse reviews the result, records the date, result and any clearance in the employee health file, and tells the Administrator only that the employee is cleared or not cleared.

No employee, intern or volunteer who has not been cleared works with individuals. A person with a positive result or symptoms is referred to a licensed health practitioner and is not permitted at the site until written clearance is received.
The Nurse tracks due dates for repeat screening and any required annual symptom review in the Employee Health Tracker and notifies employees at least 30 days before they are due.
An employee who misses a required screening is removed from duties involving individuals until it is completed and cleared.

Employees must tell the Nurse or Administrator immediately of any symptom of communicable disease, such as persistent cough, fever or weight loss, or of a diagnosis that may affect individuals. The Nurse consults with the licensed health practitioner and the local health department as needed.
The Nurse determines whether an employee may continue working, needs modified duties or must stay away, and documents the decision.

The Nurse keeps all employee health records in a locked file or restricted electronic folder separate from the personnel file (PER-06). Access is limited to the Nurse, the Administrator when required for a health and safety decision, and regulators entitled to see them.

If an individual or other staff may have been exposed to a communicable disease by an employee, the Nurse contacts the local health department promptly, follows its direction, notifies exposed individuals and their representatives as appropriate, and documents the action (HS-04).

After any exposure to blood or other body substances, the employee washes and flushes the area immediately, reports to the supervisor and Nurse at once, and is sent for medical evaluation as soon as possible. The Nurse documents the exposure and follow-up in the confidential file and an incident report if required (REC-05).

Employees receive training on preventing and managing significant-risk body substance exposure, including HIV, as required by 14 NYCRR 633.8, in orientation and annually (PER-02). Attendance is recorded in the training record.

The agency offers hepatitis B vaccination and other measures required by the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard to employees with occupational exposure risk, and records acceptance or written declination in the employee health file.
Annually, the Nurse audits employee health files for current screening and clearance and reports gaps to the Administrator.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures no uncleared person works with individuals, supports the Nurse, and keeps health files separate from personnel files.
Maintains the TB control procedure, reviews results, tracks due dates, manages exposure follow-up and keeps confidential health records.
Does not schedule employees who have not been cleared and sends symptomatic staff to the Nurse.
Complete screening on time, report symptoms and exposures promptly, and follow infection control practices.

documentation: Employee health file for each person with screening dates, results and written clearances
Employee Health Tracker with due dates
Records of removal from duty and return-to-work clearance
Exposure incident and follow-up records
Hepatitis B vaccination acceptance or declination
Training records for body substance exposure and HIV training (PER-02)
Annual health file audit

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: All personnel files of employees, interns and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME], and the Administrator, Residence Manager and Nurse who create and maintain them.
policies.purpose: To ensure a complete, current, accurate and confidential record exists for every person who works at the IRA, so the agency can show that staff are qualified, screened, trained, certified and evaluated.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(ix) (personnel policies and procedures) and 686.6(a)(2)(ix)(a) (recruitment and hiring process, qualifications, education and skills, job descriptions, description of duties and responsibilities, and job performance evaluations), by requiring that these items be documented in each file.

[AGENCY NAME] keeps a personnel file for every employee. Each file holds: the application and résumé; the job description with description of duties and responsibilities; documentation of required qualifications, education and skills; reference checks; job performance evaluations; the outcome of the criminal history check and registry checks (kept in the confidential background file described in PER-04); medication administration certification and recertification records; and training records.

Training records must be current and available for review, and the agency monitors the type, frequency and amount of training each employee receives. Employees may be asked in interview whether they agree that the records are accurate (14 NYCRR 633.8(b)(3)). Under 14 NYCRR 633.17, staff may administer medication only if they hold a job description with direct care duties and have completed an OPWDD-approved course and practicum and been certified or recertified within the year. The agency keeps those certification dates current and removes uncertified staff from medication duties.

Personnel files are confidential. Employee health records are kept separately (PER-05), as are background check results. The retention period for personnel records has not been verified by the agency. No personnel record will be destroyed until the Administrator has confirmed the required retention period in writing with OPWDD and the Office of the Medicaid Inspector General. Until then all personnel records are retained.

definitions.definition: The record for one employee, intern or volunteer holding hiring, qualification, job description, evaluation, certification and training documents.
A separate restricted file with criminal history check and registry results and related decisions (PER-04).
Documented completion of an OPWDD-approved medication course and practicum, with certification or recertification within the past year.
A dated record of each training an employee completes, the subject, the length and the trainer, kept current to show required initial and annual training.
The agency mechanism used to monitor the type, frequency and amount of training and upcoming due dates for each employee.

procedures: At hiring, the Administrator opens a personnel file and checks it against the Personnel File Checklist. The checklist lists every required document and the date each is added.

Each file contains the signed job description with duties and responsibilities, and the written qualifications, education and skills required for the position. The Administrator verifies and notes proof of education, licenses and credentials before the first shift.
The Administrator records reference checks and the hiring decision rationale in the file (PER-01).

The Authorized Party records in the confidential background file the date and acceptable outcome of the criminal history and registry checks, with any written review (PER-04). The general personnel file shows only that the check was completed and cleared and the date.

The Administrator adds the new-hire orientation sign-in, the required training completed within 3 months of hire, and the annual retraining (PER-02) to the training record within 5 business days of each session.

The Administrator keeps and updates the training tracker for each employee, covering type, frequency, amount and next due date, and reviews it at least monthly. Training due within 30 days is reported to the Residence Manager.

The Residence Manager makes training records current and available at the site or in electronic form for review by OPWDD and other surveyors, and by the employee. During interviews, employees may be asked to confirm that the records match the training they have received.

The Nurse or Administrator keeps the medication certification record: name, job description with direct care duties, course and practicum completion date, certification date and recertification due date. The Nurse tracks the due date and alerts the Residence Manager and employee at least 60 days beforehand.
An employee whose medication certification has lapsed or is not complete is not scheduled for medication administration until recertified. The Residence Manager records the removal and return.

The Residence Manager completes job performance evaluations as provided in PER-01. The signed evaluation, the employee's comments and any improvement plan are placed in the file within 10 business days of the review.
Employee health and TB records are kept in a separate confidential employee health file (PER-05). They are not filed in the personnel file.

Personnel files are kept in a locked cabinet or access-controlled electronic system at [ADDRESS]. Only the Administrator, Nurse for health and certification items, Authorized Parties for background items, and others who need access for official purposes may open them. The Administrator logs access by outside parties such as regulators.
Employees may review the contents of their own personnel file on written request, in the presence of the Administrator or designee. Corrections are made by adding a dated note.

Twice a year the Administrator audits a sample of at least [NUMBER] personnel files, or all files if there are fewer, against the checklist. Deficiencies are corrected within 10 business days and reported to the governing body (GOV-02).

The Administrator confirms the retention period for personnel records in writing with OPWDD and OMIG. Until the period is confirmed and recorded in this manual, no personnel record is destroyed. After confirmation, records are destroyed only on the Administrator's written approval, by shredding or secure deletion, and the destruction is logged.
When an employee leaves, the Administrator records the end date and reason, closes the file, notifies the Justice Center under PER-04 and keeps the file for the retention period.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains complete personnel files and the training tracker, audits files, confirms retention requirements and controls access.
Completes evaluations, supplies attendance and training information, and ensures training records are available at the site.
Tracks medication certification and recertification and maintains employee health records separately.
Maintain background check results in the confidential background file.
Provide accurate information, attend required training and certification, and confirm their training records on request.

documentation: Personnel File Checklist for each employee
Job description, qualifications, education and skills documentation
Job performance evaluations
Criminal history check outcome (in the confidential background file)
Medication administration certification and recertification records
Training records and training tracker
File access log
Audit reports
Written confirmation of retention period from OPWDD and OMIG, and destruction log

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors of [AGENCY NAME] at or connected with the IRA, including drivers and escorts.
policies.purpose: To set clear expectations for how staff treat the people we support and their money, property and relationships. To ensure rights are never limited for staff convenience or as discipline. To prevent exploitation and abuse.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(ix) (personnel policies and procedures), which includes standards of staff conduct.

[AGENCY NAME] follows OPWDD's requirements on the conduct of employees, volunteers, family care providers and custodians. All staff must treat each individual with dignity and respect and promote positive relationships. Staff must be advised of the rights of individuals (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(6)), including freedom from abuse, corporal punishment, unnecessary mechanical restraint and unnecessary medication, privacy, use of personal money, visitors and communication, and the right to file grievances without reprisal.

Rights may not be limited for staff convenience, as a threat, as retribution or for discipline (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(7)). A rights limitation may be made only as a documented, individual, time-limited limitation for clinical purposes (633.4(a)(3)) and through the process in RIT-02.

Staff must keep professional boundaries. They may not borrow from, sell to, or accept gifts of significant value from individuals or families, use individuals' money or property for themselves, enter into romantic or sexual relationships with individuals, or involve individuals in their personal business. Staff must report suspected theft and financial exploitation of an individual according to the thresholds OPWDD sets for reportable incidents and notable occurrences (see REC-05 and REC-06) and must follow the agency's rules on handling personal funds (REC-02).

Staff receive training within 3 months of hire and annually on promoting positive relationships, abuse prevention, identification and reporting, laws and policies on protection from abuse, incident reporting, and safety and security (14 NYCRR 633.8).

definitions.definition: The limit that separates a staff member's professional role from personal, financial, romantic or other non-work relationships with an individual or their family.
Improper use of an individual's money or property for another's benefit, including theft, borrowing, misuse of benefits or pressuring an individual to give or spend money.
Money belonging to an individual, including benefits, allowances and savings, handled under REC-02.
A restriction placed on an individual mainly to make staff work easier. It is prohibited.
A limitation of rights used as punishment, threat or retribution. It is prohibited.

procedures: At hire and annually, the Administrator gives each staff member a written Code of Conduct and Boundaries summarizing this policy. The employee signs it and it is filed in the personnel file (PER-06).

Within the first week, and again after any change, the Residence Manager reviews with staff the rights of individuals and the conduct rules given to individuals at or before admission (RIT-01), and records the training.

Staff must complete the required training within 3 months of hire and annually thereafter on positive relationships, abuse prevention and reporting, incident reporting, and safety and security including fire safety (PER-02).

Staff treat individuals as adults. They use respectful language, honor privacy, knock before entering rooms, use the individual's preferred name and do not discuss individuals' personal matters in front of others.

Staff never use or threaten the loss of a right, a preferred activity, food, visitors, money or communication as a consequence for behavior or to get compliance. Any observed use is reported to the Residence Manager and handled under REC-05 and REC-06.

If a supervisor believes a limitation of rights is needed, the supervisor does not impose it. The program planning team handles the request under RIT-02, which requires it to be documented, individual, time-limited and clinical.

Staff do not accept gifts above a nominal value of $[AMOUNT], loans or money from individuals or families, and do not give personal loans or gifts. Tips, inheritances and bequests are reported to the Administrator.
Staff do not buy from, sell to, or hire individuals or use them for personal tasks. Staff do not use an individual's property, vehicle, phone, accounts or benefits.
