Staff handle individuals' funds only as provided in REC-02. This includes written receipts, two-person counts where required, and separate records for each individual. Staff never commingle personal funds with their own or the agency's.

Staff do not enter romantic or sexual relationships with individuals, including after the individual's discharge while the staff member remains involved with the individual's services, and do not share their personal social media or private contact details with individuals unless approved by the Administrator for an agreed reason.

Staff report any conflict of interest, outside relationship or family tie with an individual to the Administrator in writing before it is acted on. The Administrator decides on assignments and documents the decision.

Staff who suspect theft, missing money or property, or financial exploitation report it immediately to the Residence Manager. The Residence Manager notifies the Administrator, and the matter is evaluated for reporting under REC-05 and REC-06, including the VPCR hotline at 1-855-373-2122 if there is reasonable cause to suspect a reportable incident.

The Residence Manager secures records and receipts, reviews the individual's funds records and documents what was found. The Administrator reports to OPWDD, the Justice Center and law enforcement as required.

Staff who violate this policy are subject to discipline up to termination and, where required, referral to the Justice Center, OPWDD and law enforcement. The Administrator documents the action in the personnel file.
Staff may raise concerns about conduct, including a supervisor's, without threat of job loss under PER-03.
The Administrator reviews boundary and conduct complaints each quarter, and uses them to improve training and supervision (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Issues and enforces the Code of Conduct, decides conflicts of interest, reviews violations and ensures reports are made.
Reviews rights and conduct rules with staff, observes practice, and responds to boundary and financial concerns immediately.
Is the only body that may consider limitations of individuals' rights, under RIT-02.
Treat individuals with respect, keep boundaries, handle funds only as authorized and report suspected abuse, theft or exploitation.

documentation: Signed Code of Conduct and Boundaries in each personnel file
Training records on rights, positive relationships and abuse prevention
Conflict-of-interest disclosures and decisions
Gift disclosures
Incident reports and investigation records related to conduct, theft or exploitation
Disciplinary records
Quarterly conduct review summary

policies.title: Staffing Plan, Schedule and Supervision Coverage
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, Residence Manager, direct support staff, substitutes and any volunteers working at the OPWDD-certified IRA operated by [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To ensure enough qualified paid staff are available at the right times to supervise individuals, operate and maintain the home, and meet each person's assessed protective oversight needs, and that this is shown in a written plan and schedule.
policies.policy:
This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(ix) (personnel policies and procedures), which includes staffing.

Under 14 NYCRR 686.9(a), [AGENCY NAME] makes personnel available to supervise, operate and maintain the premises, and keeps a written staffing plan based on the number of individuals, their level of functioning and need, support staff needs and physical plant demands. The plan is site-specific and agrees with the site-specific protective oversight plan (IRA-01) and individual protective oversight assessments (IRA-02), as required by 14 NYCRR 686.16(a)(5)-(6).

A supervised IRA, as defined in 14 NYCRR 686.99, has staff onsite or proximately available whenever residents are present. In a supervised residence, staff are available whenever individuals are present. Less intensive coverage is allowed only on a documented individual assessment in the individual's plan of services (686.9(a)(4)). Where this home or any individual is served on a supportive basis, coverage follows the documented assessment of supervision need for that individual.

The agency keeps a written staffing schedule at the site showing supervision available or on call 24 hours a day (686.9(b)(1)). Section 686.9 sets no numeric staff-to-individual ratio and no awake-overnight rule. The agency therefore sets staffing levels, including overnight coverage, from the individual assessments and the staffing plan, and does not reduce coverage below what the assessments support.

Volunteers may not substitute for paid personnel (686.9(a)(3)). Family and friends of individuals are not counted as volunteers. If volunteers are used, the agency keeps a written volunteer utilization plan (686.9(b)(2)). Substitutes must meet the training and qualification requirements in IRA-03.

definitions.definition: The written plan, based on number of individuals, level of functioning and need, support staff needs and physical plant demands, that sets who is staffed at the site and when.
The written schedule at the site showing the names of staff and times, with supervision available or on call 24 hours a day.
An IRA with staff onsite or proximately available whenever residents are present (14 NYCRR 686.99).
Supervision and support appropriate to each person's assessed need, using staff and/or technology, as described in the site-specific plan (IRA-01, IRA-02).
A trained, qualified person who fills a scheduled paid shift when regular staff are absent.
An unpaid person who assists the program. Family and friends of individuals are not counted as volunteers. Volunteers may not take the place of paid staff.

procedures: The Administrator and Residence Manager write the staffing plan before the IRA opens and before any change in occupancy. It addresses the number of individuals, their level of functioning and need, support staff needs and physical plant demands, and is signed and dated.

Before preparing the plan, they review each individual's protective oversight assessment (IRA-02) and plan of services (REC-01). Coverage by shift, including overnight, is set from those assessments, and the basis is written in the plan.

The plan states for each time period (weekday, weekend, overnight, holidays) the minimum number of paid staff, their roles, and how supervision is provided whenever individuals are present. In a supervised IRA, a staff member is onsite or proximately available whenever any individual is present.

Less intensive coverage for any individual is used only if the individual's plan of services contains a documented individual assessment supporting it. The Residence Manager checks for the assessment before any reduced coverage is scheduled.

The Residence Manager prepares a written staffing schedule at least [NUMBER] days in advance, posts it at the site and shows supervision available or on call 24 hours a day. The schedule lists each staff member, their position, hours, and the on-call supervisor with phone number [PHONE].
The Residence Manager records any change to the schedule, with the reason and the name of the replacement, in the schedule log on the day it is made.

Only staff who have completed required background checks (PER-04), orientation and training (PER-02), and, where they administer medication, current certification (REC-07, PER-06) are scheduled alone with individuals. Provisional staff are scheduled only with a trained monitor present.

When regular staff call out, the Residence Manager fills the shift first from approved, trained substitutes who meet IRA-03 requirements, then from approved overtime. A shift is never left without coverage required by the plan.

If coverage cannot be filled, the Residence Manager notifies the on-call supervisor and the Administrator immediately. The Administrator arranges coverage, including reassigning qualified staff, and documents what happened.
A staff member never leaves a shift until relieved. The relieving and departing staff hand off, and sign the shift log.

Volunteers are used only to enrich activities and are never counted toward required staffing or used in place of paid staff. Family and friends of individuals are treated as visitors and are not counted as volunteers.

If volunteers are used, the Administrator writes a volunteer utilization plan covering roles, screening, training, supervision and limits, and keeps it at the site. Volunteers who have regular and substantial unsupervised contact complete the checks in PER-04.

The Administrator reviews the staffing plan and the schedule at least every 6 months, after any significant change in an individual's need or health, after any incident that may have been related to staffing, and when occupancy changes. Changes are dated and signed.
The Administrator compares the staffing plan with the site-specific protective oversight plan (IRA-01) and the annual review of each individual's protective oversight (IRA-02) to confirm agreement.
Staff may raise concerns about staffing levels using PER-03, without threat of job loss. The Administrator logs and responds to each concern.

The schedule and staffing plan are kept at the site and made available to OPWDD and other surveyors. The Administrator reports staffing gaps and corrective actions in the quality improvement review (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Writes and approves the staffing plan, ensures qualified paid staff coverage, reviews the plan at least every 6 months and resolves coverage gaps.
Prepares and posts the written schedule, fills absences with qualified staff, records schedule changes and verifies documented assessments for any reduced coverage.
Is reachable throughout the on-call period, responds to coverage and safety issues and informs the Administrator.
Advises on health-related supervision needs that affect the staffing plan and individual assessments.
Work assigned shifts, stay until relieved, and report staffing problems immediately.

documentation: Written site-specific staffing plan with dated reviews
Written staffing schedule posted at the site showing 24-hour supervision available or on call
Schedule change log and shift logs
Individual protective oversight assessments and plan-of-services documentation supporting any less intensive coverage
Substitute roster with qualification and training records
Volunteer utilization plan, if volunteers are used
Records of coverage gaps and corrective actions
Staffing concerns log entries

policies.category: Policy approval process and governing body role (686.6(a)(2)(x))
policies.title: Organization, Governing Body and Program Director Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: All OPWDD-certified IRA sites operated by [AGENCY NAME] (supervised and supportive), the governing body, the Executive Director, and Residence Managers
policies.purpose: To state how [AGENCY NAME] is organized, who is accountable for each certified residence, and what role the governing body plays in approving the agency's policies and procedures.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(x) — the approval process for policies/procedures, including a description of the role of the governing body in that process. [AGENCY NAME] operates each residence under an OPWDD operating certificate in one of the classes listed in 14 NYCRR 619.2 [C1]: supervised community residence, supportive community residence, or individualized residential alternative (IRA). The governing body is the final authority for approving every policy and procedure in the Policy and Procedure Manual and every material revision to it. No policy takes effect until the governing body has approved it, except for the interim changes allowed in Procedure 12, which the governing body must ratify. The governing body sets policy and oversees the agency. The Executive Director, [EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR NAME], is responsible to the governing body for operating all certified sites. A named Residence Manager is responsible for day-to-day operation of each residence. Because an IRA must meet the governance requirements of 14 NYCRR 686.5 through 686.16(a)(4), the Executive Director confirms conformance with the current text of 686.5 at each annual policy review.

definitions.definition: The board of directors, or for a limited liability company the managers or members, that holds legal authority over [AGENCY NAME] and approves its policies.
The agency executive named in this policy who is accountable to the governing body for all certified residences.
The person designated in writing as responsible for the day-to-day operation of one certified residence, including supervision of direct support staff and implementation of individuals' plans.
The OPWDD certificate that authorizes [AGENCY NAME] to operate a residence in a specific class under 14 NYCRR 619.2.
Any change to a policy that alters who must do what, a deadline, a right of an individual, or a regulatory commitment. Typographical and formatting corrections are not material.

procedures: The governing body adopts written bylaws or an operating agreement that identify its members, officers, quorum and voting rules, and require it to meet at least quarterly. The Board Chair or designated manager keeps minutes.
The governing body appoints the Executive Director in writing and defines the Executive Director's authority to operate all certified sites. The appointment is filed in the governance records.

The Executive Director designates a Residence Manager for each site in writing. The designation names the site, the Residence Manager, and an alternate who is qualified under PER-01 and IRA-03 to act when the Residence Manager is absent. The designation is posted in the staff area of the site.

The Executive Director confirms that each site's operating certificate class (supervised community residence, supportive community residence, or IRA) matches how the site is actually operated, and reports any mismatch to the governing body at its next meeting. See GOV-01.

The Executive Director or a designee drafts each new policy and each material revision using the document-control format in POL-02. The draft identifies the regulatory source and the roles that carry out each step.

Before submission, the Executive Director has the draft reviewed for regulatory conformance and operational feasibility by the Residence Manager(s) and the nursing, clinical and compliance leads where the subject touches their duties.

The Executive Director submits the draft to the governing body at least 7 days before the meeting where it will be voted on. The submission includes a plain-language summary of what is new or changed, the regulation that requires it, and any staff training the change will require.

The governing body discusses the draft and votes to approve it, approve it with changes, or return it. The minutes record the policy ID, the version, the vote, and any conditions. The Board Chair or designated manager signs and dates the approved policy.

The Executive Director issues the approved policy with an effective date. Within 10 business days, the Residence Manager places the new version in the site copy of the manual, removes the superseded version to the archive file, and reviews the change with all staff. Each staff member signs a read-and-understood sheet.

At least annually, the governing body reviews the whole manual using the process in POL-02. It also reviews the manual within 90 days after any regulatory change that affects it. The Executive Director documents the check of the current 686.5 governance text and any gaps found.

At least quarterly, the Executive Director reports to the governing body on incidents and abuse allegations (REC-05), quality improvement findings (GOV-02), staffing and training status (PER-08, PER-02), survey and certification activity (GOV-01), and open grievances and appeals (APP-01, APP-02). The minutes record the report and any direction given.

If the Executive Director must change a policy before the governing body can meet because of an immediate regulatory directive or a safety risk, the Executive Director may issue a written interim change marked INTERIM. The change is brought to the governing body for ratification at its next meeting, and no later than 30 days after issue. If it is not ratified, it is withdrawn and staff are told in writing.

The Residence Manager is responsible for implementing approved policies at the site, supervising staff, keeping the staffing schedule and site records current, and reporting problems promptly to the Executive Director. The Residence Manager does not approve or waive any policy. Any request for an exception goes to the Executive Director, who refers material exceptions to the governing body.

The governing body keeps approved policies, minutes, signature pages, and annual review records for the life of the policy plus at least 6 years after it is superseded, and makes them available to OPWDD surveyors on request.

responsibilities.duty: Approves all policies and material revisions, reviews the manual at least annually, receives quarterly reports, ratifies interim changes, and appoints the Executive Director.
Presides at meetings, signs approved policies, and ensures minutes record each approval.
Is accountable to the governing body for all certified sites, drafts and submits policies, appoints Residence Managers, issues approved policies, and checks the current 686.5 governance text.
Operates the residence day to day, keeps the manual current at the site, trains staff on each issued policy, and reports compliance concerns to the Executive Director.
Checks drafts for regulatory conformance and keeps the version register.

documentation: Bylaws or operating agreement
Governing body minutes recording each policy vote
Signed and dated approved policies with version numbers
Written appointment of the Executive Director and designation of each Residence Manager and alternate
Staff read-and-understood sheets for each issued policy
Annual manual review record, including the 686.5 conformance check
Quarterly executive reports to the governing body
INTERIM change notices and ratification records

policies.category: Policy approval process and governing body role (686.6(a)(2)(x))
policies.title: Policy Review, Approval and Document Control
policies.applies_to: All policies and procedures in the [AGENCY NAME] Policy and Procedure Manual; Executive Director, Compliance lead, Residence Managers, governing body
policies.purpose: To make sure the agency develops and implements every policy required of a community residence, keeps each policy current, and controls versions so staff and surveyors always see the approved text.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2) — each community residence shall develop and implement policies/procedures that address, at a minimum, the required subject areas — and 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2)(x) — the approval process for policies/procedures, including a description of the role of the governing body. [AGENCY NAME] develops and implements written policies covering admission, discharge, review and appeal, community involvement, individual participation in decisions, records, incidents and abuse, medication, emergencies and disasters, health and safety, and personnel. Each policy follows the approval process below: draft, internal review, governing body approval, controlled issue, staff training, and implementation. The governing body approves each policy and each material revision (see POL-01). Every policy is reviewed at least annually and after any regulatory change. [AGENCY NAME] tracks changes to OPWDD Part 633, including OPWDD's amendments to 633.9 and 633.15, and revises affected policies when the amendments take effect. Every policy carries a version number, effective date, and approval signature.

definitions.definition: A policy with a policy ID, version number, effective date, approval signature, and next review date that is recorded in the version register.
The master list kept by the Compliance lead of every policy, its current version, approval date, next review date, and where copies are held.
A new or amended statute, regulation, OPWDD directive, or survey finding that affects what a policy must say.
A prior version replaced by a newer approved one. It is archived and marked SUPERSEDED.

procedures: The Compliance lead maintains a version register listing each policy ID, title, version, approval date, effective date, next review date, owner, and the required subject area it satisfies under 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(2). The register maps the required subjects to policies: admission (ADM-01 to ADM-03), discharge (DIS-01, DIS-02), review and appeal (APP-01, APP-02), community involvement (COM-01), individual decision-making (DEC-01, DEC-02), records (REC-01 to REC-08), incidents and abuse (REC-05, REC-06), medication (REC-07), emergencies and disasters (EMR-01 to EMR-03), health and safety (HS-01 to HS-07), and personnel (PER-01 to PER-08).

Each policy has a named owner, who is a manager responsible for the subject. The owner drafts changes using the standard template: purpose, policy, definitions, procedures, responsibilities, documentation, and related policies.
Each policy shows its header block on the first page: policy ID, title, version, effective date, approver, and next review date. A footer shows the page number and version on every page.
The Compliance lead checks the draft against the regulation it implements and against any related policies. The owner resolves conflicts between policies before submission.

The owner submits the draft to the Executive Director, who forwards it to the governing body under the timeline in POL-01. The governing body votes and the minutes record the vote. The Board Chair or designated manager signs the approval page.
On approval, the Compliance lead assigns the new version number, enters it in the register, archives the superseded version stamped SUPERSEDED with the date, and issues the controlled copy.

Within 10 business days of approval, the Residence Manager replaces the site binder copy, collects staff read-and-understood signatures, and schedules any needed training. Staff must be trained on a changed policy before they are expected to perform the changed duty.

Policies are reviewed at least once every 12 months. The Compliance lead sends each owner a review notice 60 days before the review date. The owner confirms in writing that the policy was reviewed and either that it is unchanged or that a revision is submitted.

The Compliance lead reviews OPWDD notices, Part 633 and Part 686 updates, and survey findings at least monthly. For any regulatory change, the Compliance lead identifies affected policies within 14 days and the owners submit revisions within 60 days, or sooner if the effective date requires. The Compliance lead tracks OPWDD's pending amendments to 633.9 and 633.15 until they are final and then updates the affected policies.
After any survey deficiency, incident review, or quality improvement finding that points to a policy gap, the owner revises the policy and submits it for approval under this process.

The Compliance lead presents the version register and the list of policies reviewed, revised, or overdue to the governing body at least annually. The governing body records its annual review of the entire manual in its minutes.

The Residence Manager keeps the full current manual at the site, available to staff and individuals at any time. The Compliance lead audits every site's binder twice a year to confirm that versions match the register.
Superseded versions and approval records are retained for at least 6 years after replacement so the agency can show which policy was in force on a given date.
No staff member may alter an approved policy, post an unapproved version, or work from an uncontrolled copy. Staff who find an error report it to the Compliance lead.

responsibilities.duty: Approves policies and material revisions and records its annual review of the manual.
Ensures the process is followed, assigns policy owners, and submits drafts to the governing body.
Maintains the version register, monitors regulatory change, issues controlled copies, and audits site binders.
Drafts, reviews annually, and revises the policy and trains staff on changes.
Keeps the site manual current, collects staff signatures, and reports errors or gaps.

documentation: Version register
Approved policies with header block, version, effective date, and approval signature
Governing body minutes recording approvals and the annual manual review
Policy owner annual review confirmations
Archive of superseded versions
Staff read-and-understood sheets and training records
Site binder audit reports
Regulatory change log, including tracking of the Part 633 amendments

policies.category: Policy approval process and governing body role (686.6(a)(2)(x))
policies.title: Policy and Procedure Manual: Contents and Public Availability
policies.applies_to: The [AGENCY NAME] Policy and Procedure Manual; all staff; individuals, parents, guardians, correspondents and the public
policies.purpose: To ensure the Policy and Procedure Manual contains every required content area, is kept at each site, and is open to the people it affects.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.6(a)(3) — the agency/facility policy/procedure manual is a public document and shall be available to individuals, parents, guardians, correspondents, staff and others — and 14 NYCRR 686.6(b)(3)(i)-(viii) — a written manual exists addressing admission and discharge, administration of records, emergencies and disasters, health and safety, personnel, review and appeal procedures, community involvement, and individuals' involvement in community residence activities. The manual is a public document. [AGENCY NAME] makes it available on request, without charge for inspection, to individuals, parents, guardians, correspondents, staff, and other interested persons. A complete current copy is kept at each site. Under 14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(8) [C12], individuals' rights and conduct rules are given to each person at or before admission and after any change, in the person's primary language. Under 633.4(a)(15), interpreters are provided at no charge.

definitions.definition: A document that [AGENCY NAME] must make available to any person who asks to see it, subject to removal of private information about individuals or staff.
A person designated by an individual, or by the individual's guardian, to receive information and notices about the individual's services.
The complete current controlled manual, in print or in a form readable on a site device, kept where staff and visitors can reach it without having to ask for a key.
The language the individual uses and understands best, including sign language and other communication methods.

procedures: The Compliance lead organizes the manual so that it contains, at minimum, the eight areas required by 14 NYCRR 686.6(b)(3): (i) admission and discharge — ADM-01 to ADM-03, DIS-01, DIS-02, SUP-01, SUP-02; (ii) administration of records — REC-01 to REC-08; (iii) emergencies and disasters — EMR-01 to EMR-03, IRA-04; (iv) health and safety — HS-01 to HS-07, REC-05 to REC-07; (v) personnel — PER-01 to PER-08; (vi) review and appeal procedures for concerns of individuals and their correspondents — APP-01, APP-02; (vii) community involvement of staff and individuals — COM-01; (viii) individuals' involvement in community residence activities — DEC-01, DEC-02.

The manual's table of contents lists each of the eight areas with the policies that satisfy them, so a reviewer can find each one. The Compliance lead updates the table of contents with each approved revision under POL-02.

The Residence Manager keeps one complete current copy of the manual at the site in a labeled binder or on a device in the common office area. The location is posted, and staff and individuals are told where it is during orientation and admission.

Staff may read the manual at any time during work hours. The Residence Manager reviews the location and contents of the manual with every new hire during orientation and records it in the training record. See PER-02.

Any individual, parent, guardian, correspondent, or other person who asks to see the manual is shown it. The Residence Manager or Executive Director provides it within 2 business days of a request, in print or electronic form. If a person asks for a copy, the agency provides it and does not charge for providing it.

Before giving out the manual, the staff member checks that it contains no confidential information about any individual or staff member. The manual contains policies only. Records of individuals are never kept in it. See REC-03.

At or before admission, and again after any change, the Residence Manager gives each individual and guardian or correspondent the individual's rights and the rules of conduct required by 14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(8) in the person's primary language. The Residence Manager also advises them of the complaint contacts required by 633.4(a)(12) and of any changes to them. The date and the person who received the information are recorded in the individual's record.

If an individual or family member does not read English or needs another communication method, the Residence Manager arranges a qualified interpreter, translated materials, or an accessible format at no charge, as required by 633.4(a)(15). The agency does not rely on other individuals or on children to interpret. See RIT-03.
The Residence Manager reviews the rights and conduct rules with each individual in a way the person can understand, and records any follow-up the person needs to understand them.

The Executive Director posts a notice at each site and on the agency's public information channel, [WEBSITE OR PUBLIC CONTACT], stating that the manual is a public document and how to request it. The notice includes the agency address [ADDRESS] and phone [PHONE].
The Compliance lead checks twice a year that every site has a complete current manual with all eight required areas and that the public notice is posted. Gaps are corrected within 14 days.
The Residence Manager logs every request to see the manual, including who asked, the date, and the date the manual was provided. The Executive Director reviews the log at least quarterly for delays.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the manual is complete, public, and available at every site.
Maintains the eight-area table of contents, audits site copies twice a year, and keeps the public notice current.
Keeps the site copy, shows it to anyone who asks, provides rights and conduct rules in the primary language, and logs requests.
Know where the manual is, help individuals and visitors find it, and refer requests for copies to the Residence Manager.

documentation: Manual table of contents mapped to 14 NYCRR 686.6(b)(3)(i)-(viii)
Site copy audit records
Public availability notice and posting verification
Log of requests to see the manual
Record of rights and conduct rules given, date, language, and recipient
Interpreter or translation arrangements
Staff orientation record showing review of the manual

policies.category: IRA site-specific protective oversight plan and evacuation plan (686.16)
policies.title: Site-Specific Protective Oversight Plan
policies.applies_to: Each [AGENCY NAME] IRA site (supervised and supportive); Residence Managers, supervisors, direct support staff, nursing, and the Executive Director
policies.purpose: To require a written protective oversight plan for each IRA site that provides the supervision each person needs, and to state how that need is assessed, how substitutes are used, who may supervise, and how the plan is reviewed.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.16(a)(5) — each IRA facility shall ensure the provision of, or provide as its minimum responsibility, protective oversight appropriate to the person's needs. It also meets 686.16(a)(6) — the site-specific written plan for protective oversight — including (a)(6)(i) assessment of each person's need for the amount and type of supervision, using staff and/or technology as appropriate; (a)(6)(ii) use of appropriately trained substitute personnel when primary assigned personnel are unavailable; (a)(6)(iii) qualifications and training requirements of those responsible for supervision; and (a)(6)(iv) a process to review periodically, and modify as necessary, each person's continuing need for the originally recommended protective oversight. A written site-specific plan, a condition of the IRA operating certificate (OMR 248), exists for every IRA site before the site opens and is kept at the site. Under 14 NYCRR 686.99 [C2], in a supervised IRA staff are onsite or proximately available whenever residents are present. The plan states the supervision model for the site and the exact coverage each person has, and it does not reduce coverage below what an individual assessment supports. The plan is revised whenever residents' needs or staffing patterns change.

definitions.definition: The supervision, guidance, and monitoring provided to a person in a manner suited to the person's needs, so that the person is safe and receives needed help.
An IRA in which staff are onsite or proximately available whenever residents are present (14 NYCRR 686.99).
An IRA for persons who need less than continuous supervision, with the coverage and support each person needs set by individual assessment and documented in the plan of services.
Staff who cover an assigned shift or duty when the primary assigned staff are unavailable and who have completed all training required for the coverage they provide.
Devices such as door alarms, sensors, and remote monitoring used with a person's informed consent as part of a documented supervision plan, and not as a substitute for staff where staff are required.
Close enough to arrive and help promptly, as defined for each person in the plan.

procedures: Before the site opens or admits anyone, the Executive Director and the nurse write the site-specific protective oversight plan. It states the site's certification class and supervision model, the number of beds, the layout features that affect supervision (bedroom locations, stairs, bathrooms, exits), and the staffing pattern by shift.

The plan includes an assessment section: for each person admitted, the IRA-02 individual assessment determines the amount and type of supervision required, including whether it is provided by staff, by technology, or by both, and under which circumstances. The plan states the minimum coverage for each time of day.

For each person, the plan records the coverage level, for example staff present, staff awake overnight, or staff available on call with a stated response time. The Residence Manager transcribes each level into the shift assignment sheet so that staff can see it at the start of each shift.

Any technology used for supervision is listed in the plan with its purpose, who may use it, who responds to alerts and how fast, how it is tested (at least monthly), and the person's consent or the consent of the person's legally authorized representative. See DEC-02 and RIT-02 if it limits any right.

The plan sets qualifications for those who supervise: a Residence Manager who meets PER-01 qualifications, supervisors who meet IRA-03 requirements, current first aid training, completion of all required orientation and trainings under PER-02 and 14 NYCRR 633.8, medication certification where they pass medications under REC-07, and a completed criminal history check under PER-04.

The plan establishes a substitute process: a current list of approved substitutes with their training dates, the order in which the Residence Manager calls them, and an on-call supervisor for each shift with a [PHONE] number. A substitute may work alone only after the Residence Manager confirms that they meet every qualification in the plan and have reviewed each person's protective oversight plan.

When primary staff are unavailable, the Residence Manager or on-call supervisor fills the shift with an approved substitute before the outgoing staff leave. A shift is never left below the coverage the plan requires. If no approved substitute can be found, the on-call supervisor covers in person and the Executive Director is notified the same day.

Volunteers may not substitute for paid personnel. Family and friends are not volunteers for this purpose but also may not be counted toward required coverage. If volunteers are used, the volunteer utilization plan required by the staffing rules applies. See PER-08.

Every staff member with supervision duties reads the site plan and each resident's protective oversight plan, and signs that they understand it, before their first shift and whenever it changes. The Residence Manager checks this at least quarterly through observation of shifts.

The plan sets the periodic review process for each person's continuing need for the recommended oversight: at least annually, and sooner at any change in condition, behavior, medication, health, incident pattern, or a request from the person or the person's representative. The review is carried out under IRA-02. Results that change coverage are entered into the plan within 5 business days.

The Executive Director reviews the whole site plan at least annually and whenever the resident group, the building, the staffing pattern, or the supervision model changes. The review is documented with the date, the findings, and the signature of the Executive Director, and is reported to the governing body at its next quarterly meeting.
The Residence Manager keeps the current plan and the superseded versions at the site, available to staff and to OPWDD surveyors.

If a person's assessed need rises above what the plan provides, the Residence Manager adds staff coverage immediately, notifies the Executive Director and nurse the same day, and starts a plan revision. The person's plan of services is updated under REC-01.

The Executive Director tracks incidents, near misses, and missing person events for patterns that show the oversight plan is inadequate. See REC-05, BEH-03, and GOV-02. Findings lead to a revision of the plan.

responsibilities.duty: Writes and approves the site plan with the nurse, reviews it at least annually, and reports to the governing body.
Implements the plan at the site, keeps substitute and on-call lists, confirms qualifications, transcribes coverage levels to the shift sheet, and reports changes in need.
Contributes health information to each person's supervision assessment and reviews coverage after health changes.
Know each person's plan, provide the specified coverage, and report any gap at once.
Assesses each person's need and recommends type and amount of supervision.

documentation: Written site-specific protective oversight plan, dated and signed
Per-person coverage levels and shift assignment sheets
Technology supervision log and test records, if applicable
Approved substitute list with qualification and training dates
Staff signed acknowledgments of the plan and each person's protective oversight plan
Annual plan review record
Revision history and superseded versions
Incident and coverage-gap reports

policies.category: IRA site-specific protective oversight plan and evacuation plan (686.16)
policies.title: Individual Protective Oversight Assessment and Annual Review
policies.applies_to: Every person living in a [AGENCY NAME] IRA; program planning team, Residence Manager, nurse, direct support staff
policies.purpose: To make sure every person has an individual protective oversight plan based on an analysis of their need, and that the plan is reviewed at least annually, revised as needed, and integrated with the person's other services.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.16(a)(6)(i) — assessment of each person's need for the amount and type of supervision, including staff and/or technology as appropriate to the person and circumstance; 686.16(a)(6)(iv) — a process to review periodically, and modify as necessary, the person's continuing need for the originally recommended protective oversight; and 686.16(b)(3) — each person has a plan for protective oversight based on an analysis of need that has periodically, but at least annually, been reviewed, revised as appropriate, and integrated with other services received. Each person has an individual protective oversight plan completed before or at admission. It is reviewed at least every 12 months and whenever the person's condition or circumstances change. It is part of the individualized service plan (ISP) and plan of services and is written in a way that staff can implement. Where the program planning team assesses that a person needs less intensive coverage than the supervised model, the individual assessment is documented in the plan of services and the coverage is only reduced to the level the assessment supports. For IRAs with 8 or fewer beds, each ISP includes a current fire-evacuation evaluation. Under 14 NYCRR 636-1 and 636-1.4 [C39], the person-centered plan documents the person's choices, and any modification of a person's rights for supervision purposes needs a specific assessed need and justification in the plan.

definitions.definition: The written plan, based on assessment, stating the amount and type of supervision a person needs, who provides it, how it is delivered, and how it is reviewed.
The person, their family or advocate as the person chooses, the Residence Manager, nurse, clinicians, and other people the person wants involved who develop and review the person's plan of services.
A current assessment of how quickly and with what help the person can leave the building in a fire, which feeds the facility evacuation plan (IRA-04).
The individualized service plan, called the plan of services at [AGENCY NAME], that records the person's goals, supports, and services.

procedures: Before admission, the Residence Manager and nurse gather the referral material, prior assessments, medical and behavioral history, risk information, and the person's and family's information about the supports the person needs. For supportive IRAs, the supervision-need assessment under SUP-01 is part of this step.

Within 7 days of admission, and before the plan is finalized, the program planning team assesses the person's need for supervision in each area: mobility and evacuation, medical risks such as seizures and choking, behavior and elopement risk, medication, community safety, personal care, time alone at home and in the community, and ability to call for help.

The team determines the amount of supervision (continuous, awake overnight, periodic checks, on call) and the type (direct staff, technology, or both) the person needs in each setting and time of day. It records the reasons, the options considered, and the person's own preferences and views.

The team writes the individual protective oversight plan. It states what staff must do, any conditions that raise or lower coverage, who responds in an emergency, and the plan's review date. The plan is signed by the Residence Manager, nurse, and the person or representative.

If the assessment supports less intensive coverage than the supervised model, the team documents the individual assessment in the plan of services before the lower coverage begins. The Executive Director reviews and approves it in writing. Without a documented assessment, full supervised coverage continues.

The plan is integrated into the ISP. The Residence Manager makes sure the plan of services references the protective oversight plan and that the goals, risk plans, behavior supports, and health plans do not conflict with it. See REC-01 and HS-03.

For any IRA with 8 or fewer beds, the Residence Manager makes sure each ISP contains a current fire-evacuation evaluation. It is updated whenever the person's mobility, hearing, vision, cognition, or behavior changes, and the results are used to update the evacuation plan under IRA-04.

If the plan would limit a person's rights, for example by locking a door or restricting access to a room, the team follows RIT-02, documents the specific assessed need and justification in the plan under 14 NYCRR 636-1.4, and gets any needed consent. Supervision is not increased for staff convenience, as discipline, or as a threat.

The Residence Manager gives each person, and the guardian or correspondent, a copy of their protective oversight plan, in the person's primary language and format, and explains it. The person's right to participate, object, and appeal is explained under 633.4 and APP-01.

Every staff member who works with the person reads the plan and signs a review sheet before working alone with the person. The Residence Manager checks at least quarterly, by observing practice, that the plan is carried out as written in the ISP.

The plan is reviewed at least once every 12 months, no later than the anniversary of the previous review, and at the annual ISP meeting. The team reviews whether the amount and type of oversight still fit, using incident reports, nursing notes, behavior data, daily documentation, and the person's own views.

The plan is also reviewed within 14 days of any hospitalization, significant change in health, new medication with safety effects, serious incident, missing person event, change in housemates, change in ability to evacuate, or request from the person or representative.

The team documents each review: date, participants, findings, changes made or the reason none were needed, and the next review date. If it changes coverage, the Residence Manager updates the shift sheet and site plan (IRA-01) within 5 business days and informs all staff.

The Compliance lead audits plans twice a year, checking that each person has a current plan, that it was reviewed within 12 months, that the fire-evacuation evaluation is current in each ISP where required, and that staff acknowledgments are present. Overdue reviews are reported to the Executive Director the same day they are found.

responsibilities.duty: Assesses need, writes the individual plan, and reviews it at least annually and on change.
Schedules reviews, integrates the plan into the ISP, assures staff acknowledgments, and updates shift coverage.
Provides health-based risk information, and reviews the plan after any change in health.
Approves any reduction below the supervised model and receives overdue review reports.
Audits plans and fire-evacuation evaluations.
Implement the plan as written and report changes in the person's needs.

documentation: Individual protective oversight assessment and plan, signed
Documentation of individual assessment for any less intensive coverage
Annual and event-driven review records
Current fire-evacuation evaluation in each ISP where required
Staff acknowledgment sheets
Copy given to person and representative, with date
Compliance audit reports

policies.category: IRA site-specific protective oversight plan and evacuation plan (686.16)
policies.title: Supervisor and Substitute Qualifications, Training and First Aid
policies.applies_to: Residence Managers, supervisors, direct support staff who supervise, substitute and relief staff, and the Executive Director
policies.purpose: To set who may supervise individuals, what training they must have, including first aid, and how appropriately trained substitutes are used, so that every person receives protective oversight as written.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.16(a)(6)(ii) — the use of appropriately trained substitute personnel when primary assigned personnel are unavailable; 686.16(a)(6)(iii) — the establishment of qualifications and training requirements of those responsible for supervision; and 686.16(b)(4)(i)-(iii) — OPWDD verifies that parties with supervision responsibilities have received training appropriate to the protective oversight needs of the persons in the facility, including but not limited to first aid, are aware of the specifics of each person's plan for protective oversight, and that each person's plan is implemented as specified in the individualized service plan. Only staff who meet the qualifications below may supervise individuals. Staff must have current first aid training, training on each person's protective oversight plan, and all training required by 14 NYCRR 633.8 [C13]. Substitutes meet the same standards as primary staff before working alone. Volunteers may not substitute for paid personnel (14 NYCRR 686.9(a)(3) [C5]). Supervision staffing is always set by the staffing plan and schedule at the site, which shows supervision available or on call 24 hours a day (686.9(b)(1)).

definitions.definition: Any staff member, including a Residence Manager, assigned to provide or direct protective oversight during a shift.
A staff member who covers for primary assigned staff and who has been approved under this policy.
Training that teaches staff to respond to injury and sudden illness, from an approved provider, with a certificate showing the date and the expiration.
The staff scheduled to cover a shift or duty on the staffing schedule.

procedures: Minimum qualifications for supervisors: age and education or experience required in PER-01 for the position; a satisfactory criminal history check and registry clearances (PER-04); employee health and TB screening (PER-05); completion of all training in this policy; and, if they pass medications, current certification under REC-07.

Required training before a staff member supervises alone: orientation to the site and its protective oversight plan; the specifics of each resident's protective oversight plan and risk plans; emergency procedures including evacuation under IRA-04; incident reporting (REC-05); abuse prevention and reporting (REC-06); and positive behavior support (BEH-01).

First aid: every staff member who supervises must hold current first aid training, completed before they are assigned alone on any shift. The Residence Manager records the issue and expiry dates and re-trains staff before expiration. A staff member with expired first aid is not scheduled to supervise alone. If a qualified person is not available, the on-call supervisor covers.

Training under 14 NYCRR 633.8 [C13]: within 3 months of hire, each employee completes training on human growth and development, characteristics of persons served, promoting positive relationships, abuse prevention, identification and reporting, laws and policies on protection from abuse, incident reporting, and safety and security including fire safety. Each employee is retrained annually on positive relationships, abuse prevention and reporting, laws and policies, incident reporting, and safety and security including fire safety. Training on preventing and managing significant-risk body substance exposure is also given. Supervisors complete the safety and abuse prevention training before being assigned alone with individuals, regardless of the 3-month period. See PER-02.

Training specific to the person: Each supervisor receives training suited to the needs of the people living at the site, for example seizure response, choking response, mobility or transfer techniques, diabetes or other health risks, and behavior supports. The nurse or clinician delivers it and signs the competency check. See HS-03.

Awareness of each person's plan: before the first shift and after any plan change, the staff member reads each person's protective oversight plan and discusses it with the Residence Manager. The staff member signs and dates the acknowledgment. Staff who have not signed may not be assigned alone.

Substitute approval: the Residence Manager adds a person to the approved substitute list only after confirming that every qualification above is met and is documented in the personnel file. The list shows each substitute's first aid expiry, last plan review, and last training date. The Residence Manager reviews the list monthly.

Using a substitute: when primary staff cannot work, the Residence Manager or on-call supervisor calls approved substitutes from the list in the stated order. The substitute receives a shift handover covering each person's plan, current risks, medications, appointments, and any incident in the last 72 hours. The handover is documented in the communication log.

No unapproved person covers a shift. Volunteers, family members, friends of residents, and staff from other sites who have not completed site-specific training do not substitute for paid supervisors. If an unqualified person is present, the Residence Manager keeps qualified staff on duty at the required level.

The Residence Manager observes each new supervisor and each new substitute on at least one shift before they work alone. The observation checks plan knowledge, safe supervision, documentation, and emergency response, and is documented.

The Residence Manager checks, at least quarterly, that supervisors know each person's plan and that the plan is carried out as specified in the ISP. The check includes observing practice, reviewing daily documentation, and interviewing staff. Findings are recorded and gaps are corrected through coaching and retraining within 14 days.

The Residence Manager keeps a training matrix showing each staff member's dates for orientation, 633.8 training, annual retraining, first aid, medication certification, plan acknowledgments, and evacuation drill participation. The matrix is monitored so that all training is current. The Compliance lead audits it quarterly and reports lapses to the Executive Director.

Supervisors report to the Residence Manager and the on-call supervisor at once if they cannot meet the protective oversight required for any person on a shift. The Residence Manager arranges coverage and records the event. See IRA-01.

Personnel files hold proof of qualifications, training certificates, first aid cards, and plan acknowledgments. See PER-06. Staff performance evaluations assess whether supervisors implement protective oversight plans correctly. See PER-01.

responsibilities.duty: Sets minimum qualifications, ensures resources for first aid and other training, and reviews the quarterly training audit.
Approves substitutes, schedules only qualified supervisors, orients and observes new staff, and maintains the training matrix.
Provides and signs off on person-specific training and competency checks.
Maintain current training, know each person's plan, and report any inability to provide required coverage.
Audits training and substitute records quarterly.

documentation: Training matrix for all supervisors and substitutes
First aid certificates with issue and expiry dates
Training records under 14 NYCRR 633.8, including orientation and annual retraining
Signed acknowledgments of each person's protective oversight plan
Approved substitute list with qualification dates
Shift handover entries in the communication log
New-staff observation records
Quarterly supervisory check records and audit reports

policies.category: IRA site-specific protective oversight plan and evacuation plan (686.16)
policies.title: Facility Evacuation Plan, Staff and Resident Training and Evaluation
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] OPWDD-certified IRAs (supervised and supportive); all staff, substitutes and individuals residing in the home
policies.purpose: To make sure every IRA operated by [AGENCY NAME] has a written facility evacuation plan that has been put into practice. Staff and the individuals living in the home are trained on the plan and evaluated on how they carry it out, so everyone can leave safely in a fire or other emergency.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.16(b)(1) (OPWDD verification that each IRA has implemented a facility evacuation plan, and that staff and persons residing in the facility are trained and evaluated regarding their performance of the plan). [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written evacuation plan for each IRA site. The plan is implemented, not just filed. Every staff member, including substitutes, and every individual is trained on the plan and is evaluated on performing it. Evaluations are documented. Drills are run at no less than the minimum frequencies set by OPWDD ADM #2012-02, and drill logs are kept. If the evacuation plan or a drill shows that any occupants cannot evacuate in 3 minutes or less, the home also meets 14 NYCRR 635-7.2(a)(1)(iii) as required by 686.16(a)(3). Homes of 8 or fewer persons meet the 635-7.1(h)(1)(ii) building code requirement (NYC: 635-7.1(i)(1)(ii)) and 635-7.4(b)(3). Homes of 9 or more persons meet 635-7.1, 7.2 and 7.3. For homes of 8 or fewer beds, each individual's ISP contains a current fire-evacuation evaluation, and fire alarms are audible in sleeping areas with bedroom doors closed. In supportive IRAs, all occupants are also trained to evacuate (see SUP-03).

definitions.definition: The written, site-specific plan stating how all occupants leave the home safely in an emergency. It covers alarm response, assigned staff duties, each person's assistance needs, exit routes, a safe meeting place and who calls for help.
A practice exercise of the evacuation plan. Under ADM #2012-02 these are generally procedurally synonymous.
A documented review, by a trained observer, of how well each staff member and each individual carried out their part of the plan, with corrective retraining when needed.
The time needed for all occupants to reach a point of safety. A time of more than 3 minutes triggers 14 NYCRR 635-7.2(a)(1)(iii).
An evaluation of each individual's ability to evacuate. It is kept in the person's ISP for IRAs of 8 or fewer beds.

procedures: Before the home opens, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and the Residence Manager write a site-specific evacuation plan for the home. It states the number of certified beds, exits, alarm locations, primary and secondary routes, a designated outside meeting place and the home's [ADDRESS].

The plan identifies each individual's evacuation needs (mobility, vision, hearing, behavior, medication, communication, need for prompting or physical help) from the person's fire-evacuation evaluation and protective oversight assessment (IRA-02). It assigns a staff member to help each person who needs help.

For homes of 8 or fewer persons, the Residence Manager makes sure each ISP contains a current fire-evacuation evaluation and updates it at least annually, and whenever the person's condition or abilities change.

The Residence Manager has the plan reviewed against the correct building-code tier: 635-7.1(h)(1)(ii) and 635-7.4(b)(3) for 8 or fewer persons (NYC: 635-7.1(i)(1)(ii)), or 635-7.1, 7.2 and 7.3 for 9 or more persons. The review is documented.

The plan is timed. The first full drill after admission, and each later full drill, records total evacuation time. If any drill or evaluation shows that occupants cannot evacuate in 3 minutes or less, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] notifies the OPWDD certification area office and ensures that 635-7.2(a)(1)(iii) is met before further certification activity.
The plan is posted in a visible place in the home. Floor-plan evacuation maps are posted at each exit route and in common areas, in formats accessible to the individuals living there.

New staff and substitutes are trained on the plan during orientation, before working alone, and the Residence Manager signs off on a hands-on walkthrough. This is recorded in the personnel record (PER-02).

Each individual is trained on the plan in a way that fits their communication and learning style within [NUMBER] days of admission and after any plan change. Training is repeated in each drill. The training and the person's response are documented.

The Residence Manager sets a drill schedule using the minimum number, spacing and variations required by OPWDD ADM #2012-02. The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms the schedule against the current ADM text and records it in the drill log. Drills are run on different shifts, including when individuals are asleep, to the extent ADM #2012-02 requires or allows.

If a drill is varied for a reason ADM #2012-02 allows (for example, when conditions make a full evacuation unsafe), the reason is recorded in the drill log. The minimum number of full evacuation drills is still completed. Where the home is certified under the Health Care chapters of the Life Safety Code, defend-in-place is not used for non-fire evacuations.

A trained staff member conducts each drill. They sound the alarm, time the drill and observe each person. They record the date, time, shift, type of drill, who took part, time to a point of safety, problems and any individual who needed extra prompting.

Each staff member and each individual is evaluated on their performance in at least one drill in each cycle set by the schedule. The evaluation notes whether the person performed their role correctly (for example, alarm response, route, meeting place). A person who does not perform correctly is retrained within [NUMBER] days and re-evaluated.

In homes of 9 or more persons, the Residence Manager makes sure all heat and smoke-detecting alarm devices are tested quarterly as required by 635-7.3(e)(i)(1), and keeps the test documentation. The same schedule is used in smaller homes. In homes of 8 or fewer beds, staff check weekly that alarms are audible in every sleeping area with the door closed, and record the check.

Problems from drills, such as slow evacuation, blocked exits, alarms not heard or staff errors, are corrected promptly. The Residence Manager records the corrective action and its date on the drill log, and the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews drill logs monthly.

The plan is reviewed at least annually, and also after any drill failure, building change, change in the individuals living in the home, change in staffing pattern or real emergency. The review is signed and dated by the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

When OPWDD staff verify implementation, the Residence Manager shows the current plan, the drill logs, staff and individual training records and evaluations, alarm test records and fire-evacuation evaluations in the ISPs.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the plan, confirms the drill schedule against ADM #2012-02, reviews drill logs monthly, and makes sure corrections and OPWDD notifications are made.
Writes and updates the plan, trains staff and individuals, schedules and conducts drills, documents evaluations and retrains where needed.
Know the plan, take part in drills and perform their assigned evacuation duties, and report hazards or blocked exits at once.
Helps identify medical or mobility needs that affect evacuation and the 3-minute evacuation time.
Take part in training and drills with support, and tell staff of concerns about leaving the home safely.

documentation: Written facility evacuation plan and annual review sign-off
Drill schedule and drill logs (date, time, shift, evacuation time, participants, problems, corrective action)
Staff and substitute training records and sign-offs
Individual training records and performance evaluations
Fire-evacuation evaluations in each ISP (homes of 8 or fewer beds)
Alarm test and audibility records
Records of OPWDD notifications if the 3-minute time is not met

policies.title: Supportive IRA Referral, Intake and Supervision-Need Assessment
policies.applies_to: Supportive IRAs only (use only where the residence is certified as a supportive IRA); admissions staff, Residence Manager, nurse and the admission review team
policies.purpose: To set out how [AGENCY NAME] receives referrals, completes intake, assesses each applicant's need for supervision, and decides on admission to a supportive IRA, where staff are typically not onsite at all times.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.8(a)(4) (the agency/facility shall develop policies and procedures governing referral, intake and admission) and 14 NYCRR 686.8(a)(5) (these policies shall specifically address how the agency will assess and meet the applicant's need for supervision in the supportive residence and shall include the admission criteria listed in 686.8(b)(1)). [AGENCY NAME] admits to a supportive IRA only when a documented assessment shows that the person's supervision needs can be met by the supports the home actually has. These include staff visits, on-call staff and technology. Because staff are typically not onsite at all times, the assessment looks at what the person can do safely when no staff are present. Every placement requires approval of the OPWDD DDRO Director before admission, using OPWDD's Request for Approval to Fill a Residential Opportunity. Admission follows 14 NYCRR Subpart 636-3 and 24-ADM-03, including OPWDD's Emergency Need, Substantial Need and Current Need categories. Vacancies are reported promptly so each is first considered for people with Emergency Need. The admission criteria in 686.8(b)(1) are applied exactly as written in the regulation and are listed on the agency's admission checklist.

definitions.definition: An IRA where staff are not required to be onsite at all times. Supervision and support are matched to the individual's assessed need. This differs from a supervised IRA, where staff are onsite or proximately available whenever residents are present (14 NYCRR 686.99).
A written assessment of the applicant's ability to stay safe and manage daily life when staff are not present, and of the supports needed to meet the gap.

definitions.term: Emergency Need, Substantial Need, Current Need
definitions.definition: The categories OPWDD assigns to people seeking residential opportunities under Subpart 636-3 and 24-ADM-03.
OPWDD Developmental Disabilities Regional Office Director approval of a placement, obtained before admission.

procedures: Admissions staff log each referral on the day it is received: date, referral source, applicant name, OPWDD need category if known, and contact information for the applicant and any legal representative.

The Residence Manager acknowledges the referral within [NUMBER] business days and explains to the applicant and their representative how a supportive IRA works, including that staff are typically not onsite at all times.
Admissions staff report each vacancy promptly to OPWDD as required by 24-ADM-03, and consider referrals so that people with Emergency Need are considered first.

The Residence Manager collects referral records: current plan of services or person-centered plan, medical and medication records, behavioral and psychiatric history, incident history, functional assessments, guardianship or health care proxy documents, and information on income and benefits.

The admission review team (Residence Manager, nurse, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and, when available, the applicant's care manager) meets with the applicant and their representative and visits the home. The applicant decides whether they want to live there, and alternatives considered are recorded.

The nurse and Residence Manager complete a written supervision-need assessment covering: ability to recognize and respond to emergencies and use the telephone or emergency alert; medication management; mobility and evacuation; risk of wandering or elopement; ability to take part in meals, hygiene and household routines; and safety in the community and when alone.

The assessment states how the home will meet each identified need: frequency and timing of staff visits, who the trained substitute is, on-call coverage, technology supports, and training the person needs. If the need cannot be met with the home's actual supports, the applicant is not admitted. The team records this and tells the applicant and referring party in writing.

The team checks the applicant against each admission criterion listed in 14 NYCRR 686.8(b)(1) using the admission checklist. Reasons for acceptance or non-acceptance are written down. No one is excluded for a reason that is discriminatory (see ADM-03 and RIT-03).

If the team recommends admission, the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] submits OPWDD's Request for Approval to Fill a Residential Opportunity to the DDRO Director, with required supporting information. The person is not admitted until DDRO Director approval is in the file.

Admission is confirmed in writing to the individual and their representative. This includes the written disclosure of charges and rights (see ADM-03 and RIT-01) and the individual's supervision plan from the assessment.

Before moving in, the Residence Manager makes sure the individual's plan of services (REC-01) records how supervision will be provided, who the visiting staff and emergency contacts are, and the evacuation training the person needs (SUP-03).

Before relying on any documentation or minimum-service guidance in OPWDD ADM #2002-01 (including any stated minimum days of service), the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] confirms with the OPWDD area office that it is current. The confirmation is dated and filed. Until then, [AGENCY NAME] documents each day's service in the way required by the current OPWDD guidance it has verified.
The Residence Manager reviews the supervision-need assessment at [NUMBER] days after admission, then at least annually, and whenever the person's condition, behavior or the home changes (see IRA-02).
The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews referral and admission logs quarterly to check timeliness, vacancy reporting and consistency of decisions.

responsibilities.duty: Makes the final admission decision, submits the request for DDRO Director approval and reports vacancies.
Receives referrals, leads the intake visit, completes the supervision-need assessment with the nurse and keeps the referral file.
Assesses health, medication and emergency-response ability and advises on what supervision is needed.
Take part in intake, state their choices and preferences, and make the final decision to move in.
Approves each placement before admission.

documentation: Referral log and all referral records
Written supervision-need assessment and the plan for meeting each need
Admission checklist applying each criterion in 686.8(b)(1)
Record of alternatives considered and the individual's choice
Request for Approval to Fill a Residential Opportunity and DDRO Director approval
Vacancy report records
Written notice of admission decision
Dated confirmation of the current status of ADM #2002-01 guidance

policies.title: Supportive IRA Discharge Criteria
policies.applies_to: Supportive IRAs only; Residence Manager, nurse, Administrator, the individual's planning team
policies.purpose: To set discharge criteria for a supportive IRA that describe the independence a person is working toward, the circumstances that could lead to a more restrictive setting, and the protections that prevent discharge to an unsuitable or unavailable setting.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.8(a)(7)(i)-(iii). (i) [AGENCY NAME] describes, for each individual, the level of independent functioning that would appropriately permit the person to live independently, and identifies the activities and experiences that would promote that independence. (ii) [AGENCY NAME] describes potential problem circumstances or declining functioning that might result in discharge to a more restrictive program. (iii) [AGENCY NAME] does not discharge a person except to a setting that can more appropriately meet the person's needs and that is actually available at the time of the projected discharge. A person is never discharged because of staff convenience, as a penalty, or in a way that leaves the person without a place to live. The individual takes part in every discharge decision and keeps the right to review and appeal (see APP-01).

definitions.definition: Living in a home of the person's choice with no more than the community, natural and paid supports the person selects, without a certified residential program.
A setting with more supervision or fewer personal freedoms than the supportive IRA, such as a supervised IRA or a more structured setting.
The receiving setting has confirmed in writing that it has a vacancy, has been approved by the necessary authorities, and can accept the person on the projected discharge date.
Written statements, individualized to the person, covering the three elements in 686.8(a)(7)(i)-(iii).

procedures: Within [NUMBER] days of admission, the Residence Manager and planning team write the individual's discharge criteria with the person. They are filed with the plan of services (REC-01).

The criteria describe the skills and supports that would permit independent living, such as managing money, medication, cooking, transportation, using emergency services and keeping a household. Each is described in terms of what the person can do now.

The team lists the activities and experiences that will build that independence, such as skill training, community trips, travel training, supported employment or volunteer experiences (COM-01), and records who will provide each and when.

The team lists the problem circumstances or loss of functioning that could lead to a more restrictive setting, such as repeated unsafe situations when alone, declining health or mobility, repeated emergency use, or behavior posing a serious danger that supportive supports cannot address. These are written individually and in plain language.

The criteria state that before any move to a more restrictive program, [AGENCY NAME] will first try additional supports available in the supportive IRA: more staff visits, technology, retraining, a behavior support plan (BEH-01), nursing review or a revised plan of services.

The Residence Manager reviews the criteria with the individual at each plan review and at least annually. Changes are recorded and dated, and the individual receives a copy in a format they understand.
If a person shows signs under item 4, the Residence Manager convenes the planning team promptly and documents what happened, supports tried and results.

Before any discharge is proposed, the team confirms with the individual and representative whether they agree. If the person objects, the person is told of the right to review and appeal (APP-01) and, where applicable, the right to object under 633.12 (RIT-02). Discharge is not carried out while a required review is pending, unless there is an immediate danger to health or safety, and that is documented.

The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] identifies the proposed receiving setting and confirms in writing with the receiving provider and OPWDD that the setting can meet the person's needs, is approved, and is actually available on the projected discharge date. Written confirmation is kept in the file.

If no suitable setting is available, the person stays in the supportive IRA, and the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] and care manager continue to look for a setting. The case is reviewed at least every [NUMBER] days and documented.
The discharge itself follows DIS-02, including a discharge plan, transfer of records with consent, medications, personal funds and belongings, and follow-up.
The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews all discharges to more restrictive settings in quality improvement review (GOV-02) to see whether earlier supports could have helped.

responsibilities.duty: Approves discharge decisions, confirms the receiving setting's availability in writing and reviews discharges for quality improvement.
Writes and reviews individual discharge criteria with the person, convenes the planning team and tracks supports provided.
Advises on health-related decline and how it affects the person's ability to remain in the home.
Take part in setting criteria and discharge decisions, and may object, appeal and choose among available options.

documentation: Individualized discharge criteria (all three elements) in the plan of services
Records of annual and event-driven reviews
Records of supports tried before any move to a more restrictive program
Planning team notes and the individual's response
Written confirmation of receiving setting availability on the projected discharge date
Notice of rights to review and appeal

policies.title: Supportive IRA Visitation, Emergency Contacts and Evacuation Training
policies.applies_to: Supportive IRAs only; Residence Manager, visiting and on-call staff, substitutes, individuals living in the home
policies.purpose: To make sure that in a supportive IRA, where staff are typically not onsite at all times, someone trained is always available to visit residents, every resident knows whom to call, and every occupant can evacuate in an emergency.
policies.policy: This policy meets 14 NYCRR 686.8(a)(12)(i)-(iv). (i) A trained person is available to visit each person in the supportive IRA in the absence of the assigned case manager. (ii) Each person is told whom to call in an emergency or other unusual or unsettling circumstance. (iii) All occupants of the home are trained to evacuate in emergencies. (iv) The other information specific to supportive operations is set out in this policy, including after-hours coverage and review of visit data. This policy works with the facility evacuation plan (IRA-04) and the site protective oversight plan (IRA-01), under which the home's protective oversight is matched to each person's assessed need.

definitions.definition: A staff member or trained substitute who has completed [AGENCY NAME]'s orientation, the individual's plan-specific training, emergency response and first-aid training required for supervisors (IRA-03) and who can visit when the case manager is not available.
A large-print or picture-based card, or equivalent accessible format, listing whom to call in an emergency and in other unusual or unsettling situations, with phone numbers.
Any event that worries or confuses the person, such as a stranger at the door, a lost key, loss of power, feeling ill, a disagreement with a housemate, or a missed visit.

procedures: The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] designates in the staffing plan (PER-08) at least one trained visiting person and one trained back-up for each shift or day, for each supportive IRA.

Each individual's plan of services states the frequency, timing and purpose of visits, set from the supervision-need assessment (SUP-01). It also states who visits when the assigned case manager is absent.

Before working alone, each visiting person and substitute completes orientation on the home, each individual's plan, emergency response, medication support where applicable, rights, incident reporting and the evacuation plan. The Residence Manager signs off. This is filed in the personnel record.

A visiting person who cannot attend a scheduled visit notifies the Residence Manager or on-call supervisor at once, and the visit is covered by the back-up. No scheduled visit is skipped without the individual being contacted and the reason documented.

The Residence Manager makes sure each individual receives an emergency contact card at admission and whenever contacts change. It lists 911, the on-call supervisor [PHONE], the Residence Manager [PHONE], the care manager [PHONE], and the OPWDD number (866) 946-9733 for complaints, along with any other complaint contacts required under RIT-01.

Staff teach each person how and when to call, using practice calls, role play, or whatever method suits the person's communication. Staff write down how well the person did. Training is repeated at least [NUMBER] times a year and after any real event.
Each person is told in plain language that they may call if something unusual or unsettling happens, not only in a medical emergency. Staff respond kindly and the call is never treated as a nuisance.
