The on-call supervisor answers the line at all times when staff are not onsite. If a call is not answered, the call goes to a back-up within [NUMBER] minutes. The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] tests the system monthly and records results.

On admission and at least [NUMBER] times a year, all occupants are trained to evacuate the home, as set out in IRA-04. This includes the alarm, exits, meeting place, and calling 911. Each person's performance is observed and recorded.

Visiting staff record each visit: date, time, who was seen, how the person was, medication or health observations, safety checks, emergency contacts reviewed, and any follow-up. Concerns are reported the same day to the Residence Manager.
Any incident, injury or allegation seen or learned about on a visit is handled under REC-05 and REC-06 without delay.

The Residence Manager reviews visit and call records monthly for missed visits, repeated calls from the same person or signs a person's need for supervision has increased. Findings go to the planning team and the supervision-need assessment is updated (IRA-02).
The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews all supportive IRA visit coverage, emergency contact training and evacuation training quarterly in quality improvement (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Assigns trained visiting persons and back-ups, runs the on-call system and reviews coverage quarterly.
Trains staff and individuals, issues emergency contact cards, reviews visit records and updates plans.
Make scheduled visits, document them, respond to calls and report concerns the same day.
Take part in training, keep their contact card and call when they need help.

documentation: Staffing plan listing visiting persons and back-ups
Training sign-offs for visiting staff and substitutes
Emergency contact cards and records of delivery
Individual training records on emergency calls and evacuation
Visit logs and on-call logs
Monthly on-call system test records
Evacuation drill and training records (see IRA-04)

policies.title: Individual Rights and HCBS Settings Requirements
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] IRAs (supervised and supportive); all staff, individuals, representatives and families
policies.purpose: To make sure every individual living in a [AGENCY NAME] IRA is told of their rights, can use them, and lives in a home that meets the HCBS settings requirements for waiver-funded residential habilitation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects and protects the rights of every individual under 14 NYCRR 633.4 and the HCBS settings requirements of 42 CFR 441.301(c) and 14 NYCRR Subpart 636-1. Rights are given in writing at or before admission, and again after any change, in the person's primary language (633.4(a)(8)). Staff are advised of the individuals' rights (633.4(a)(6)). The rights include: a safe and sanitary environment; freedom from abuse, corporal punishment, unnecessary mechanical restraint and unnecessary medication; confidentiality; a written individualized plan with the right to take part, object and appeal; choice of physician and dentist; information on sexuality and family planning; religion; voting; use of personal money; a balanced diet; own clothing; privacy; storage; request for an alternative residence; grievances without reprisal; visitors and communication; a health care proxy; and gender expression. Individuals have access to food at any time. The residence is chosen by the individual and the alternatives considered are documented in the plan. Interpreters are provided at no charge (633.4(a)(15)). Rights are limited only under RIT-02.

definitions.definition: The rights and responsibilities listed in 14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(4), together with the HCBS settings protections that apply to OPWDD waiver services.
Federal and state requirements, including 42 CFR 441.301(c) and Subpart 636-1, that residential settings give the person real community access, choice, privacy and control.
The individual's written plan of services, developed with the person, which documents choice of residence, alternatives considered, supports and any rights modification.
The language the person uses and understands best, including sign language, or another form of communication.

procedures: The Residence Manager gives each individual, and their representative, a written statement of rights and the conduct rules at or before admission, and after any change. It is read aloud or explained in the person's primary language and in an accessible format. The person signs or the method of acknowledgement is noted.
Before admission, the Residence Manager gives the person written information on the supplies and services provided and the charges (633.4(a)(4)(xv)), as set out in ADM-03.

At admission, and whenever they change, the Residence Manager tells each person of the contacts for complaints (633.4(a)(12)): the OPWDD number (866) 946-9733, the agency grievance contact [PHONE], and [OTHER COMPLAINT CONTACTS]. Contacts are posted where individuals can see them.

The Residence Manager uses qualified interpreters or translators, at no charge to the person, wherever a person's primary language is not English or the person uses sign language or other communication supports (633.4(a)(15) and RIT-03).
Rights training is part of orientation for every employee and substitute, and is repeated yearly (633.4(a)(6)). Staff sign that they were advised of the individuals' rights (PER-02).

Staff support each individual to use their rights every day: choosing their physician and dentist, clothing, daily routines, religious practice, voting (including help to register and get to the polls), visitors and communication at times of their choosing, privacy in bedroom and bathroom, and keeping their belongings in secure storage.

Food is available at any time. Individuals may get food and drink without asking permission or waiting for set meal times. Staff do not lock food, remove it or limit it. Any restriction is allowed only under RIT-02 and 14 NYCRR 636-1.4.

The person-centered plan records that the residence was chosen by the individual and lists the alternatives considered. The plan is updated when it is not working and when the person's functional needs are reassessed (REC-01).

The Residence Manager provides the person with information on sexuality and family planning, and respects gender expression, including choice of clothing, name and pronouns, as part of the person's privacy and dignity.

A person may request a written copy of the plan, and may ask in writing to see their clinical record (633.4(a)(10), MHL 33.16). The Residence Manager sends the request to the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] the same day. If access is denied, the person is told of the right to review by the OPWDD Clinical Record Access Review Committee (REC-08).
Persons with a health care proxy are supported to follow its terms, and staff meet the duties set out in 633.4(a)(11) (DEC-02).
Individuals can request an alternative residence at any time. The request is recorded and referred to the planning team and care manager within [NUMBER] business days, with the outcome recorded.
No one is punished or retaliated against for using their rights, raising a concern, or filing a grievance (APP-02).

The Residence Manager audits the home monthly for rights and settings compliance (access to food, privacy, visitors, own clothing, storage, posted contacts) and records findings. The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reviews audits quarterly in quality improvement (GOV-02).
Staff who violate an individual's rights are subject to discipline under PER-07, and reports of abuse or neglect go through REC-06.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure rights and HCBS settings requirements are met in every home, handles record access requests and reviews audits.
Gives rights information, ensures interpreters, supports daily use of rights and audits the home monthly.
Know and respect individuals' rights and support each person to use them.
Take part in decisions, speak up about concerns and use grievance routes.

documentation: Signed or documented acknowledgement of rights and conduct rules, with date and language used
Written disclosure of charges, supplies and services
Posted complaint contacts and record of changes
Staff rights training and acknowledgement
Person-centered plan documenting choice of residence and alternatives considered
Interpreter use records
Requests for record access and outcomes
Monthly rights and settings audits

policies.title: Rights Restrictions, Modifications and Due Process
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] IRAs (supervised and supportive); all staff, planning teams, individuals and representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure that an individual's rights are limited only when absolutely necessary, individually, for a limited time and for clinical reasons. The limit must be supported by an assessed need and justified in the person-centered plan, and the person must keep the ability to object and appeal.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not limit any right of an individual except as allowed by 14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(3): the limitation must be documented, individual, time-limited and for clinical purposes only. For rights that are HCBS settings rights, a modification requires a specific assessed need and justification in the person-centered service plan under 14 NYCRR 636-1.4 and 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4)(vi)(F). Rights are never limited for staff convenience, as a threat, as retribution, or for discipline (633.4(a)(7)). Restrictive or intrusive interventions, and any limits connected to behavior support, also follow 14 NYCRR 633.16, BEH-01 and BEH-02. The person has the right to object under 633.12 and to a review and appeal of the plan (APP-01). Access to food at any time is the starting point, and any restriction must run from least restrictive to most restrictive through the person-centered planning process and be justified under 636-1.4.

definitions.definition: Any restriction of, or interference with, a right listed in 14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(4), including a limit on food, visitors, communication, money, privacy or movement.
A change to an HCBS settings right that is supported by a specific assessed need and justified in the person-centered service plan (636-1.4).
A purpose based on an assessed health, safety or treatment need of the individual, not the convenience or preference of staff.

definitions.term: Human rights committee / informed consent committee
definitions.definition: The committees described in 14 NYCRR 633.16 that review behavior-related plans and restrictions and informed consent.
Has a stated end date and review schedule, after which it ends unless the team renews it with a new documented justification.

procedures: No staff member may limit a right on their own. A limit may only be proposed by the person's planning team, led by the Residence Manager and the clinician or nurse concerned, and approved by the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

Before any limit is proposed, the team identifies the specific assessed need or risk, with data such as incident reports, medical findings or a functional behavior assessment. The need is described individually, not as a house rule.

The team documents less intrusive supports and positive interventions already tried, and why they did not work. A limit is not considered unless the less restrictive options have been tried or are shown to be inadequate.

The team chooses the least restrictive option that addresses the need. For food, the options run from all foods at all times (the starting point) to the most restrictive, and each step up needs a justification under 636-1.4.

The proposed limit is written into the person-centered plan with: the right affected; the specific assessed need; the justification under 636-1.4; the less restrictive options tried; how the person's condition and the limit will be monitored, with data collected and reviewed; a time limit with a review date; assurance that the limit will cause no harm; and the person's informed consent.

The plan must be explained to the person in the primary language and accessible form, and the person or representative has the right to take part, to object and to appeal. Informed consent is obtained under DEC-02. If the person does not agree, the limit is not put in place without following the required review process, and the objection is recorded.

If the limit relates to behavior support or involves a restrictive or intrusive intervention, it is reviewed by the committees and meets the requirements of 14 NYCRR 633.16 before use (BEH-01, BEH-02).

The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] approves the plan in writing before the limit starts, apart from emergency actions needed to prevent immediate danger, which follow EMR-01 and BEH-02 and are reported and documented.
Staff are trained on each limit that affects the person they support, and are told that it applies only as written. Staff apply it consistently and record each use as the plan requires.

The team reviews each limit at least every [NUMBER] days, and at each plan review, using the data collected. Limits that are no longer needed or are not working are ended or changed promptly, and the plan is updated (REC-01).
Limits that end on their date lapse automatically unless the team renews them with a new written justification and renewed consent.

The person is told in writing of the right to object under 633.12, to file a grievance (APP-02) and to a review and appeal of the plan (APP-01), and of the complaint contacts, including OPWDD (866) 946-9733. A person who objects is never retaliated against.

The Residence Manager checks monthly that no unauthorized or undocumented limits exist in the home, such as locked food, withheld visitors, controlled phone use, or blanket rules. Any found are corrected the same day, and staff involved are retrained or disciplined under PER-07.

A limit used for staff convenience, as a threat, as retribution, or for discipline is a violation of 633.4(a)(7). It is reported to the [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] immediately and handled as a possible abuse or neglect matter under REC-06.
The [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] reports the number and type of active limits quarterly to the governing body and in quality improvement review (GOV-02).

responsibilities.duty: Approves or denies proposed limits, ensures committee review where needed, and reviews the list of active limits quarterly.
Leads the planning team, collects data, writes the plan content, trains staff on each limit and checks monthly for unauthorized limits.
Provides the clinical assessment that supports the need and the review of effects on the person.
Apply limits only as written, record use, and never create or enforce limits on their own.
Take part in planning, give or withhold consent, and may object, grieve and appeal.

documentation: Person-centered plan section for each limitation: right affected, assessed need, justification, less restrictive options tried, data plan, time limit, consent and review dates
Assessments and data supporting the need
Informed consent records
Committee review records where required under 633.16
Notice of rights to object, grieve and appeal
Monthly audit records of unauthorized limits
Records of renewals or endings of limits

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Communication Access
policies.applies_to: All individuals receiving services at [AGENCY NAME] IRA sites (supervised and supportive), their families, legal representatives and advocates, and all employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors
federal: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act
policies.purpose: To make sure every individual and representative can understand, communicate about and take part in their services and rights without discrimination, and without paying for language or communication supports.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate against any individual or applicant on the basis of race, color, national origin, language, disability, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, age or any other protected characteristic, consistent with the ADA and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act. Interpreter and language-access services are provided at no charge to the individual or representative (14 NYCRR 633.4(a)(15)). Rights and conduct rules are given at or before admission, and again after any change, in the individual's primary language (633.4(a)(8)). The agency advises individuals of complaint contacts on admission and whenever those contacts change (633.4(a)(12)). The agency provides reasonable accommodations and assistive supports for individuals with communication, hearing, vision, literacy or other sensory needs, so that rights information, the plan of services, consent discussions and everyday choices are understood. Gender expression is respected as an individual right under 633.4(a)(4). No individual's rights are limited because of a communication difficulty or a language barrier.

definitions.definition: The language or mode of communication the individual (or legal representative) uses and understands best, including American Sign Language, a communication device or pictures.

Supports that let a person receive and express information, such as interpreters, translated or easy-read documents, large print, braille, captioning, assistive listening devices and augmentative/alternative communication (AAC).
A person who is competent in both languages and in the subject matter. Other residents, and family members acting against the individual's wishes, are not used as interpreters.
A person lawfully authorized to make decisions for the individual, such as a health care proxy agent, guardian or surrogate.

procedures: At referral and again at intake, the Program Director or designee asks the individual and representative their primary language, preferred mode of communication, and any hearing, vision, literacy or AAC needs. These are recorded on the intake record.

Before admission, the Program Director arranges a qualified interpreter or translated materials when the individual or representative needs them. The agency pays all costs, and no charge is passed to the individual or family.

At or before admission, staff give the individual and representative the written rights and conduct rules in the primary language or in an accessible format (plain language, pictures, braille, large print, audio or sign language). Staff explain them aloud and document who was present, the format used and the date.
After any change to rights, conduct rules or complaint contacts, the Program Director re-issues the changed information in the primary language within [10] business days and documents the re-issue.

At admission and as contacts change, staff advise the individual and representative how to make a complaint, including the agency grievance process and the outside contacts listed in APP-02, in the primary language.

The Program Director records each individual's communication profile in the plan of services (how the person expresses yes/no, pain, distress, preferences and choices, and what supports staff must use). The profile is added to the plan under REC-01.

Direct support staff use the communication profile every shift. Staff supply AAC devices, picture schedules, glasses, hearing aids and other supports, keep them charged and working, and report broken or missing equipment to the Residence Manager the same day.

The agency uses a qualified interpreter, not another resident, for consent, medical appointments, rights restrictions, grievances, incident interviews and plan meetings. Family members may help only if the individual agrees. The staff member records who interpreted.
If a document cannot be translated before a deadline, staff read and explain it orally through an interpreter, document that, and deliver the written translation as soon as it is available.

The Residence Manager makes accommodations for meetings, such as sign language interpreters, captioning, accessible rooms, extra time and a support person. The Program Director arranges any accommodation within [5] business days of a request, or sooner when it is urgent.

Staff may not refuse, delay or reduce services, discourage rights use, or treat an individual differently because of language, disability, or protected status. Any employee who observes this reports it to the Program Director immediately. Possible abuse or neglect is also reported under REC-06.

The Program Director reviews each new hire's and substitute's training on the communication needs of the individuals they support. Orientation under PER-02 includes this policy, how to reach interpreter services and how to use each person's AAC.
The agency posts a notice of nondiscrimination and the interpreter-access contact, [PHONE], in a visible, accessible place at each site and in the admission packet.
Staff report any complaint of discrimination or denied communication access to the Program Director. The complaint is handled as a grievance under APP-02 and cannot lead to reprisal.

Each year, with the annual plan review, the Program Director confirms each communication profile is current, and reports language and communication access requests, delays and complaints to the quality improvement review under GOV-02.

responsibilities.duty: Arranges interpreters and translations at no charge, approves accommodations, reviews complaints, and reports trends to quality improvement.
Makes sure communication profiles and supports are in place and working each shift, and trains staff on each person's communication methods.
Use each person's communication supports, never use other residents as interpreters, and report barriers or discrimination immediately.
Makes sure interpreters and accessible formats are used for health teaching, consent discussions and medication information.
Makes sure the agency funds language access and hears reports on discrimination and access complaints.

documentation: Intake record showing primary language and communication needs
Receipt of rights and conduct rules, with date, language/format, interpreter used and recipient's signature or documented acknowledgment
Communication profile in the plan of services
Interpreter and translation request log, with no-charge confirmation
Accommodation requests and outcomes
Complaint contact notices given at admission and after changes
Orientation and training records on communication access
Discrimination or access complaints and grievance files

policies.title: Positive Behavior Support
policies.applies_to: All individuals receiving services at [AGENCY NAME] IRA sites, and all staff who support them, including supervisors, substitutes, nursing staff and clinicians
policies.purpose: To support people through positive, person-centered approaches that address the reasons behind challenging behavior, protect rights and dignity, and meet 14 NYCRR 633.16 for behavior support in OPWDD-certified residences.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses positive behavior support as its approach to challenging behavior. Behavior support follows 14 NYCRR 633.16. Each behavior support plan is based on a functional behavior assessment, is written as a component of the individual's plan of services, and is developed by the program planning team with the individual and representative. Functional behavior assessments and behavior support plans are written, approved and supervised by staff who meet the Level 1 or Level 2 Behavioral Intervention Specialist qualifications in 633.16. Plans are reviewed by the behavior plan/human rights committee, with informed consent as required. No plan may include aversive conditioning. No individual's rights are limited for staff convenience, as a threat, as retribution or as discipline (633.4(a)(7)). Any rights limitation in a plan is documented, individual, time-limited and for clinical purposes only (633.4(a)(3)). Interventions classed as restrictive or intrusive are governed by BEH-02.

definitions.definition: A structured assessment that identifies what a behavior communicates or achieves for the person (its function), the settings and triggers around it, and the person's strengths, health, communication and preferences.
A written plan, part of the plan of services, that sets out preventive supports, skills to teach, replacement behaviors, how staff respond, and how data are collected and reviewed.
The committee that reviews behavior plans and any rights limitations or restrictive interventions for appropriateness, rights protection and consent. It follows 633.16.

definitions.term: Behavioral Intervention Specialist (BIS), Level 1 and Level 2
definitions.definition: A clinician who meets the qualifications for Level 1 or Level 2 in 633.16 and is authorized to develop or supervise behavior support plans at that level.
Use of pain, discomfort, humiliation or other noxious stimuli as a consequence to change behavior. It is prohibited.
The people who develop and review the plan of services, including the individual, representative, advocates the individual chooses, and relevant agency staff and clinicians, as composed under 633.16.

procedures: The Residence Manager or nurse refers an individual for behavior support when a behavior puts the person or others at risk, limits community participation, or recurs despite usual supports. The referral is in writing to the Program Director.
The Program Director first confirms with the Nurse that medical, pain, sleep, medication and other health causes have been ruled out or addressed, and documents the review.

A qualified Behavioral Intervention Specialist (Level 1 or Level 2, as the plan requires) completes a functional behavior assessment that includes direct observation, staff and family interviews, record review and baseline data. The agency completes it [within 30 days] of the referral unless an emergency requires faster action.

The program planning team, including the individual and representative, meets to review the assessment and set the plan's goals. The team includes the individual's preferences and strengths and explains the plan in terms and a format the person understands (see RIT-03).

The BIS writes the behavior support plan as a component of the plan of services, covering prevention strategies, environmental changes, teaching of replacement skills, reinforcement, and a consistent staff response. The plan names each behavior in observable terms and states how data are collected.

The BIS checks that the plan does not include aversive conditioning, or any practice that limits rights for staff convenience, threat, retribution or discipline. Any proposed rights limitation is written as documented, individual, time-limited and clinical, with a review date.

Before the plan is put in use, the Program Director sends it to the behavior plan/human rights committee for review. When the plan includes any restrictive or intrusive intervention, the steps in BEH-02 also apply. Required informed consent is obtained from the individual or legal representative and documented under DEC-02.

The BIS trains every staff member who works with the individual, including substitutes and overnight staff, on the plan before they implement it. Staff sign a training roster. No staff member implements a plan they have not been trained on.

Direct support staff carry out the plan consistently and record the required behavior and intervention data on each shift under REC-01. Staff report any concern about the plan, or any injury, to the Residence Manager the same shift.

The BIS reviews the data at least monthly, and meets with the Residence Manager and the Nurse to check whether the plan is working, whether staff are following it, and whether health changes or medication changes have affected behavior.

The program planning team and the committee review each plan at least annually, and sooner after an incident, a significant change in condition or medication, a rights complaint, or when data show the plan is not working. Changes are documented and staff are retrained.

The agency works to reduce and remove any rights limitation or restrictive intervention as soon as the individual's progress allows. The committee reviews each limitation on its documented time limit and ends it when no longer clinically justified.

The individual or representative may object to the plan or any rights limitation and appeal under APP-01 and the objection process referred to in 633.4(a)(9). The Program Director records the objection, informs the person of their right to an advocate and handles it without reprisal.

The Program Director confirms at least annually that behavior support practices match the current text of 633.16, including the operative subdivisions that govern approvals and consent, and records the comparison in the policy review under POL-02.
The Program Director reports behavior plan and committee activity (number of plans, restrictive interventions, rights limitations, objections) to the quality improvement review under GOV-02.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure plans are developed, reviewed and approved, that staff qualified as a Level 1 or Level 2 BIS are used, and that no aversive or prohibited practice is in any plan.
Completes functional behavior assessments, writes and supervises plans, trains staff and reviews data monthly.
Reviews plans and rights limitations, checks consent, and ends limitations that are no longer justified.
Makes sure staff are trained, plans are followed, data are recorded and concerns are raised.
Screens for medical and medication causes and monitors any behavior medication.
Implement the plan exactly as trained, record data, and report problems or unsafe practices.

documentation: Behavior referral and medical rule-out review
Functional behavior assessment
Behavior support plan within the plan of services
Behavior plan/human rights committee minutes and approvals
Informed consent documentation
Staff training rosters for each plan
Daily behavior and intervention data
Monthly BIS data review notes
Annual plan reviews and rights limitation review dates
Objections and appeals
BIS credential verification

policies.title: Restrictive Interventions, Restraint and Seclusion
policies.applies_to: All individuals receiving services at [AGENCY NAME] IRA sites and all employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors who may support an individual in crisis
policies.purpose: To protect individuals from unnecessary or improper restrictive interventions, to set the narrow conditions in which any such intervention may be used under 14 NYCRR 633.16, and to make sure improper use is reported immediately.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses restrictive or intrusive interventions only as 14 NYCRR 633.16 permits, only after the reviews and consents that regulation requires, and only as a last resort. Interventions classed as restrictive or intrusive under 633.16 include restrictive physical intervention, exclusionary time-out, mechanical restraining devices (including modified clothing used as a restraint), and behavior medication without a co-occurring psychiatric diagnosis. Individuals have the right to freedom from abuse, corporal punishment, unnecessary mechanical restraint and unnecessary medication (633.4(a)(4)). The agency prohibits seclusion, meaning confining a person alone in a locked or blocked space, and prohibits aversive conditioning. Staff use protective physical intervention only to prevent imminent serious harm and only with training. Deliberate inappropriate use of restraints is abuse or neglect, and inappropriate use of restraints is a significant incident. Both are reported to the Justice Center Vulnerable Persons' Central Register (VPCR) at 1-855-373-2122 and to OPWDD as required under Part 624. No intervention is used for staff convenience, as a threat, as retribution or for discipline (633.4(a)(7)).

definitions.definition: An intervention classed as such by 633.16, including restrictive physical intervention, exclusionary time-out, mechanical restraining devices, behavior medication without a co-occurring psychiatric diagnosis, and other methods the agency designates.
The least intrusive physical contact used briefly to protect a person or others from imminent harm, as defined in 633.16.
A device or item (including modified clothing) that restricts a person's movement or access to their body.
Removing a person from an activity to a space they may not freely leave, as classed in 633.16.
Confining a person alone in a space they cannot leave. The agency does not use it.
A reportable incident category under Part 624, which includes inappropriate use of restraints, reported to VPCR and OPWDD.

procedures: The Program Director states in writing, at orientation and annually, which interventions are restrictive under 633.16, which the agency prohibits (seclusion, aversive conditioning, and any restraint used for convenience, threat, retribution or discipline), and who may approve any exception.

Before any restrictive intervention is included in a plan, the BIS documents that positive supports were tried or are insufficient, that the intervention is the least restrictive method that will work, and its clinical purpose and time limit.

The behavior plan/human rights committee reviews and approves the intervention, and informed consent is obtained from the individual or legal representative. Both are documented, and all approvals required by 633.16 are in place before use. Without these approvals, no restrictive intervention is used except as an emergency under the following steps.

Only staff trained and currently certified in the agency's approved physical intervention curriculum, and in the individual's plan, may use protective or restrictive physical intervention. The Program Director keeps current training and certification dates.

In an emergency, staff first use verbal de-escalation, remove triggers and give space. Staff use physical intervention only when there is imminent risk of serious physical harm and less intrusive methods have failed or cannot work, use the least force needed, and release as soon as the risk ends.

Staff never use a restraint that blocks breathing or circulation, never hold a person face down, never use pain, never restrain as punishment or for staff convenience, and never use a mechanical restraint or modified clothing unless it is in an approved plan.

During any physical intervention, one staff member monitors the person's breathing, color and distress and stops immediately if there is any sign of medical danger. Staff call 911 for any sign of injury, breathing difficulty or medical emergency under EMR-01.

Immediately after any physical or mechanical intervention, staff make sure the person is safe, offer comfort, and notify the Residence Manager. The Nurse or a clinician checks for injury as soon as possible and the same shift, and staff record the check.

Behavior medication is given only on a prescriber's order and only with consent. Staff do not give or ask for any medication to control behavior for staff convenience. The Nurse reviews any behavior medication without a psychiatric diagnosis against 633.16 and informs the committee.

Any employee who sees or suspects inappropriate use of a restraint reports at once to the Residence Manager or Program Director and, for deliberate misuse that may be abuse or neglect, directly to VPCR at 1-855-373-2122. Staff do not wait for supervisor approval.

The Program Director reports a deliberate inappropriate use to VPCR and OPWDD immediately and begins protective steps (separating staff from the individual, medical care, preserving evidence). Inappropriate use that is not deliberate is reported as a significant incident to VPCR and to OPWDD as Part 624 requires. See REC-05 and REC-06.

The Program Director notifies the individual's representative and others as required by Jonathan's Law and Part 624 timeframes in REC-05, and tells the individual about their right to an advocate and to object.

Within [24 hours] of any intervention, staff complete an incident report. It describes the antecedents, steps tried, the intervention used, how long it lasted, who took part, the person's condition before and after, and injuries.

The Program Director holds a debrief within [3] business days with staff and, when appropriate, the individual, to learn what happened and what to change. The BIS reviews the behavior support plan under BEH-01, and the team decides whether it needs revision.

The committee and the quality improvement review (GOV-02) examine all restrictive interventions each quarter, including frequency, duration, staff involved, injuries, and any pattern for a person, shift or site, and set corrective action.

Before the agency finalizes this policy, and at each annual review, the Program Director compares it with the current operative text of 633.16 (including its approval, consent, time-limit and review requirements) and documents any change made under POL-02.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure no unapproved restrictive intervention is used, keeps training current, reports incidents, and leads the debrief and review.
Justifies and writes any approved intervention in the plan and revises the plan after use.
Reviews and approves restrictive interventions and time limits and monitors their use.
Checks for injury after any intervention, reviews behavior medication and oversees medical response.
Supervises on-site practice, verifies staff are trained, and ensures same-shift reporting and documentation.

responsibilities.role: All employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors
responsibilities.duty: Use only permitted methods and report any improper use immediately.

documentation: List of restrictive and prohibited interventions
Committee approvals and informed consent
Physical intervention training and certification records
Incident reports and post-intervention injury checks
VPCR report numbers and OPWDD reports
Debrief records and plan revisions
Quarterly review of restrictive interventions
Annual comparison against 633.16

policies.title: Missing Person and Elopement
policies.applies_to: All individuals receiving services at [AGENCY NAME] supervised and supportive IRA sites and all staff, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors
policies.purpose: To make sure a missing individual is found quickly and safely, to protect the individual's freedom to move in the community, and to make sure each event is reported and reviewed as required by Part 624.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] responds immediately when an individual is missing, meaning absent from the residence or from supervision without the planned arrangement and whose whereabouts are unknown. Under current Part 624 categories, a missing person is handled as a significant incident, and the agency confirms the current text of 14 NYCRR 624.3 at each annual policy review. All employees, interns, volunteers, consultants and contractors report to the CEO or designee immediately, and reportable incidents and serious notable occurrences are also reported to OPWDD immediately, as Part 624 (624.5) requires. Each individual's elopement risk and supervision level are set in the individual's protective oversight plan (IRA-02) and plan of services. Adults who come and go by choice are not treated as missing when they follow their plan; their freedom is protected under RIT-01 and any limitation must follow RIT-02.

definitions.definition: An individual who is not where the plan says they should be, who has not returned by an agreed time or been in contact, and whose location and safety are unknown.
Leaving the residence, a vehicle, an activity or the supervision a person's plan requires, in a way that exposes the person to danger or breaks their supervision plan.
The individual's assessed risk of leaving supervision, with the supervision level and strategies, recorded in the protective oversight plan.
[ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or the person the agency designates in writing to receive reportable incidents at all hours.
An agreed arrangement, mostly for supportive IRA residents, stating when and how the person will report in or return when away.

procedures: At admission and at each annual review, the Nurse, Residence Manager and the individual's team assess elopement risk, using history, communication, medical conditions, medications, traffic and water awareness, community skills and past events. The result goes in the protective oversight plan under IRA-02 and SUP-01.

The Program Director records for each person the supervision level, preventive supports (door alarms, line-of-sight, escort in community), a recent photo and physical description, preferred places, and the check-in plan. The information is kept where staff can find it quickly and is shared on a need-to-know basis.

Staff learn each person's risk level at orientation and at shift change. The Residence Manager makes sure the supervision level is staffed under PER-08 and that alarms and safeguards are tested at least [weekly], with results documented.

When staff cannot find an individual, or the person has not returned by the agreed time, the staff member in charge immediately checks the residence, grounds, vehicle and activity areas and calls the person's phone if they have one. Another staff member keeps supervising the remaining residents.

For an individual at high risk, or when there are signs of danger such as weather, traffic, water, medical vulnerability, or distress, staff call 911 immediately. In all other cases, staff call 911 if the person is not located within [15] minutes, or sooner if the individual's plan says so.

The staff member in charge notifies the Residence Manager and the CEO or designee immediately by phone, and the Program Director checks that OPWDD and, where required, the Justice Center VPCR (1-855-373-2122) have been notified immediately. Staff do not delay reporting while searching.

The Program Director or designee notifies the individual's legal representative, family or others entitled to notice, as soon as possible, in line with REC-05 and Jonathan's Law timeframes, and tells them what the agency and police are doing.
Staff give the police the description, photo, medical needs, communication method and likely locations, and stay in contact with the police and the Program Director until the person is found.

The Program Director sends additional staff to search when safe and staffing allows, and keeps the site covered so remaining individuals remain supervised. The agency does not leave the house without required supervision.

When the individual is found, staff check that the person is safe, offer comfort and do not punish. The Nurse assesses for injury, dehydration, exposure and medication needs, and staff call 911 if care is needed. Staff notify police, the Program Director, the CEO or designee and the representative that the person has been found.

Staff complete the incident report before the end of the shift and enter it in the incident management system in line with REC-05. The Program Director updates the OPWDD incident entry at least monthly until the matter is closed, as Part 624 requires.

The Program Director determines whether neglect may have contributed, such as inadequate supervision, a failure to follow the plan or a failed alarm. Possible abuse or neglect is reported to VPCR and investigated under REC-05 and REC-06.

Within [3] business days, the Program Director and the team review why the event occurred, check that supervision matched the elopement risk level, and update the protective oversight plan, plan of services and any behavior support plan (BEH-01). Any new limitation on movement is handled under RIT-02 and not used for convenience.

The Program Director reviews every missing person event, near-miss and alarm failure in the quarterly quality improvement review under GOV-02, and corrects trends by person, site, time of day or staffing level.
The Program Director holds a missing-person drill or tabletop exercise at each site at least [annually] and makes sure all staff, including new and substitute staff, know how to respond.

responsibilities.duty: Is reachable at all hours, receives immediate reports, and makes sure OPWDD and VPCR notifications are made.
Oversees search, notifications, investigation, plan revision and quarterly review.
Keeps risk information, alarms and staffing in place, and leads the on-site response.
Assesses risk factors and conducts the medical check after the person is found.
Follow the supervision level, search immediately, call 911 when required and report without delay.

policies.title: Licensure, Certification, Provider Agreements and Temporary Use Beds
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] governing body, Administrator, Program Director and all IRA sites operated by the agency
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] operates each IRA only under a valid OPWDD operating certificate and active Medicaid and waiver enrollment, within certified capacity and class, and keeps the agency in good standing with OPWDD and the Department of Health.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] operates each community residence only under a current OPWDD operating certificate for the class of certificate it holds. The classes listed in 14 NYCRR 619.2 are supervised community residence, supportive community residence and individualized residential alternative (IRA). The IRA operating certificate application (OMR 248) is triennial, with a maximum term of three years, and the agency renews on the calendar schedule OPWDD sets. OPWDD lists processing time as 90 to 120 days, so the agency starts renewal early. The agency never admits above certified capacity. It uses temporary use beds only if they are designated on the operating certificate for an IRA of four or more beds, and those beds count toward certified capacity (14 NYCRR 686.15). Before opening a new site or changing capacity, the agency follows the Mental Hygiene Law 41.34 site selection process as applied to IRAs by OPWDD regulation. Medicaid and waiver enrollment is maintained through eMedNY under community residence category of service 0269, with an IRS SS-4 letter (a W-9 is not accepted) and certification of a Provider Compliance Program. The agency notifies OPWDD of changes in ownership and completes the required criminal history check of owners and operators.

definitions.definition: The OPWDD certificate that authorizes the agency to operate a specific residence, for a stated class, address and capacity, for a stated term.
An OPWDD-certified residence, supervised or supportive, that provides room, board and individualized protective oversight for individuals with developmental disabilities.
A bed in an IRA of four or more beds that is designated on the operating certificate for temporary use. It counts toward certified capacity (686.15).
The agency's written compliance program that must be certified for Medicaid enrollment.
The eMedNY enrollment category for community residences.
Any transfer, sale or change of control of the agency or its operating entity requiring notice to OPWDD.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a licensure calendar that lists, for each site, the operating certificate class, address, certified capacity, any temporary use beds, effective date and expiration date. The Program Director reviews the calendar each month.

Before opening a site, the Administrator determines whether Mental Hygiene Law 41.34 site selection requirements apply to the site's bed count and supervision level, completes any required notices and documents the result.

The Administrator submits the IRA operating certificate application (OMR 248) with all supporting documents the application requires, including documentation of the site, physical plant, program, staffing and governance. The Administrator keeps copies and a submission log.

The Administrator starts each renewal at least [180] days before the certificate expires, because OPWDD lists processing time of 90 to 120 days. The Program Director completes a self-review of policies, records, staffing, training and the physical plant before submitting.

The agency does not admit or retain individuals at a site until the operating certificate is issued for that site, and does not exceed certified capacity or operate a class of residence it is not certified for.
The Administrator posts or makes the operating certificate available at each site as required, and gives a copy to the governing body.

If the agency wishes to designate temporary use beds, the Administrator confirms the IRA has four or more beds, requests the designation on the operating certificate, and counts the beds toward certified capacity. The agency uses a temporary use bed only after the designation takes effect, and admission follows ADM-01 and ADM-02.
Before any change in capacity, address, class, program or physical plant, the Administrator notifies OPWDD and obtains approval before the change takes effect.

The Administrator enrolls with eMedNY under category of service 0269 and the OPWDD waiver provider enrollment. The enrollment package includes an IRS SS-4 letter (not a W-9), certification of the Provider Compliance Program and any application fee due. The agency checks whether the fee applies or is waived and records the answer.

The agency maintains the provider agreement and waiver approval with OPWDD and the Department of Health, and keeps enrollment information (address, owners, contacts, bank information) current in eMedNY. The Administrator makes updates within [30] days of any change.

The Administrator reports any planned change in ownership or control to OPWDD before it takes effect, and cooperates with any criminal history check required of owners, operators and managing employees. The agency also confirms Medicaid and certification continuity for individuals served.

The Administrator confirms that required insurance, workers' compensation, unemployment insurance registration, business registration and building approvals are in place and renewed for each site, and records the dates in the licensure calendar.

The agency cooperates fully with OPWDD certification surveys and visits, provides records on request, and sends the plan of correction for any deficiency by the deadline OPWDD sets. It uses the process in GOV-02 to track and, when appropriate, dispute deficiencies.
The Administrator reports any threat to the operating certificate or enrollment (denial, citation, suspension, audit finding) to the governing body within [2] business days.

The Program Director confirms at least annually that the number of individuals admitted, the class of certificate and the temporary use bed designations match the operating certificate, and records the check in the quality review.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees licensure and enrollment, approves ownership changes and receives reports on citations.
Keeps certificates and enrollment current, files applications and renewals, and notifies OPWDD of changes.
Makes sure each site operates within certified class and capacity, and prepares for surveys and renewals.
Maintains eMedNY enrollment information and the certified Provider Compliance Program.
Keeps the certificate available at the site and does not accept admissions without Program Director approval.

documentation: Operating certificate for each site and licensure calendar
OMR 248 application and submission log
MHL 41.34 site selection review
Temporary use bed designation records and capacity log
eMedNY enrollment, category 0269 confirmation, IRS SS-4 letter and Provider Compliance Program certification
Provider agreements with OPWDD and the Department of Health

policies.title: Quality Improvement, Data Review and Mortality Review
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] governing body, Administrator, Program Director, quality improvement committee and all IRA sites
policies.purpose: To use incident, death, claims and survey data to find problems early, correct them, and protect the health, safety and rights of individuals, and to keep the Provider Compliance Program active.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] runs a quality improvement program that reviews incidents, notable occurrences and deaths at least quarterly. Serious notable occurrences include the death of any person receiving services regardless of cause, and sensitive situations as the agency defines them (14 NYCRR 624.4). Minor notable occurrences and reportable incidents are reviewed under the reporting, recording, investigation, review and monitoring rules of 14 NYCRR 624.5. Every death of an individual receives a mortality review. The agency also tracks Jonathan's Law notification and access to incident information, performs internal quarterly samples of claims and service documentation as part of its Provider Compliance Program, because OMIG disallows a claim if documentation does not match the rate code billed, and tracks any deficiency under OPWDD Division of Quality Improvement's deficiency dispute process (effective 4/1/2024). Results go to the governing body, and corrective actions are tracked to completion.

definitions.definition: The agency group, including the Administrator, Program Director, Nurse, a clinician and [ROLE] that reviews data and directs corrective action.
A death of any person receiving services regardless of cause, or a sensitive situation as defined in agency policy, including possible criminal acts by an individual (624.4).

An event such as suspected theft or financial exploitation over $15 and up to $100 (isolated, no card involved), or an injury needing treatment beyond first aid by a physician, dentist, PA or NP (624.4).
A structured review of the circumstances, care and any contributing factors of an individual's death, to find lessons and prevent other deaths.
The check that each billed unit of service is supported by documentation that fits the rate code billed.
The OPWDD Division of Quality Improvement process, effective 4/1/2024, by which a provider may dispute a survey deficiency.

procedures: The Administrator appoints a QI committee and a QI coordinator. The committee meets at least quarterly and keeps minutes.

Before each quarterly meeting, the QI coordinator compiles data from the incident management system on all reportable incidents, serious and minor notable occurrences, deaths, injuries needing medical treatment, medication errors, restraints and restrictive interventions, missing person events, grievances and rights complaints, by site, individual, staff shift and type.

The committee reviews each category for trends, repeat events, late reports, open investigations, items not updated at least monthly in the OPWDD system until closure, and whether required notifications were made.

The committee reviews every death. The Program Director confirms that the death was reported as a serious notable occurrence and, if it is also a reportable incident, that it was reported both ways. The committee holds a mortality review within [30] days of the death, or sooner if the facts are available.

The mortality review looks at the person's health history, recent change in condition, response to symptoms, medication, nursing oversight, emergency response, advance directives, supervision and any contributing factors. The review produces written findings and recommended changes, and the Program Director tracks them.

The Program Director confirms for each incident that the family or representative was given the notification and access to information required by Jonathan's Law, and that the date and method are recorded. The committee reports any late or missed notice and corrects the cause. The agency confirms the statute's current notice timeframes together with 624.5 at each annual review.

The committee reviews incident investigations for timeliness and completeness, that investigations continue to a substantiated or unsubstantiated finding even if the employee leaves, and that employees were notified of this rule.

Each quarter, the Billing/Compliance Officer pulls a random sample of residential habilitation claims for each site and compares the documentation to the rate code billed (daily notes, attendance and presence, plan of services, signatures, units). The Program Director reviews the findings.

When a claim is not supported by documentation, the Billing/Compliance Officer stops further billing of the same kind until the cause is corrected, corrects or voids the claim, and repays any overpayment through the process the Medicaid program requires. The steps are documented under GOV-03.

The Program Director tracks every OPWDD survey deficiency, including the due date for the plan of correction and the deadline for any dispute under the OPWDD Division of Quality Improvement deficiency dispute process (effective 4/1/2024). The Administrator decides within the deadline whether to dispute and records the decision and result.

For each finding in any review, the committee assigns a corrective action with a responsible person, a due date and a way to measure whether the action worked. The QI coordinator tracks all actions on an open-items log, and unresolved items stay on the agenda until closed.

The committee reviews the physical plant, emergency drills, staffing, training completion and individual outcomes (health, community participation, rights) at least quarterly, using data from HS-01, EMR-02, PER-02 and REC-01.

The Administrator reports a written QI summary to the governing body each quarter, including deaths, serious notable occurrences, claims sample results, open deficiencies and corrective actions. The governing body documents its review and any direction.
The QI coordinator protects confidentiality of individual information in all QI materials under REC-03, and uses de-identified data wherever possible.
The agency may not retaliate against any employee who reports a problem or participates in a review. Staff concerns are handled under PER-03.
Each year the committee reviews the QI plan itself and the policy, and updates it under POL-02.

responsibilities.duty: Receives quarterly QI reports, directs action on serious problems and reviews mortality findings.
Appoints the QI committee, decides on deficiency disputes and makes sure corrective actions are carried out.
Prepares incident and death data, leads mortality reviews, confirms Jonathan's Law notice and tracks deficiencies.
Compiles data, keeps minutes and the corrective action log.
Runs quarterly claims and documentation samples as part of the Provider Compliance Program and corrects errors.
Provides clinical review for deaths, injuries and change-in-condition events.

documentation: QI committee minutes and quarterly data reports
Incident, notable occurrence and death summaries
Mortality review records and recommendations
Jonathan's Law notification tracking
Quarterly claims and documentation sample results and corrective action
Deficiency tracking log, plans of correction and dispute decisions
Corrective action log
Quarterly governing body report and acknowledgment

policies.title: Medicaid Compliance, Billing and Service Documentation
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] OPWDD-certified Individualized Residential Alternative (IRA) sites, supervised and supportive, paid for residential habilitation under the OPWDD HCBS waiver (Medicaid). Applies to the Administrator, Billing Compliance Officer, Program Director, Residence Managers, nursing staff, Direct Support Professionals (DSPs) and anyone who creates, reviews or submits service records or claims.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] bills Medicaid only for residential habilitation that was actually delivered, is supported by contemporaneous documentation that matches the rate code billed, and is consistent with each person's plan of services. The policy also keeps the agency's Medicaid enrollment, its Provider Compliance Program and its audit readiness in good standing. No official checklist items are assigned to this policy; it supports the licensure, quality and records policies listed under Related.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will claim Medicaid payment for IRA residential habilitation only when (1) the agency is approved by OPWDD and DOH and enrolled in Medicaid for the service (C43, C53); (2) the service was delivered to an eligible person living in a certified site; and (3) the documentation on file supports the specific rate code billed. For supervised IRAs, the agency bills residential habilitation as a daily unit using the rate code that matches the person's status for that day: service day, therapeutic/non-medical leave day, or retainer/medical leave day (C45). The agency will not bill retainer days beyond 14 per person per rate year (C45). The agency understands that it has one provider-wide residential habilitation rate (C44) and will not bill any site- or person-specific rate that has not been issued to it. The agency understands that OMIG audits IRA residential habilitation claims and that a claim is disallowed when documentation does not match the code billed (C47). Where a requirement in this policy rests on guidance that may be dated or whose current status is not confirmed (ADM #2014-01 retainer-day cap, ADM #2002-01 documentation guidance, any supportive IRA minimum-day rule, and electronic visit verification), the Billing Compliance Officer will confirm the current rule in writing with OPWDD before relying on it, and will follow the stricter reading until confirmed (C45, C46). Services billed must also be consistent with the person's plan of services and with federal HCBS setting requirements (42 CFR 441.301(c)) and federal Medicaid payment requirements (42 USC 1396b(l)).

definitions.definition: The OPWDD HCBS waiver service delivered in a certified community residence (IRA) that supports the person's skills, health, safety and community participation as described in the person's plan of services (C43).
The unit of billing for supervised IRA residential habilitation: one unit per person per day, under the rate code that applies to that day (C45).
A day on which the person receives residential habilitation in the IRA and the documentation supports billing the service-day rate code (C45).

A day billed under the therapeutic/non-medical leave rate code when the person is away from the IRA for a reason that qualifies under current OPWDD guidance (for example, an approved home visit). The Billing Compliance Officer confirms qualifying reasons with OPWDD (C45).

A day billed under the retainer/medical leave rate code to hold the person's place during a qualifying absence such as a hospital stay. Limited to 14 days per person per rate year, subject to confirmation that the cap is still in effect (C45).
The Medicaid rate period used by OPWDD for retainer-day counting. The Billing Compliance Officer records its exact start and end dates in the retainer-day tracker.
The agency's written program for preventing, detecting and correcting Medicaid billing and documentation errors and fraud, certified as part of Medicaid enrollment (C53).
The single residential habilitation rate that applies to the provider rather than to an individual site or person (C44).

procedures: Enrollment: Before billing any claim, the Administrator confirms that [AGENCY NAME] holds OPWDD approval and DOH approval as a waiver provider and is enrolled with eMedNY. The community residence enrollment is filed under category of service 0269 (C43, C53). The Administrator keeps the approval letters and enrollment confirmation in the Governance file.

Enrollment documents: When filing or updating enrollment, the Administrator submits an IRS SS-4 letter (a W-9 is not accepted) and the certification of the Provider Compliance Program (C53). The Administrator pays the Medicaid enrollment application fee unless a waiver applies (for example, existing Medicare or other-state Medicaid enrollment, or a hardship waiver), and files the waiver or payment proof.

Designation: The governing body designates a Billing Compliance Officer [BILLING COMPLIANCE OFFICER NAME] who has authority to hold claims, request corrections and report directly to the Administrator and governing body on compliance matters.

Provider Compliance Program: The Billing Compliance Officer maintains the written Provider Compliance Program, reviews it at least annually, trains all staff who document or bill at hire and annually, and records attendance in each personnel file (see PER-02, PER-06).

Eligibility and admission check: Before the first billing day for a person, the Billing Compliance Officer confirms the OPWDD-approved placement and admission date (see ADM-01, ADM-02), active Medicaid eligibility, and that the person's plan of services is in place (see REC-01). A claim is not released for any day before these are confirmed.

Rate setup: The Billing Compliance Officer confirms the provider-wide rate issued to [AGENCY NAME] (C44) and enters only that rate and its related rate codes in the billing system. Any change to the rate is documented from the OPWDD or DOH notice.

Daily documentation: On every shift, the DSP on duty documents the person's presence or absence, the residential habilitation supports provided, and any health or behavior event, in the daily record before the end of the shift (see REC-01). Entries are dated, timed, signed or electronically attributed to the staff member, and are never pre-filled or copied forward.

Absence documentation: When a person is away from the IRA, staff record the date and time of departure and return, the reason (home visit, hospital admission, other), who was told, and who approved the absence. Hospital stays are also recorded with admission and discharge dates from the hospital paperwork (see EMR-01).

Selecting the rate code: Each month, before billing, the Residence Manager completes a day-by-day census for each person showing the code for every day: service day, therapeutic/non-medical leave day, or retainer/medical leave day (C45). The Billing Compliance Officer compares the census with the daily notes and absence records, and any day whose documentation does not support the code is corrected or not billed (C47).

Retainer-day control: The Billing Compliance Officer keeps a running retainer-day tracker per person per rate year. When a person reaches 10 retainer days, the Billing Compliance Officer notifies the Program Director and the person's team. No retainer day beyond 14 is billed (C45). Before relying on the cap in any new rate year, the Billing Compliance Officer confirms in writing with OPWDD that ADM #2014-01 is still in effect and records the response.

Supportive IRA rules: For any supportive IRA, the Billing Compliance Officer confirms with OPWDD, in writing, which billing method and any minimum-day requirement currently apply before any claim is submitted. ADM #2002-01 is treated as dated guidance and is not relied on until its current status is confirmed (C46).

Electronic visit verification: The Billing Compliance Officer asks OPWDD in writing whether electronic visit verification applies to IRA residential habilitation, records the answer, and implements any required system within the deadline OPWDD sets. Until confirmed, the agency continues daily documentation as above.

Pre-submission review: Before each claim batch is submitted, a second person who did not prepare the census reviews a sample of days per site against the source notes. The sample size and any errors found are recorded on the review form. The Billing Compliance Officer approves the batch in writing.

Submission and reconciliation: Claims are submitted through eMedNY only by authorized users. Within 30 days of each remittance, the Billing Compliance Officer reconciles payments to claims submitted, investigates denials and short payments, and records the cause and correction.

Overpayments and errors: When staff or the Billing Compliance Officer discover a claim that was billed in error or was not supported (for example, wrong rate code, undocumented day, retainer days over the cap), the Billing Compliance Officer stops related billing, quantifies the error, informs the Administrator within 2 business days, and corrects or voids the claim. Repayment is made promptly and within the timeframe required by law and by direction from OPWDD, DOH or OMIG.

Audit readiness: The Billing Compliance Officer keeps a current audit binder or electronic folder for each site containing the census, daily notes, absence records, plans of services, and rate-code support. When OMIG, OPWDD or DOH requests records, the Billing Compliance Officer logs the request, notifies the Administrator the same day, and produces complete records by the due date (C47). Requests for more time are made in writing before the deadline.

Internal monitoring: Each quarter, the Billing Compliance Officer audits at least 10% of billed person-days (and at least 5 days per person) across sites, reports error rates by site and by cause to the Administrator, and reports results to the governing body and the quality improvement process (see GOV-02). Corrective action is assigned with a due date and rechecked within 60 days.

Prohibited practices: Staff must not alter, back-date or create records after the fact to support a claim, bill for a day the person was not in the service or qualifying leave status, bill for services not in the plan of services, or pressure staff to change documentation. Anyone who observes such a practice reports it to the Billing Compliance Officer or Administrator. Staff may report concerns without fear of retaliation (see PER-03).
Records retention and access: Billing and service records are kept in accordance with REC-08 and applicable Medicaid record-retention requirements, and are protected under REC-03.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, appoints the Billing Compliance Officer, receives quarterly compliance reports, and ensures resources for compliance.

Maintains OPWDD/DOH approval and eMedNY enrollment (category of service 0269), files enrollment documents and the Provider Compliance Program certification, and acts on overpayment and audit findings.

responsibilities.role: Billing Compliance Officer [BILLING COMPLIANCE OFFICER NAME]
responsibilities.duty: Controls rate codes, retainer-day tracking, pre-submission review, reconciliation, internal audits, and written confirmations from OPWDD on unconfirmed rules (retainer cap, supportive IRA rules, EVV). Handles audit requests.
Ensures sites document consistently, that plans of services match services billed, and that corrective actions are carried out.
Reviews daily notes each week, completes the monthly day-by-day census, and ensures absences and returns are documented.
Complete accurate, timely, contemporaneous documentation each shift and never alter or back-date entries.
Document health-related absences and hospital admissions and discharges so the correct leave code can be applied.

documentation: OPWDD and DOH approval letters, eMedNY enrollment confirmation (category of service 0269), IRS SS-4 letter and Provider Compliance Program certification
Written Provider Compliance Program and annual review record
Compliance training attendance records
Placement approval, Medicaid eligibility check and billing start date for each person
Daily service notes and absence/return records
Monthly day-by-day rate-code census with Residence Manager and Billing Compliance Officer sign-off
Retainer-day tracker by person and rate year
Written OPWDD confirmations on ADM #2014-01 status, supportive IRA rules and EVV applicability
Pre-submission review forms, claim batches, remittances and reconciliation logs
Overpayment and error log with corrections and repayments
Quarterly internal audit reports and corrective action plans
Audit and records-request log with copies of records produced

documents.title: 14 NYCRR § 686.6 - Administration (policy/procedure manual content required of each community residence)
documents.form_number: None. No OPWDD policy checklist form was found; 14 NYCRR 686.6 is the section that lists the required written policies.
